Rethinking Batch Composition: 
Promoting feature diversity for Speech Enhancement
Mingchi Hou
Ina Kodrasi
††thanks: This work was supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation project 200021_215187 on “Pathological Speech Enhancement”.
Abstract
Speech enhancement systems are commonly trained using randomly sampled mini-batches, which may contain limited diversity in intrinsic acoustic characteristics of the clean speech signals. Motivated by previous findings linking clean speech characteristics to enhancement performance, we propose a feature-stratified mini-batch sampling strategy that divides training examples into quantiles according to a clean-speech characteristic and enforces equal representation within each mini-batch. Experiments across two large-scale English and Spanish speech datasets and a smaller dataset containing neurotypical and pathological speech demonstrate improvements over standard random mini-batch sampling across multiple objective enhancement metrics. Ablation studies demonstrate that the gains are robust across training runs, while their magnitude depends on the acoustic characteristic used for stratification. The proposed strategy requires no modification to the enhancement model or training objective, providing a simple and complementary approach to speech enhancement training.
Index Terms: speech enhancement, mini-batch composition, intrinsic acoustic feature
††address: 1Idiap Research Institute, Switzerland 
2École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Switzerland
1 Introduction
Speech enhancement (SE) aims to improve the quality and intelligibility of speech degraded by noise, reverberation, and other acoustic distortions.
A broad range of deep learning-based approaches has been developed for this task, including discriminative and generative approaches.
Discriminative approaches learn a mapping from degraded to clean speech through, e.g., spectral mask estimation [1] or spectral coefficient estimation [2], whereas generative approaches formulate SE as a probabilistic generation problem using diffusion [3], flow matching [4], or Schrödinger Bridge [5].
Despite their overall strong performance, these approaches can exhibit substantial performance differences across input conditions, with a range of factors, such as e.g., acoustic degradation (noise type, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)) [6] or characteristics of the target speaker [7], contributing to this variability.
This challenge has motivated efforts to improve SE robustness and generalization.
For example, robustness to different acoustic conditions has been addressed by explicitly accounting for noise type and SNR [8, 9] or by using mixture-of-experts architectures in which different model components can specialize to different acoustic conditions [10].
To achieve consistent performance across speakers, speaker-aware and personalized SE approaches have been proposed that condition enhancement on speaker embeddings or that adapt models to individual speakers [7, 11, 12, 13].
Beyond explicitly targeting robustness to acoustic conditions or different speakers, improvements to SE generalization have also been pursued through alternative loss functions [14], training targets [15, 16], and model architectures [17, 18], as well as through strategies for improving the quality and scale of training data [19].
Despite these advances, recent studies have shown that certain speech samples remain challenging for state-of-the-art SE models, even when the noise type, SNR, and speaker are fixed [20, 21, 22]. This suggests that an important source of enhancement difficulty lies in the intrinsic characteristics of the clean speech signal itself. In our previous work [22], we demonstrated that clean speech characteristics such as formant structure and loudness can be strongly correlated with SE performance, even when the noise type, SNR, and speaker are controlled.
To the best of our knowledge, this source of variability has never been considered in the design of SE training strategies. Specifically, training data are typically presented to SE models through randomly sampled mini-batches, without explicitly considering the distribution of intrinsic speech characteristics within each batch. Although random sampling provides unbiased coverage of the training set over many iterations, individual mini-batches can still differ substantially in their acoustic composition. For speech data with high intrinsic variability, a randomly sampled batch may consequently cover only a limited region of the acoustic feature space, causing individual gradient updates to be dominated by a restricted range of enhancement difficulty.
In this work, we propose to explicitly control the distribution of intrinsic clean speech characteristics within each mini-batch to improve SE training and performance. To this end, we propose a simple plug-and-play feature-stratified sampling strategy.
For each training sample, we extract a user-defined clean speech characteristic (such as e.g., the mean formant frequency or the mean loudness) and partition the training data into quantiles based on its value. Each mini-batch is then constructed with an equal number of samples from each quantile. Importantly, the selected characteristic is used solely to determine the composition of the mini-batch and is not provided as an input to the SE model.
We evaluate the proposed strategy on discriminative and generative SE approaches across two languages, i.e., English and Spanish, and across two speaker populations, i.e., neuortypical and pathological.
Across these various datasets, we observe consistent improvements in multiple objective SE metrics when the proposed feature-stratified sampling strategy is used for training.
The main contributions of this work are:
1. 
We introduce feature-stratified batch sampling for SE, a simple plug-and-play training strategy that explicitly promotes diversity in intrinsic clean speech characteristics within each mini-batch.
2. 
We demonstrate consistent performance improvements across two SE paradigms, two languages, and two speaker groups, using four objective SE metrics.
3. 
We show that the improvements are robust to stochastic variations in mini-batch sampling, and that their magnitude depends on the clean speech characteristic used for stratification. In particular, characteristics that are strongly associated with SE performance provide greater benefits, suggesting that stratification is most effective when it promotes diversity along acoustic dimensions related to enhancement difficulty.
2 Speech Enhancement
The noisy microphone signal y⁡(t)y(t) at time tt is given by the sum of the clean speech signal s⁡(t)s(t) and the noise signal n⁡(t)n(t), i.e.,
y⁡(t)=s⁡(t)+n⁡(t).y(t)=s(t)+n(t).
(1)
In the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain, (1) is given by
Y⁡(f,k)=S⁡(f,k)+N⁡(f,k),\displaystyle Y(f,k)=S(f,k)+N(f,k),
(2)
where Y⁡(f,k)Y(f,k), S⁡(f,k)S(f,k), and N⁡(f,k)N(f,k) denote the complex-valued STFT coefficients of the noisy, clean speech, and noise signals, respectively, and ff and kk denote the frequency bin and time frame indices.
The objective of SE is to recover the clean speech signal from its noisy observation. Depending on the modeling paradigm, this objective can be formulated as a direct regression problem or as a generative mapping problem between noisy and clean speech. In this work, we consider representative state-of-the-art models from both paradigms, which are briefly described below. Their implementation and training configurations are detailed in Section 4.
2.1 Speech enhancement models
Complex-valued spectrogram-based regression (CR):  CR follows a discriminative regression formulation in which a deep neural network predicts the real and imaginary components of the clean speech STFT from the corresponding noisy STFT [23]. The predicted complex-valued spectrum is transformed back to the time domain, and the model is optimized using the mean square error between the reconstructed signal s^​(t)\hat{s}(t) and the clean signal s⁡(t)s(t).
Schrödinger Bridge-based model (SB):  In contrast to direct regression, SB formulates SE as a generative transport problem learning a stochastic path between the noisy observation and the corresponding clean speech representation [24, 5]. Unlike conventional diffusion-based approaches which progressively perturb clean speech toward a predefined noise distribution [3], SB learns this path directly from the paired noisy and clean representations.
The model is trained with a weighted data-prediction objective defined in both the time and STFT domains. Further details of the SB formulation are provided in [5].
2.2 Training procedure
State-of-the-art SE models are conventionally trained using mini-batches formed by randomly sampling training examples.
We consider a training set 𝒟\mathcal{D} consisting of NN pairs of clean-noisy examples, i.e.,
𝒟={(si,yi)}i=1N,\mathcal{D}=\{(s_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N},
where sis_{i} denotes the ii-th clean signal and yiy_{i} denotes the corresponding noisy observation. Standard SE training constructs a mini-batch by randomly sampling BB examples from 𝒟\mathcal{D}.
We use this random sampling strategy as the baseline for training the CR and SB models and compare it against the proposed stratified sampling strategy described in Section 3.
3 Proposed method
Conventional random sampling treats all training examples equally, irrespective of their intrinsic speech characteristics. Our previous analysis showed that intrinsic properties of clean speech are correlated with enhancement gains [22], suggesting that the distribution of such characteristics in the training data may influence how effectively an SE model learns across different types of speech. This motivates us to investigate whether explicitly controlling the distribution of intrinsic speech characteristics during training can improve model generalization.
We therefore propose a stratified mini-batch sampling strategy that balances the representation of a (user-defined) clean speech characteristic across training batches. The approach is independent of the specific characteristic used for stratification and modifies only how training examples are sampled.
3.1 Speech characteristics
We extract intrinsic speech characteristics from the clean training utterances using the openSMILE toolkit [25]. Let f⁡(si)f(s_{i}) denote the value of a selected characteristic for the clean signal sis_{i}. The characteristic is computed once for each training utterance and is used solely to determine its sampling group, i.e., it is not provided as an input to the enhancement model. In our experiments, we consider the mean third formant frequency F3F_{3} (cf. Section 5.1) and the standard deviation of the fundamental frequency f0f_{0} (cf. Section 5.2) as speech characteristics for stratification.
3.2 Stratified mini-batch sampling
For a given batch size BB, we propose to choose the number of quantiles JJ such that BB is divisible by JJ. The empirical distribution of the selected characteristic f⁡(si)f(s_{i}) over the training set is divided into JJ quantiles, denoted by Q1Q_{1}, …\ldots, QJQ_{J}. Each training example is assigned to exactly one quantile according to its characteristic value.
Each mini-batch is constructed by randomly sampling B/JB/J utterances from each quantile. Sampling is performed without replacement within an epoch, while the examples are reshuffled between epochs. Thus, each mini-batch contains an equal representation of utterances spanning the range of the selected clean speech characteristic, rather than reflecting a potentially imbalanced distribution.
The quantile boundaries are computed once using the training set and remain fixed throughout training. The same sampling procedure can be applied independently to any SE model, allowing the effect of stratified sampling to be evaluated without modifying the underlying SE architectures, training objectives, or optimization procedures.
The proposed strategy can be implemented using a custom sampler in standard deep learning data loading frameworks.
4 Experimental settings
4.1 Datasets
Clean speech signals.  To assess the generalizability of our findings across languages, we use two clean speech datasets, i.e., the English Wall Street Journal (WSJ0) dataset [26] and the Crowdsourced Latin American Spanish (CROWD) dataset [27]. WSJ0 is a commonly used benchmark for SE [3, 5], containing 28.628.6 hours of speech from 120120 speakers. We use the standard WSJ0 split, with 101101, 1010, and 88 speakers assigned to the train, validation, and test sets, respectively.
Since the CROWD dataset is larger, we select subsets of it with a comparable duration and the same number of speakers as the different WSJ0 splits.
To assess the impact of the proposed batch sampling strategy across neurotypical and pathological speaker groups, we additionally use the PC-GITA dataset [28]. PC-GITA contains 2.82.8 hours of speech from 5050 individuals with Parkinson’s disease and 5050 neurotypical controls. Each speaker produces 1212 utterances, comprising 1010 sentences, one read text, and one monologue. Given the limited amount of available speech, we use speaker-independent 1010-fold cross-validation for the PC-GITA dataset [13, 22]. In each fold, 80%80\%, 10%10\%, and 10%10\% of the speakers are assigned to the training, validation, and test sets, respectively.
For each dataset, all recordings are downsampled to 1616 kHz and the SE models are trained and evaluated independently using only the corresponding training, validation, and test data.
Noisy mixtures.  Noisy mixtures are constructed using four environmental noise categories from CHiME3 [29], i.e., bus, cafe, pedestrian area, and street. Noise recordings are first downsampled to 1616 kHz before mixture generation. A random segment of a randomly selected noise category is added to a clean speech signal. The mixture SNR is sampled uniformly from −6-6 dB to 1414 dB. This procedure follows the noise-mixing protocol commonly adopted in previous SE studies [23, 5].
4.2 Model architectures and training
Following [23], signals are transformed to the STFT domain using a window size of 510510 samples, a hop length of 128128 samples, and a Hann window. The STFT coefficients are then compressed using α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and β=0.33\beta=0.33 as in [5].
Both the CR and SB models use the NCSN++M U-Net architecture, a lighter configuration of NCSN++ [30, 23]. The CR model removes the noise-conditioning layers, resulting in 22.122.1 million trainable parameters, whereas the SB model retains these layers, resulting in 25.225.2 million trainable parameters. In addition, SB uses exponential moving average with a decay rate of 0.9990.999 [5], a variance-exploding noise schedule with σmin=0.7\sigma_{\min}=0.7 and σmax=1.82\sigma_{\max}=1.82, and 5050-step SDE sampling.
Training is performed using the Adam optimizer, a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}, and a maximum of 10001000 epochs. Training stops if the validation loss does not decrease for 2020 consecutive epochs.
For the WSJ0 and CROWD dataset, models are trained on an NVIDIA H100 GPU. For the PC-GITA dataset, models are trained on an RTX 3090 GPU.
4.3 Evaluation
SE performance is evaluated using four established objective metrics, i.e., extended short-time objective intelligibility (ESTOI)[31], wideband perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ)[32], frequency-weighted segmental signal-to-noise ratio (fwSSNR)[33], and scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SI-SDR)[34]. The clean speech signal is used as the reference signal for all metrics. To facilitate comparisons across datasets, we report the improvement in these objective metrics, i.e., Δ\DeltaESTOI, Δ\DeltaPESQ, Δ\DeltafwSSNR, and Δ\DeltaSI-SDR, relative to the noisy mixture.

5 Experimental Results
This section evaluates the effectiveness of the proposed stratified mini-batch sampling strategy and examines the factors that influence its performance and robustness. We first compare the proposed strategy with standard random mini-batch sampling across the considered SE models and speech datasets (Section 5.1). For these main experiments, the mean value of F3F_{3} is used as the acoustic characteristic for stratification, motivated by its strong correlation with SE performance observed in our previous work [22]. We then conduct two ablation studies. First, we investigate whether the choice of acoustic characteristic affects the benefit of stratification by comparing mean F3F_{3} with the standard deviation of the fundamental frequency f0f_{0}, which showed little or no correlation with SE performance in our previous work (Section 5.2). Second, we assess whether the observed improvements are robust to stochastic variations in mini-batch composition by comparing random and stratified sampling across multiple training runs (Section 5.3).

Table 1 compares the performance of the CR and SB models trained using standard random mini-batch sampling and the proposed stratified mini-batch sampling using a batch size B=8B=8 and J=4J=4 quantiles. For mini-batch sampling, training utterances are stratified according to their F3F_{3} value.
Models are separately trained and tested on the English WSJ0, Spanish CROWD, and Spanish PC-GITA datasets. For PC-GITA, test performance is reported separately for neurotypical and pathological speakers.
For the WSJ0 dataset, stratified sampling improves the performance of both the CR and SB models, with the largest gains observed for the CR model, particularly in E-STOI and fwSSNR.
Improvements for the SB model are more modest across all metrics.
For the CROWD dataset, stratified sampling improves the performance of both the CR and SB models, but the improvements are more pronounced for the SB model, particularly for PESQ, fwSSNR, and SI-SDR.
For the PC-GITA dataset, stratified sampling improves the performance of the CR model for both neurotypical and pathological speakers, with the largest gains observed in E-STOI and fwSSNR. In contrast, the SB model achieves performance comparable to random sampling, with only minor differences between the two strategies. The consistent gains of the CR model across both speaker groups indicate that the proposed sampling strategy also benefits pathological speech.
Overall, stratified mini-batch sampling maintains or improves performance across both SE models, all three datasets, and both neurotypical and pathological speaker populations, with the magnitude of the gains depending on the dataset, model architecture, and evaluation metric. The strategy requires virtually no additional computational cost and leaves the enhancement model, training objective, data, and optimization procedure unchanged, modifying only how training examples are selected to form mini-batches. Therefore, it provides a simple and complementary means of improving SE training and performance without additional model complexity.
5.2 Effect of the acoustic characteristic used for stratification
The mean F3F_{3} was selected as the stratification feature for the results in Section 5.1 based on its strong correlation with SE performance reported in our previous work [22]. To examine whether the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy depends on this correlation, we additionally consider the standard deviation of the fundamental frequency f0f_{0} as the stratification feature, which exhibits little or no correlation with SE performance [22]. As an exemplary setting for this ablation study, we consider the CR model trained and evaluated on the English WSJ0 dataset.
Table 2 compares the performance of the CR model on WSJ0 when using mean F3F_{3} and the standard deviation of f0f_{0} for stratification. The mean F3F_{3} results are repeated from Section 5.1 to facilitate a direct comparison.
It can be observed that stratification based on mean F3F_{3} yields considerable improvements over the standard deviation of f0f_{0} for E-STOI and fwSSNR, whereas PESQ and SI-SDR remain comparable. This suggests that the effectiveness of stratification is not determined simply by introducing greater acoustic diversity within a mini-batch. Instead, the diversity appears to be more beneficial when it is introduced along a dimension that reflects differences in enhancement difficulty.
5.3 Robustness to stochastic mini-batch sampling
The results in Section 5.1 are obtained from a single training run. Since stochastic mini-batch sampling can lead to different mini-batch compositions across training runs, we additionally examine whether the observed performance differences between random and stratified sampling are robust to such variations. To this end, we train the CR model on the English WSJ0 dataset using three independent training runs, with the same random seeds applied to both sampling strategies. For stratified sampling, the mean F3F_{3} is used as the stratification feature.
Table 3 reports the resulting performance across the three runs.
The results show that stratified sampling consistently outperforms random sampling across all four metrics. The relatively small standard deviations across runs indicate that these improvements are consistent across different random seeds, suggesting that the benefit of stratified sampling is robust to stochastic variation in mini-batch composition.
6 Conclusion and Outlook
In this paper, we proposed a simple feature-stratified mini-batch sampling strategy for training SE models. The strategy divides the training data according to a clean-speech characteristic strongly correlated with SE performance, i.e., the mean F3F_{3}, and enforces equal representation of its quantiles within each mini-batch. The proposed strategy improves SE performance across multiple models, datasets, and evaluation metrics, although the magnitude of the gains varies across experimental conditions.
The proposed method requires no modification to the enhancement architecture, loss function, or training procedure, and can be readily incorporated into existing training pipelines. Future work will explore joint diversification based on multiple acoustic characteristics, curriculum learning strategies, effects of different batch sizes and number of quantiles, as well as subjective evaluation of the resulting enhanced speech.
7 Compliance with Ethical Standards
This research study was conducted retrospectively using human subject data made available in [26, 27, 28]. Ethical approval was not required as confirmed by the license attached with the data.

## 核心摘要

语音增强需从带噪观测中恢复干净语音，即使噪声类型、信噪比和说话人固定，不同干净语音样本的增强难度仍受其固有声学特征影响。随机采样的小批量可能只覆盖声学特征空间的局部区域，使梯度更新偏向特定难度范围。为此论文提出按干净语音特征分层的批量采样，仅改变训练样本组成而不改模型结构、损失与优化流程，可直接替换采样器。该方法先用openSMILE提取每句干净语音选定特征值，再按训练集经验分布将其划分为分位数，得到各样本的分组标签。组装小批量时从各分位数等量抽取且不放回，使每批均匀覆盖不同特征区间，特征只决定分组而不输入增强模型。在英语WSJ0上三次重复训练复数谱回归模型的平均结果中，分层采样以第三共振峰均值为特征时扩展短期客观可懂度改善值ΔE-STOI为0.27，高于随机采样的0.24。增益幅度随数据集、模型和指标变化，在PC-GITA上薛定谔桥生成模型与随机采样基本相当，结论限于所测四类CHiME3噪声混合、信噪比范围、语言和人群，尚未验证其他批量大小、分位数、联合特征与主观听感，方法几乎不增加额外计算成本。

DuET: Note–Frame Dual Encoding for Piano Performance-to-Score Transcription
Wei Zeng
Affiliation: School of Computing, National University of Singapore
Email: w.zeng@u.nus.edu
Ye Wang♯Integrative Sciences and Engineering Programme, NUS Graduate School
Affiliation: School of Computing, National University of Singapore
Email: dcswangy@nus.edu.sg
Abstract
Transcribing expressive piano performances into scores requires interpreting individual note timings within an underlying metrical structure. However, score attributes are associated with notes, whereas beats may occur without coincident note onsets. We introduce DuET, a Dual-Encoder Transformer that jointly learns note-level performance MIDI-to-score (PM2S) transcription and frame-level beat and downbeat tracking. Bidirectional cross-attention connects note and frame encoders, while an autoregressive decoder alternates between their representations to predict structured score attributes. We further introduce TimeRoPE and Time–Pitch Rotary Positional Encoding (TPRoPE) to establish a shared performance-time reference and explicitly encode relative temporal and pitch relationships. Evaluations on ASAP, a classical piano dataset, and our curated Gangqinpu dataset, which spans multiple genres with a focus on popular piano music, demonstrate improvements in score timing and notated duration. Compared with the strongest baseline on each dataset, DuET reduces MUSTER mean error from 6.56% to 3.64% on Gangqinpu and from 11.30% to 11.22% on ASAP. Ablations support the benefits of frame-level context, time-based positional encoding, and decoder-history masking. Code, weights, and demos are available at https://github.com/wei-zeng98/DuET.
1 Introduction
Automatic piano transcription converts piano performances into symbolic representations. These representations are useful for music analysis, education, and downstream music information retrieval (MIR) tasks such as expressive performance rendering. Based on their inputs and outputs, transcription tasks can be grouped into audio-to-MIDI [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], audio-to-score (A2S) [6, 7, 8, 9], and performance MIDI-to-score (PM2S) [10, 11, 12]. Audio-to-MIDI transcribes audio into notes with performance onset times and durations, whereas A2S and PM2S aim to produce notated scores from audio and performance MIDI, respectively. Despite substantial progress in audio-to-MIDI transcription, accurately producing a notated score remains an open problem.
The first challenge in score transcription is that mapping performance time to score time requires interpreting individual note timings within a broader rhythmic context. Under expressive timing, the same performed time interval may correspond to different score-time intervals depending on tempo and metrical context. Accurate PM2S transcription therefore requires modeling not only the temporal relationships among notes but also their alignment with the underlying metrical structure. Beat and downbeat tracking [13, 14] provides supervision for this metrical context, but its prediction granularity differs from that of note-level score transcription. Score attributes are associated with individual notes, whereas beat positions are represented on a frame-level time grid, including frames without any note onset.
A second challenge lies in representing the relative positions of notes in a musically meaningful way. Sequence-index distances do not directly reflect temporal separation: consecutive notes may occur simultaneously or be separated by a substantial time interval. Although timing encodings based on inter-onset intervals (IOIs) [11, 10] explicitly represent adjacent-note distances, non-adjacent temporal distances require accumulating the intervening IOIs. More fundamentally, notes occupy a two-dimensional time–pitch space, as illustrated by a piano roll. Serializing these notes into a one-dimensional sequence preserves their individual attributes, but the resulting sequence order does not explicitly encode relative temporal and pitch distances.
Beyond these modeling challenges, recent neural PM2S studies have primarily relied on publicly available classical piano datasets such as ASAP [15]. However, the practical need for score transcription is particularly strong for popular piano music, where corresponding sheet music is often less readily available than for classical repertoire. This motivates training and evaluation across both classical and popular piano music.
In this paper, we present a complete piano A2S pipeline comprising audio-to-performance MIDI transcription, PM2S transcription, and score formatting. We use Transkun v2 [2] and MuseScore 4 [16] for the first and final stages, respectively, and focus our methodological contributions on the intermediate PM2S stage. We formulate PM2S transcription as a one-to-one mapping between input performance notes and notes in a structured score representation. The mapping preserves note identities and pitches while predicting musical attributes, including score onsets and durations, staff and voice assignments, meter and key signatures, and grace-note labels.
Under this formulation, we introduce DuET (Dual-Encoder Transformer), which integrates frame-level beat tracking with note-level PM2S transcription. To accommodate their different prediction granularities, DuET uses a note encoder to model individual notes and their relationships, and a frame encoder to capture temporal context on a regular time grid. Bidirectional cross-attention allows the two branches to exchange information, while alternating decoder cross-attention combines note relationships with metrical context for score prediction. This architecture enables joint learning from note-level score supervision and frame-level beat/downbeat supervision. To establish a common temporal reference across note and frame representations, we introduce TimeRoPE, which encodes relative performance-time distances within and across the two branches. We further propose Time–Pitch Rotary Positional Encoding (TPRoPE) to explicitly encode both relative temporal distances and pitch intervals in note attention.
DuET achieves the lowest MUSTER mean error among the compared methods on ASAP and Gangqinpu, as well as the lowest onset, offset, duration, and staff-assignment errors on both datasets. Ablation studies examine the contributions of dual encoding, positional encoding, decoder memory access, and masking. Our main contributions are:
• 
We introduce DuET, a note–frame dual-encoder Transformer that jointly learns frame-level beat and downbeat tracking and note-level PM2S transcription through bidirectional encoder cross-attention and alternating decoder cross-attention.
• 
We introduce a shared performance-time coordinate system through TimeRoPE and propose TPRoPE to explicitly encode relative temporal and pitch relationships in note attention.
• 
We evaluate DuET on classical piano performances from ASAP and our curated Gangqinpu dataset, which spans multiple styles with a focus on popular piano music. DuET achieves the lowest MUSTER mean error among the compared methods on both datasets. We provide inference code, pretrained weights, and an interactive audio-to-score demo.
2 Related work
2.1 Piano performance MIDI-to-score transcription
Early PM2S methods used probabilistic models to estimate rhythmic structure and notation attributes [17, 18, 19]. Neural approaches subsequently introduced recurrent networks for joint note-value and voice estimation [20] and beat-based rhythm quantization [10]. More recently, Transformer encoder–decoder models have formulated PM2S transcription as sequence-to-sequence prediction of structured scores [11, 21, 12, 22].
Within this progression, metrical information has been incorporated in different ways. Liu et al. [10] explicitly predict beat and downbeat labels at note onsets and use dynamic programming to infer beats without coincident note onsets. This additional inference addresses the mismatch between note-based predictions and a metrical grid that extends beyond note onsets. Several Transformer encoder–decoder models infer metrical structure implicitly through note-associated score positions and measure information [11, 12]. Wachter et al. [21] take another approach, conditioning rhythm quantization on an externally supplied beat and downbeat grid. When this grid is unavailable, a separate beat tracker is required, and its errors can propagate through beat-based preprocessing into quantization. DuET jointly learns frame-level beat tracking and note-level score prediction, providing direct supervision at both granularities without requiring an externally supplied beat grid at inference.
Beyond metrical modeling, repertoire coverage remains limited. Prior work has largely evaluated PM2S transcription on classical piano datasets, such as ASAP [15], while Shibata et al. [19] also examined popular piano music. Although Wachter et al. [21] additionally explored jazz guitar, their piano evaluation remained focused on classical repertoire. We complement these studies by training and evaluating DuET on both classical and popular piano music.
2.2 Positional encoding in symbolic music
Relative positional information is important for modeling relationships in symbolic music. Music Transformer [23] introduced efficient relative attention to capture dependencies over long musical sequences. RoFormer [24] subsequently introduced rotary positional encoding (RoPE), which applies position-dependent rotations to queries and keys so that their attention scores depend on relative positions. Beyer and Dai [11] adopted RoPE in a Transformer encoder–decoder for PM2S transcription, combining sequence-position encoding with compound note representations.
These positional encodings primarily describe sequence-index relationships, rather than explicitly modeling both performance-time distances and pitch intervals. In computer vision, two-dimensional RoPE has been investigated to encode spatial relationships [25]. We adapt this multidimensional principle to symbolic music through TPRoPE, using time and pitch coordinates for note attention and a shared performance-time reference across note and frame representations.
3 Methodology
3.1 Task formulation
We study PM2S transcription within a three-stage A2S pipeline. We use Transkun v2 [2] to obtain performance MIDI from audio and MuseScore 4 [16] to produce the final notation in MusicXML format. Our model addresses the intermediate PM2S stage, predicting the musical attributes of a structured score representation. Additionally, we jointly learn frame-level beat and downbeat tracking as an auxiliary task to support metrical understanding. Notation and engraving decisions, including pitch spelling and beaming, are delegated to MuseScore 4.
Performance MIDI input.
For an input window, we represent the performance as a sequence of NN notes:

Notes are ordered by performance onset, retaining their original input order for simultaneous notes. From the same note sequence and available sustain-pedal messages, we derive a piano-roll representation 𝐑=(r1,…,rT)\mathbf{R}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{T}), where TT is the number of frames. We jointly learn beat and downbeat tracking on the same time grid as 𝐑\mathbf{R}. We model the aligned mapping using an encoder with an autoregressive decoder:

3.2 DuET architecture

As illustrated in Figure 1, DuET consists of a note encoder, a frame encoder, and a note-aligned autoregressive decoder. The two encoders accommodate different prediction granularities: score attributes are associated with individual notes, whereas beat tracking requires temporal coverage beyond note onsets. Bidirectional cross-attention connects the encoder branches, and alternating decoder cross-attention combines their output memories for score prediction. An auxiliary beat/downbeat head supervises the final frame representations.
Input embeddings.
DuET uses separate embedding modules for the note sequence 𝐗\mathbf{X} and piano-roll representation 𝐑\mathbf{R} defined in Section 3.1, producing representations of the same hidden dimension. For each note, a learned pitch embedding is concatenated with a linear projection of its continuous performed duration in seconds and velocity normalized to [0,1][0,1] by division by 127127. Performance onset is represented through positional encoding rather than note embedding to model relative timing independently of the absolute time origin. Unlike IOIs, which explicitly encode only adjacent-note intervals, this encoding directly represents temporal distances between any pair of notes. Pitch is included in both note embedding and positional encoding to capture absolute pitch identity and relative pitch intervals, respectively. The positional encoding is detailed in Section 3.3.
For the frame branch, each frame of 𝐑\mathbf{R} contains four pitch-wise features over the 88 piano keys (MIDI pitches 21–108): binary key-held activity, pedal-extended activity, binary note onsets, and onset velocities normalized by 127. Two additional features encode the sustain-pedal state and the availability of pedal information, yielding a 354-dimensional input per frame. Two temporal convolutional layers with GELU activations map 𝐑\mathbf{R} into frame embeddings. Both layers use a kernel size of 55, stride 11, and padding 22, preserving the 20 ms frame interval without temporal downsampling.
Dual encoder.
The encoder comprises eight coupled layers, each with separate note and frame branches. Each layer first applies self-attention independently within the two branches, followed by bidirectional cross-attention. In note cross-attention, queries come from the note branch and keys and values from the frame branch; frame cross-attention reverses these roles. Both cross-attention modules use the note and frame states produced by self-attention, without using each other’s updated outputs. A separate SwiGLU feed-forward network completes each branch, with pre-layer normalization and residual connections applied around each attention and feed-forward module. The final states are normalized at the encoder output and further normalized to form note memory 𝐌N∈ℝN×d\mathbf{M}^{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} and frame memory 𝐌F∈ℝT×d\mathbf{M}^{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} for the decoder, where NN and TT are the numbers of notes and frames, respectively, and dd is the hidden dimension. This interaction allows note representations to incorporate temporal context and frame representations to incorporate note relationships.
Frame-level objectives.
We attach prediction heads to the final frame-encoder representations, before the additional normalization used to construct decoder memory 𝐌F\mathbf{M}_{F}. These heads predict beat/downbeat classes, within-bar beat indices, and the cosine and sine components of bar phase, providing three complementary supervision signals:
ℒframe=ℒbeat+0.5​ℒindex+0.1​ℒframe​-​phase.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{frame}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{beat}}+0.5\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{index}}+0.1\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{frame\text{-}phase}}.
(5)
Here, ℒbeat\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{beat}} is a weighted three-class cross-entropy loss for non-beat, ordinary beat, and downbeat predictions, using Gaussian soft targets with a standard deviation of one frame and class weights (1,5,5)(1,5,5). ℒindex\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{index}} is a soft-target cross-entropy loss for the beat index within a bar, supervised around reliable beat annotations. ℒframe​-​phase\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{frame\text{-}phase}} is the squared error between predicted and target cosine and sine components of normalized bar phase, with targets interpolated between adjacent reliable beats. Each loss is normalized by its effective supervision weight, excluding padded frames and unreliable annotations.
Note-aligned decoder.
The decoder comprises eight layers arranged as four successive layer pairs. Each layer applies causal self-attention, cross-attention, and a SwiGLU feed-forward network, with pre-layer normalization and residual connections. Cross-attention alternates between note memory 𝐌N\mathbf{M}^{N} in odd-numbered layers and frame memory 𝐌F\mathbf{M}^{F} in even-numbered layers, allowing each layer pair to combine note relationships with temporal context. Decoder self-attention uses IndexRoPE, while cross-attention uses TPRoPE for note memory and TimeRoPE for frame memory, with query coordinates taken from the corresponding input note (see Section 3.3). Separate attribute heads map the final normalized decoder state to categorical distributions for the predicted score fields, producing them in parallel at each note step. An additional pitch head provides auxiliary supervision during training.
Note-level objectives.
The decoder is supervised by categorical score-attribute prediction, auxiliary pitch prediction, and note-phase consistency:
ℒnote=∑a∈𝒜λa​ℒa+ℒpitch+0.1​ℒnote​-​phase,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{note}}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\lambda_{a}\mathcal{L}_{a}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pitch}}+0.1\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{note\text{-}phase}},
(6)
where 𝒜\mathcal{A} contains the eleven predicted score fields in Table 1, excluding the copied pitch. Each ℒa\mathcal{L}_{a} is a cross-entropy loss, with λa=0.2\lambda_{a}=0.2 for key signature, voice, and grace-note status, and λa=1\lambda_{a}=1 otherwise. The auxiliary loss ℒpitch\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pitch}} supervises input-pitch prediction from the decoder state. The note-phase loss measures expected circular onset error within the reference bar using the predicted onset-integer and onset-fraction distributions, and is applied only to non-grace notes with valid timing annotations. Each loss is normalized over its valid supervised notes; padding, conditioning-prefix records, and unknown labels are excluded.
The overall training objective combines note-level and frame-level supervision:
ℒ=ℒnote+ℒframe.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{note}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{frame}}.

3.3 TimeRoPE and TPRoPE
DuET assigns positional coordinates according to the information represented by each attention module. Figure 2 illustrates how the same notes receive different coordinates under IndexRoPE, TimeRoPE, and TPRoPE.

IndexRoPE uses sequence indices, TimeRoPE uses scaled performance timestamps, and TPRoPE uses both performance timestamps and pitch coordinates. The dashed vertical lines indicate the 20 ms frame grid; note onsets need not coincide with this grid.
TimeRoPE.
TimeRoPE replaces frame and note indices with a shared performance-time coordinate u=(t−tstart)/Δu=(t-t_{\mathrm{start}})/\Delta, where tstartt_{\mathrm{start}} is the input-window start and Δ=0.02\Delta=0.02 seconds. Dividing by Δ\Delta expresses elapsed time in units of the 20 ms frame interval. For frames, tt lies on this regular grid; for notes, it is the continuous performance onset, without rounding or quantization. For example, the onset of x2x_{2} in Figure 2 is 0.0260.026 seconds, giving a non-integer coordinate of 1.31.3. Applying rotary encoding to projected queries and keys makes the positional contribution to attention depend on uj−ui=(tj−ti)/Δu_{j}-u_{i}=(t_{j}-t_{i})/\Delta. This shared coordinate system represents elapsed time within and across the two branches. Values remain unchanged, as in standard RoPE [24]. Since each frame represents activity across multiple pitches and has no unique pitch coordinate, TimeRoPE is used in frame self-attention, both directions of encoder cross-attention, and decoder cross-attention to frame memory.
TPRoPE.
Unlike frames, each note has a unique pitch coordinate in addition to its performance onset. TPRoPE therefore encodes both temporal and pitch relationships within every attention head. For a head dimension dhd_{h}, the first dh/2d_{h}/2 components of each projected query and key form the time subspace, and the remaining dh/2d_{h}/2 components form the pitch subspace. The coordinates are continuous window-relative time ti−tstartt_{i}-t_{\mathrm{start}} in seconds and centered pitch pi−60p_{i}-60 in semitones. Unlike TimeRoPE, time is not divided by Δ\Delta, because the temporal rotary periods are specified directly in seconds. The two subspaces are rotated independently:

(8)
where [⋅;⋅][\cdot;\cdot] denotes concatenation and 𝐪it,𝐪ip∈ℝdh/2\mathbf{q}_{i}^{t},\mathbf{q}_{i}^{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}/2} are the time and pitch components of the projected query. Each subspace contains dh/4d_{h}/4 rotary pairs, with rotation angle 2​π​x/P2\pi x/P for coordinate xx and period PP. The periods are geometrically spaced from 0.10.1 to 6464 seconds for time and from 1212 to 256256 semitones for pitch. Keys undergo the same transformation, making the positional contribution to attention depend on relative performance-time distances tj−tit_{j}-t_{i} and pitch intervals pj−pip_{j}-p_{i}. Values remain unchanged. TPRoPE is used in note self-attention and decoder cross-attention to note memory, where each decoder query uses the onset and pitch of its corresponding input note.
IndexRoPE.
Decoder self-attention uses standard sequence-index RoPE, termed IndexRoPE, to represent score-record order. Unlike the performance coordinates used in encoder and cross-attention modules, these indices identify autoregressive decoding positions. A causal mask prevents attention to future decoder positions.
3.4 Windowing and continuation
During training and inference, we process performances using windows containing preceding context and new notes to transcribe. The new region spans [s,s+W)[s,s+W) in performance time, where ss is its start time and WW its duration in seconds, and includes notes whose onsets fall within this interval. We use W=32W=32 seconds. The preceding context includes performance inputs and a conditioning prefix of score records from up to four preceding bars. The encoders process both context and new inputs, while the decoder conditions on the score prefix to predict new records. Training uses reference score records as the prefix, with note-level losses applied only to new records.
At inference, windows advance through non-overlapping new regions. Each window takes its prefix from the most recent four bars of the accumulated predictions, together with the corresponding performance context. The first window has no score prefix. Prefix records remain unchanged, and only new predictions are appended, ensuring that each input note is transcribed once.
3.5 Score reconstruction
After processing all windows, we reconstruct a full score from the accumulated note records. Relative bar indices are converted to full-piece indices using each window’s anchor. Each note predicts a bar length, time signature, and key signature. For each bar, we discard candidate tuples whose bar length does not accommodate all predicted within-bar note onsets, and select the most frequent remaining tuple. Empty bars inherit the preceding time and key signatures, with their lengths determined by the inherited meter.
Starting from score time zero, bar lengths are accumulated to obtain the bar starts AbA_{b}. Each note is then placed at τi=Abi+qi+fi\tau_{i}=A_{b_{i}}+q_{i}+f_{i}, retaining its input pitch and predicted duration, staff, voice, and grace-note status. The resulting structured score is converted into notation using MuseScore 4, which handles pitch spelling, accidental display, stem directions, beaming, and tie reconstruction.
4 Experimental setup
Datasets.
We use (n)ASAP [26], the note-aligned extension of ASAP [15], and our curated Gangqinpu dataset11
 1
 We plan to publicly release Gangqinpu and document its construction in a forthcoming dataset paper. for training and evaluation, with additional training data from PERiScoPe [27].
(n)ASAP provides expressive piano performances paired with symbolic scores, note alignments, and beat annotations, focusing on Western classical repertoire.
Gangqinpu contains 18,787 performance–score pairs, spanning popular, classical, and other musical styles, with performance MIDI transcribed from audio using Transkun v2.
We additionally use PERiScoPe data imported through PianoCoRe [28]; its web-collected performances were also transcribed using Transkun v2, reducing differences attributable to the choice of transcription system.
We prepare note correspondences and metrical supervision to support joint score prediction and beat tracking.
For Gangqinpu and (n)ASAP, training, validation, and test splits are defined at the piece level, using cross-dataset work groups to prevent overlap.
Masking.
During training, we apply bar-level masking to the performance-note input with probability 0.1, replacing the content embeddings of all notes within each selected bar with a learned mask embedding.
The corresponding current-note pitch embeddings supplied to the decoder are also masked, while the original onset and pitch coordinates used by RoPE are retained.
Independently, we mask each shifted decoder-history note embedding with probability 0.75 using a separate learned mask embedding, excluding BOS and padding positions [11].
Prediction targets remain unchanged, and both masking mechanisms are disabled during evaluation and inference.
Training configuration.
We use a hidden dimension of 512512, eight attention heads, and a SwiGLU [29] intermediate dimension of 14081408. DuET is trained from random initialization for 5050 epochs using AdamW [30] with a peak learning rate of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} and weight decay of 0.010.01. Each epoch samples 20,00020{,}000 windows. Training uses two GPUs with 1616 windows per GPU, giving a global batch size of 3232 without gradient accumulation. The learning rate follows a cosine decay schedule with linear warmup over the first 5%5\% of training steps. Gradients are clipped to a norm of 11.
5 Results
5.1 PM2S transcription performance
We report PM2S transcription results on 59 performances from the ASAP test split and common-valid subsets of 79 performances from the Gangqinpu test split. We compare DuET with MuseScore, the J-pop and classical configurations of Shibata et al. [19], neural beat tracking [10], and the Transformer model of Beyer and Dai [11], using MUSTER [31, 20] and ScoreSimilarity [32, 33]. ASAP baseline results are taken from Beyer and Dai [11]. For quantitative evaluation, DuET predictions are serialized directly to MusicXML without MuseScore post-processing; MuseScore 4 is used for visualization.
As shown in Table 2, DuET achieves the lowest MUSTER mean error on the Gangqinpu test split, reducing it from 6.56%6.56\% for the strongest baseline to 3.64%3.64\%. It also achieves the lowest errors across all four reported ScoreSimilarity metrics. On ASAP, DuET obtains a MUSTER mean error of 11.22%11.22\%, compared with the published Transformer result of 11.30%11.30\%, with lower onset, offset, duration, and staff-assignment errors. Its missing-note and extra-note errors remain higher than those of several baselines. Across both datasets, the most consistent gains lie in score timing and notated duration.

5.2 Ablations
We examine encoder branches, positional encoding, decoder memory access, and masking in Table 3 and Table 4. PM2S results use fixed common-valid subsets of 39 ASAP and 72 Gangqinpu performances, retained from the original ablation suite. Beat tracking uses all 59 ASAP and 100 Gangqinpu test performances.
Encoder branches and joint supervision.
Removing the frame branch increases MUSTER mean error from 8.68%8.68\% to 10.50%10.50\% on ASAP and from 3.07%3.07\% to 3.64%3.64\% on Gangqinpu. Onset and offset errors also increase on both datasets, supporting the value of frame-level temporal context. Duration results are mixed: DuET achieves lower ScoreSimilarity duration error on ASAP, whereas Note encoder only performs better on Gangqinpu. Among the dedicated trackers, adding the note branch improves beat F1 on both datasets but reduces downbeat F1. Full DuET achieves higher beat and downbeat F1 than both dedicated trackers on ASAP, whereas both trackers perform better on Gangqinpu. Tracker checkpoints are selected using beat metrics and score models using score metrics, so these differences cannot be attributed solely to joint supervision.
Positional encoding.
Index / Alternating yields higher MUSTER mean error than DuET on both datasets, despite additionally receiving inter-onset intervals as input features. This suggests that performance-based positional encoding can improve transcription accuracy in the proposed architecture. With alternating memory access, Time–Pitch RoPE reduces MUSTER mean error relative to time-only RoPE from 13.68%13.68\% to 8.68%8.68\% on ASAP and from 3.57%3.57\% to 3.07%3.07\% on Gangqinpu. However, its effects under single-memory decoding are mixed: Time–Pitch RoPE improves mean error with note memory on ASAP, but increases it with note memory on Gangqinpu and with frame memory on both datasets. Thus, the benefit of pitch-aware encoding depends on decoder memory access and the dataset.
Decoder memory access.
With Time–Pitch RoPE, alternating access to both memories achieves lower MUSTER mean error than either Note memory or Frame memory on both datasets. This supports allowing the decoder to access both note relationships and frame-level temporal context. With time-only RoPE, however, both single-memory variants achieve lower mean error than alternating access on both datasets. Several single-memory variants also obtain lower duration errors than DuET. These results indicate that the effectiveness of memory access depends on the positional encoding.
Masking.
DuET uses encoder-input bar masking and decoder-history note masking at rates of 10%10\% and 75%75\%, respectively (see Section 4). Removing either masking mechanism increases MUSTER mean error on both datasets. Removing decoder-history masking also substantially increases onset error, consistent with its role in reducing reliance on preceding score attributes. The combined setting nevertheless does not minimize every metric: removing input masking improves Gangqinpu note-deletion and note-insertion errors, and some masking variants achieve higher beat F1.
5.3 Qualitative analysis
For qualitative analysis, we randomly selected an excerpt from a piano performance on YouTube22
 2
 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UkLJl8lEChY and transcribed it into performance MIDI using Transkun v2. Figure 3 compares the scores reconstructed from this MIDI by DuET and two neural baselines. DuET produces a more regular rhythmic organization, with consistent 4/44/4 meter and relatively simple note values. Beyer and Dai [11] predict changes between 3/43/4 and 4/84/8 and introduce triplet groupings, while the model of Liu et al. [10] produces frequent tuplets, fragmented rests, and overlapping voices. These examples illustrate how different interpretations of expressive performance timing can lead to substantially different score structures. DuET yields a more coherent and readable transcription in this excerpt, although visual simplicity alone does not establish transcription accuracy.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of score excerpts reconstructed from the same performance MIDI: (a) DuET, (b) Beyer and Dai, and (c) Liu’s PM2S. All outputs are rendered with MuseScore 4.
6 Conclusion
We presented DuET, a dual-encoder Transformer for piano PM2S transcription that combines note-level score prediction with frame-level metrical supervision. Bidirectional encoder cross-attention and alternating decoder cross-attention integrate note relationships with temporal context, while TimeRoPE and TPRoPE represent relative performance time and pitch intervals. Experiments on ASAP and Gangqinpu show consistent improvements in timing-related metrics, with a substantial reduction in overall transcription error on Gangqinpu. Ablations demonstrate the value of the frame branch and decoder-history masking, although the benefits of pitch-aware encoding and memory integration vary across datasets and metrics. Future work will improve downbeat transcription accuracy, and extend evaluation to broader musical styles.

## 核心摘要

表现性钢琴演奏转谱需要把演奏时间映射到乐谱时间，输入是带音高、秒级开始时间和时值的演奏音符序列，输出是与输入音符一一对应的乐谱记录，包含小节内起始位置、记谱时值、谱表、声部、拍号、调号和装饰音标记，难点是表情性速度变化下相同演奏间隔对应不同乐谱间隔，而节拍可能出现在没有音符开始的时刻。同一音符序列连同延音踏板导出20ms网格的钢琴卷帘，音符序列作为音符编码器输入建模音符间关系，卷帘作为帧编码器输入建模含空拍时刻的时间上下文。双向交叉注意力让两个分支的中间表示互为键值交换信息，输出的音符记忆保留音符级关系、帧记忆保留逐帧节律覆盖。自回归解码器逐音符交替读取两种记忆并并行预测该音符的乐谱属性，帧记忆另经辅助头直接接受帧级节拍与下拍监督。共享演奏时间旋转位置编码把音符连续开始时间和帧网格时间放在同一坐标系，时间-音高旋转位置编码在音符注意力中同时编码相对时间距离和音程。与已有做法相比，该工作不需要外部输入节拍网格，也不用在音符位置做动态规划推断空拍。在Gangqinpu测试集上，DuET相对最强基线把MUSTER平均误差从6.56%降到3.64%，在ASAP上从11.30%降到11.22%，timing相关误差下降最为一致。结论适用于古典ASAP与偏流行风格的Gangqinpu钢琴曲目，ASAP上的缺音符和多余音符误差仍高于部分基线，原文未披露训练、推理或部署成本。

Full-Duplex Interaction with Speech, Expressions and Gestures
Siyin Wang

Abstract
Human face-to-face conversation requires coordinating speech, gestures and expressions across both speaking and listening. We present ELLSA 2, an end-to-end full-duplex dialogue model that jointly optimizes speech interaction and streaming gesture-expression generation. An autoregressive, chunk-wise synthesizer combines pretrained acoustic features with distinct listening and speaking hidden states from the dialogue backbone and speech synthesizer, enabling continuous non-verbal generation even when the model is verbally silent. To translate dialogue understanding into vivid semantic gestures, we introduce contextual semantic calls and template guidance, separating whether to invoke an available semantic gesture from how to realize it. We also establish a curated data and evaluation pipeline for dialog-aware co-speech gesture generation and investigate reference-based multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as automatic judges. Experiments show that ELLSA 2 remains highly competitive with open-source full-duplex speech interaction models and outperforms cascaded baselines across dialog-aware gesture and expression metrics. Semantic template guidance further significantly improves semantic gesture quality. Strong system-level correlations with human judgments support these reference-based scores as useful preliminary metrics for full-duplex and semantic gesture assessment. Together, these results advance dialogue modeling from spoken responses toward coordinated multimodal interaction.
1 Introduction
Human dialogue is more than an exchange of spoken responses. A speaker may spread their hands to convey spatial extent or raise their eyebrows in surprise; a listener may nod or smile without taking a turn. Such behaviors convey meaning and organize interaction even when no words are spoken. Natural human-machine conversation therefore calls for a comprehensive dialogue model that coordinates speech, gestures and facial expressions across speaking and listening. This requires treating non-verbal behavior as part of the dialogue process itself, rather than as simple animation added after a spoken response.
Recent full-duplex speech models support concurrent listening and speaking, moving beyond fixed-turn interaction (Défossez et al., 2024; Roy et al., 2026). Meanwhile, gesture and facial-animation models generate non-verbal behavior from supplied speech, and recent systems extend these capabilities to conversational settings
(Chu et al., 2026; Nagano et al., 2026; Lim et al., 2026). The remaining question is not simply how to produce more output modalities, but how dialogue understanding can coordinate them. Listening reactions require the interlocutor’s context; semantic gestures require deciding whether a particular action fits the intended response. These requirements motivate jointly learning spoken interaction and visible behavior with a unified dialogue model.
We introduce ELLSA 211
 1
 ELLSA denotes an Expressive LLM that Listens, Speaks, and Acts. Data preparation and evaluation pipeline, as well as the training and inference codes of standalone gesture-expression generator are released in https://github.com/bytedance/SALMONN/tree/ELLSA2., an end-to-end full-duplex dialogue model that jointly optimizes speech interaction and streaming gesture-expression generation. Its synthesizer uses autoregressive, interleaved chunk-wise language modeling to generate upper-body, hand and expression codes from both listening and speaking representations. Alongside pretrained acoustic features, it incorporates hidden states from the LLM backbone for the listening stream and from the speech synthesizer for the speaking stream. Gesture and expression generation remains active during verbal silence, supporting non-verbal listener responses within the same dialogue process. A carefully designed curriculum training strategy is adopted to progressively integrate multiple modalities into a unified model.
We further leverage dialogue understanding to generate gestures with explicit semantic meaning. Such gestures are sparse in conversational recordings, where non-semantic gestures can dominate learning. We therefore decouple whether to invoke a semantic gesture from how to realize it. A contextual semantic-call head uses intermediate hidden states to determine whether a semantic action is appropriate. An accepted call retrieves a curated exemplar to guide ongoing body and hand generation. Otherwise, generation proceeds freely. This enables a single synthesizer to support both free and template-guided modes while keeping facial expressions and mouth articulation conditioned on the current dialogue. Experiments show that ELLSA 2 remains highly competitive on speech interaction and outperforms cascaded baselines on gesture and expression metrics, especially in generating semantic gestures, highlighting the effectiveness of joint dialogue modeling.
Assessing this communicative function requires evaluation beyond geometric quality and rhythmic alignment, while repeated human assessment is costly (Kucherenko et al., 2024). We therefore establish a curated data and evaluation pipeline comprising conversational training data with expression supervision, a semantic exemplar library and a human-verified test set covering full-duplex behaviors and semantic gestures. Our evaluation measures speaking-listening activity, prosodic alignment, full-duplex behavior, and gesture semantics. We also investigate MLLM-as-a-judge as preliminary automatic metrics, examining their system-level agreement with human judgments.
Our contributions are threefold:
• 
We propose ELLSA 2, the first end-to-end full-duplex dialogue model that jointly optimizes speech, gesture and expression generation, enabling continuous dialogue-conditioned non-verbal behavior along with speech interaction.
• 
We introduce contextual semantic calls and template guidance, supported by a curated exemplar library, to separate semantic gesture decision from realization. This method significantly improves semantic gesture quality.
• 
We establish a data curation and evaluation pipeline for dialog-aware co-speech gesture generation, including a human-verified benchmark and reference-based MLLM metrics whose correlations with human judgments support preliminary system-level assessment.
2 Related Work
2.1 End-to-end full-duplex speech interaction
End-to-end speech models (Zeng et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2025) bypass the mandatory text interface of cascaded recognition–dialogue–synthesis systems (Serban et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025), which may lose paralinguistic cues important for natural interaction. Full-duplex models further enable concurrent listening and speaking through different modeling paradigms, including dual-model monitor–generator architectures in VITA (Fu et al., 2025) and Freeze-Omni (Wang et al., 2025), continuous speech generation in Moshi (Défossez et al., 2024) and PersonaPlex (Roy et al., 2026), or explicit dialogue-state prediction in SALMONN-omni (Yu et al., 2025). Recent work has also begun to incorporate action-related modalities: ELLSA adds visual perception and robotic manipulation to full-duplex interaction (Wang et al., 2026), while ViBES (Zhang et al., 2026) separately supports speech interaction and co-speech gesture generation through multitask modeling. MIBURI (Mughal et al., 2026) and DyaPlex (Nagano et al., 2026) condition gestures on frozen representations from speech interaction models. In contrast, ELLSA 2 jointly optimizes speech, gestures and expressions within a unified end-to-end framework. Gestures and expressions enrich conversational vividness and expressiveness, while the speech interaction backbone directly supports contextually appropriate non-verbal generation.
2.2 Co-speech gesture and expression generation
Co-speech gesture generation synthesizes body movements and, in some cases, facial expressions conditioned on speech. Most approaches use skeleton- or joint-level representations, such as SMPL-H (Romero et al., 2017) and SMPL-X (Pavlakos et al., 2019). Modeling paradigms span GPT-style autoregressive decoding (Liu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024), diffusion-based denoising (Chen et al., 2024b; Chen et al., 2024a), and more efficient flow-matching approaches (Xu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025c). Dyadic gesture generation explicitly models two-person interactions by conditioning on both the speaker’s and interlocutor’s speech (Zhao et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2026). Similar conditioning has been explored for facial expressions (Peng et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2026; Lim et al., 2026), making these settings better suited to real-world conversations. Following this direction, ELLSA 2 unifies speech, gesture, and facial expression generation within an end-to-end full-duplex dialogue framework. We further leverage the speech interaction backbone to support gestures with explicit semantic meaning, which enrich conversational vividness and immersion but remain challenging for conventional co-speech models (Zhang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025b). Finally, we investigate evaluation protocols for dyadic conversational gesture generation through evaluation subsets and objective metrics, particularly MLLM-as-a-judge.
3 Methodology
3.1 Streaming Dialogue Gesture and Expression Generation
To make non-verbal behavior generation more suitable for real-time human–machine interaction, we develop a dialogue-aware streaming gesture and expression module. Here, dialogue-aware means that generation is conditioned not only on the model’s speech, but also on the incoming speech from the interlocutor, while streaming ensures that non-verbal behaviors can be generated online to satisfy the latency requirements of real-time interaction. We realize both properties through autoregressive, interleaved chunk-wise language modeling, as illustrated in Figure 1. The model operates at fixed 0.8 s intervals, receiving both speaking and listening speech representations and generating the corresponding gestures and facial expressions. Within each chunk, the modalities are organized into an interleaved sequence in the order of speaking audio, listening audio, and gesture/expression tokens. This formulation leverages the sequence-modeling capability of the LM to maintain long-range conversational context and jointly fuse information across modalities, facilitating coordinated gesture and expression generation. Meanwhile, the causal attention structure naturally supports streaming generation when the model is executed in a chunk-wise autoregressive manner.
For gesture and expression representations, raw body motion is represented using SMPL-H (Romero et al., 2017), while facial expressions are parameterized using FLAME (Li et al., 2017). We factorize the generation target into upper-body, hand and facial-expression components, and encode each component using region-specific RVQ-VAE (Lee et al., 2022). Lower-body motion is excluded because of unreliable supervision under limited visibility, following observations in prior work (Peng et al., 2026). The RVQ-VAE encoder downsamples the original 30 Hz motion sequences into gesture latents at 7.5 Hz, whereas the speech encoder and connector produce speech representations at 12.5 Hz. Consequently, for each 0.8 s chunk, the generator receives 10 speaking-speech embeddings and 10 listening-speech embeddings and predicts 6 motion latent steps. Each latent step contains 18 codebook indices: six for the upper body, six for the hands, four for non-mouth facial expressions, and two for mouth-related expression. Separate prediction heads generate these indices in parallel at each temporal step. The model maintains a 20 s streaming context window. When the context cache is refreshed, the final three chunks are retained as history to preserve temporal continuity. Since accurate mouth articulation is particularly important for natural face-to-face interaction, we further apply an SVD-based reversible decomposition to isolate an eight-dimensional subspace that contributes most strongly to mouth motion, enabling mouth-related articulation to be modeled separately from other facial dynamics. Details are provided in Appendices A.1–A.2.
Figure 1: ELLSA 2 jointly models full-duplex speech, gesture, and facial expression generation. The gesture-expression synthesizer conditions on hidden states from both user and model speech and autoregressively generates discrete gesture and expression codes every 800 ms. It supports two generation modes: free generation and guided generation, which additionally incorporates optional semantic gesture guidance for more semantically grounded gesture generation.
3.2 Speech Interaction with Gesture and Expression Generation
Full-duplex interaction enables the model to listen and speak concurrently throughout the dialogue. ELLSA 2 follows the full-duplex temporal framework of SALMONN-omni (Yu et al., 2025). Instead of generating responses only at discrete conversational turns, the model operates continuously over fixed temporal blocks. Multimodal representations are interleaved within each block to support synchronized processing across modalities. At each time step, the dialogue backbone consumes the latest input-speech representation and generates the corresponding textual output. The resulting hidden states are subsequently used to drive both the streaming speech synthesizer and the gesture–expression generator, thereby enabling true end-to-end modeling. Consequently, text, speech, gesture and expression are jointly produced within a unified, online dialogue process.
We integrate non-verbal behavior generation into the speech interaction backbone through hidden-state conditioning. Specifically, intermediate representations from the speech interaction backbone are directly provided as conditioning inputs to the gesture–expression generator. For the speaking stream, we use hidden states associated with the output speech tokens produced by the streaming speech synthesizer. These representations encode both the semantic content and acoustic realization of the model’s outgoing speech. For the listening stream, we use hidden states generated by the LLM backbone while processing incoming speech embeddings, which capture both the current acoustic context and the inferred dialogue state of the interlocutor. Both conditioning hidden states are extracted from the final layer of their respective modules.
Gesture and expression generation remains continuously active, while regular text tokens trigger speech synthesis whose hidden states provide the speaking-stream condition. When the backbone emits <silence>, the synthesizer is inactive and this condition is replaced with a learnable null representation. The listening stream remains active throughout, enabling non-verbal listener responses during verbal silence rather than restricting generation to spoken-response turns. This persistent processing of listening stream further highlights the importance of full-duplex modeling in building comprehensive dialogue models. The model must generate gestures and expressions continuously, including during the listening state, where it produces nonverbal listener responses while remaining verbally silent. In contrast, turn-based models typically do not process input speech unless they are activated to generate a spoken response.
3.3 Contextual Semantic Calls and Template Guidance
We further investigate how the dialogue backbone can benefit gesture generation by enabling gestures with explicit semantic meaning through exemplar guidance. Semantic gestures can substantially enhance the interaction experience by providing vivid visual cues that complement spoken content. However, learning such gestures directly from large-scale conversational data is challenging because semantically explicit gestures are relatively sparse and often require high-level contextual understanding. Under standard training, the much larger proportion of non-semantic motion can dominate the learning objective, encouraging the model to prioritize rhythmic alignment with speech rather than semantic grounding. To address this imbalance, we decouple whether to invoke a semantic gesture from how to realize it. Specifically, the dialogue backbone first determines whether the current conversational context calls for a semantic gesture. Once triggered, a high-quality exemplar conveying the corresponding meaning is retrieved and used to guide the gesture generator toward a semantically consistent realization.
We implement this mechanism by attaching a semantic call head to an intermediate hidden representation of the dialogue backbone. At each candidate token step, the head performs a binary prediction indicating whether a semantic gesture is appropriate in the current context. When the semantic call is activated, the corresponding high-quality semantic gesture exemplar is introduced as an additional guidance signal for gesture generation. Concretely, the exemplar tokens are inserted into the interleaved speech–motion sequence at the beginning of the corresponding chunks, allowing the gesture generator to condition on both conversational context and exemplar motion.
An important requirement is that the semantic call decision must be available before the corresponding gesture is generated. Otherwise, exemplar retrieval and guidance would introduce additional latency. This requirement is naturally supported by the thinker–talker architecture adopted in ELLSA 2. Because text generation and speech synthesis proceed asynchronously, with text generation running ahead of speech realization, the model can perform semantic-call prediction on look-ahead textual representations before the corresponding speech and gesture outputs are produced. The selected exemplar can therefore be prepared in advance and subsequently used to guide gesture generation in synchronization with speech. This design makes semantic gesture guidance compatible with real-time streaming interaction and highlights an additional advantage of integrating gesture generation with a full-duplex dialogue backbone that provides look-ahead linguistic context.
3.4 Multimodal Curriculum Training
We adopt a curriculum training strategy to progressively integrate multiple modalities into a unified model. The gesture-expression generator is first trained in three stages. In Stage 1, we align the speech modality with the pretrained language model through a streaming ASR objective. In Stage 2, the text targets within each chunk are replaced with gesture tokens, enabling the model to learn streaming co-speech gesture generation. In Stage 3, facial expression tokens are further introduced, resulting in a unified generator for joint co-speech gesture and expression generation. This progressive training procedure reduces the difficulty of directly learning multimodal generation from scratch and allows each newly introduced modality to build upon previously established representations.
Full-model integration then follows four stages. Stages 1–2 establish full-duplex speech interaction following SALMONN-omni (Yu et al., 2025), first connecting the streaming speech encoder to the LLM and then introducing the streaming speech synthesizer. In Stage 3, the speech dialogue model is kept frozen, while only the gesture–expression connector and generator are optimized. This stage focuses on representation alignment: the non-verbal generation module learns to interpret and utilize hidden representations produced by the pretrained speech dialogue model without perturbing its established interaction behavior. In Stage 4, the speech interaction and non-verbal generation components are jointly optimized, allowing the internal representations of the dialogue model to further adapt to multimodal behavior generation. Since the speech dialogue model has already acquired strong interaction capabilities, its learning rate is lower than that of the gesture-related parameters. This conservative update strategy enables the dialogue representations to adapt to gesture and expression generation while minimizing interference with previously learned speech interaction capabilities. Full settings are given in Appendix A.6.

4 Experimental Setup
4.1 Training and Test Data Preparation
To build and evaluate a high-quality dialogue-aware gesture–expression generation module, careful curation of both training and evaluation data is essential. We therefore summarize our data curation pipeline and practical observations in Figure 2, with the aim of facilitating future research in this direction. For training, we select only a subset of Seamless Interaction (Agrawal et al., 2025) through speaker-level filtering. Human gesturing is inherently variable: for the same utterance, a speaker may produce expressive hand movements, subtle rhythmic motion, or almost no visible gesture, all of which are natural behaviors. However, not all such data are equally informative for learning a gesture generator. In particular, speakers exhibiting predominantly static motion provide weak supervision for distinguishing speaking and listening behaviors and may bias the model toward generating overly still motion. We therefore design a filtering pipeline that selects speakers with clearly visible speaking gestures and pronounced differences between speaking and listening states. This process retains 81 speakers from the original 3,401. Further details are provided in Appendix B.1. Because the original Seamless Interaction dataset does not provide off-the-shelf facial-expression annotations, we additionally construct a dedicated pipeline to recover FLAME-based facial parameters (Li et al., 2017). The pipeline consists of expression estimation using KaoLRM (Zhu et al., 2026), invalid-detection filtering, and crop stabilization of the recovered parameters. These steps produce temporally stable facial-expression supervision suitable for streaming generation. Additional details are given in Appendix B.2.
For the semantic exemplar library used in template-guided generation, we develop a separate curation pipeline consisting of semantic event proposal, pose screening, action-family canonicalization, diversity selection and phrase disambiguation. The resulting library contains 3,227 high-quality exemplars spanning 1,125 action families and indexed by 2,072 semantic phrases. Details of the construction procedure are provided in Appendix B.3. We further construct a dialogue-aware evaluation set to better reflect the requirements of interactive gesture generation. Existing test sets primarily emphasize gestures produced while speaking and therefore provide limited coverage of listening–speaking transitions and explicit semantic gestures, both of which are important for natural dialogue. Our test set consequently focuses on these two important aspects: full-duplex conversational behaviors and semantic gestures. The curation pipeline first applies conventional gesture-based metrics for pre-filtering, followed by MLLM-based screening and final human verification. The resulting human-verified benchmark contains 138 clips, including 67 full-duplex examples covering full-duplex behaviors such as backchannels, overlaps and interruptions, as well as 71 semantic examples. All samples have high-quality groundtruth gestures which will further serve as anchors in MLLM and human evaluation. Further details are provided in Appendix B.4.
