4.2 Evaluation Measures
We evaluate ELLSA 2 across three modalities: speech, gesture and expression. For speech and expression, we largely follow established evaluation protocols. For gesture generation, however, conventional metrics do not fully capture the requirements of dialogue-aware interaction. We therefore design a set of objective metrics targeting both speaking–listening dynamics and semantic appropriateness, complemented by subjective human evaluation.
Speech and Expression
For speech interaction, we report S2T accuracy and transcribed S2S answer accuracy on Llama Questions (Nachmani et al., 2024), Web Questions (Berant et al., 2013), and TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), together with GPTScore on AlpacaEval (Chen et al., 2024c). To evaluate full-duplex interaction capability, we additionally report the turn-taking success rate on each speech interaction benchmark. For expression, lip vertex error (LVE) and mean head distance (MHD) evaluate speaking-related facial geometry, while upper-face deviation (FDD) and jaw-pose deviation (JDD) characterize state-dependent dynamics across speaking and listening frames. As for speech interaction baselines, we choose Moshi (Défossez et al., 2024), PersonaPlex (Roy et al., 2026), Freeze-Omni (Wang et al., 2025) and SALMONN-omni (Yu et al., 2025). For expression baselines, we include both speaking-only baselines such as ARTalk (Chu et al., 2025) and MIBURI (Mughal et al., 2026), and dyadic baselines like UniLS (Chu et al., 2026) and DualTalk (Peng et al., 2025). Detailed protocols are provided in Appendices C.1 and C.5.
Gesture
For gesture evaluation, we introduce four metrics covering different aspects of dialogue-aware gesture generation, as illustrated in Figure 2. Two metrics operate directly on motion representations, while the other two employ MLLMs to evaluate rendered interaction videos. For baselines, we include both speaking-only baselines such as GestureLSM (Liu et al., 2025c) and MIBURI (Mughal et al., 2026), and dyadic baselines like ConvoFusion (Mughal et al., 2024) and audio2photoreal (Ng et al., 2024).
The first two metrics focus on conversational state awareness and speech–gesture synchronization. The speaking–listening activity ratio, RSL=ES/ELR_{\mathrm{SL}}=E_{S}/E_{L}, compares the mean motion displacement during speaking and listening segments, measuring whether the generated gestures exhibit appropriate activity differences across conversational states. Prosodic alignment AA measures rhythmic correspondence by contrasting the onset–gesture correlation of the matched speech with that of a negative speech sample drawn from a different session. Compared with direct rhythmic-alignment measures, this contrastive formulation reduces the possibility that excessively active motion obtains an artificially high score. We further validate AA on the GENEA benchmark (Kucherenko et al., 2024), where it exhibits stronger agreement with human judgments than commonly used rhythmic metrics such as BeatAlign. Further details are provided in Appendix C.2.
The remaining two metrics use MLLMs to assess rendered videos from a dialogue perspective. The duplex score DD evaluates full-duplex conversational behavior, including interaction timing and the appropriateness of gestures across speaking and listening states, whereas the semantic score SS evaluates whether visible gestures convey the intended semantic meaning. For each evaluation, the judge receives both the generated clip and its temporally synchronized human reference. The reference serves as contextual evidence for appropriate conversational behavior. Gemini-2.5-Pro and Seed independently evaluate each clip twice at 5 fps, and the average scores across trials and judge models are reported. Human annotators independently evaluate the same two dimensions using the corresponding scoring criteria. In this work, we treat human judgments as the gold standard for evaluating gesture quality. We then analyze the agreement between MLLM-based scores and human ratings. The observed correlations suggest that MLLM-based evaluation can serve as a preliminary automatic metric. Detailed protocols are provided in Appendices C.3 and C.4.

5.1 Speech Interaction
Table 1 shows that ELLSA 2 is highly competitive with current open-source full-duplex speech interaction models while additionally generating gestures and facial expressions. Gesture Generation
Table 2 shows that ELLSA 2 generates strong dialog-aware gestures across speaking/listening state distinction, rhythmic alignment, duplex behavior, and semantic expression. The jointly optimized ELLSA 2 achieves the best alignment score and the highest human-rated duplex score, while consistently outperforming the standalone generator in human duplex evaluation. With semantic guidance, ELLSA 2 further achieves the best speaking/listening activity ratio as well as the highest semantic scores under both human and MLLM evaluations. In particular, semantic guidance substantially improves the human semantic score from 2.014 to 2.711, demonstrating that the proposed semantic template guidance effectively enhances the generation of visible semantic gestures. Meanwhile, the two ELLSA 2 variants remain comparable on the other metrics, suggesting that the semantic improvement is achieved without compromising general dialog-aware gesture quality. Agreement Between MLLM and Human Evaluation
We further validate the reliability of MLLM-as-a-judge for dialog-aware co-speech gesture evaluation, with the results reported in Table 3. The correlation between human annotators exceeds 0.9 for both duplex and semantic evaluation, indicating strong agreement in system-level judgments. Mean pairwise MLLM–human correlations are also consistently high, reaching 0.806/0.904 for duplex/semantic quality. When averaging the scores across MLLM judges and human annotators, the correlations further increase to 0.853 and 0.919, respectively. These results demonstrate that aggregated MLLM judgments are strongly correlated with human evaluations at the system level, suggesting that MLLM-as-a-judge can serve as a useful preliminary metric for efficient evaluation and rapid model comparison in dialog-aware co-speech gesture generation. 6 Conclusion
We presented ELLSA 2, a full-duplex dialogue model that jointly generates speech, gestures, and facial expressions during both speaking and listening. By leveraging shared dialogue representations to guide all output modalities, joint optimization preserves competitive full-duplex speech interaction while improving gesture and expression generation. We further introduced semantic template guidance, which consistently improves semantic gesture quality while maintaining facial expression articulation. Finally, we established a curated data and evaluation pipeline for dialog-aware co-speech gesture generation focusing on full-duplex behaviors and semantic gestures. Correlation analysis with human judgments further supports reference-based MLLMs as useful preliminary system-level metrics for evaluating duplex and semantic gesture quality. We hope our work will facilitate further research on multimodal full-duplex interaction.

AI tools were also used to support the implementation of data-curation pipelines, including speaker filtering for gesture training data and construction of the semantic exemplar library. The interfaces used for human annotation and the demonstration page were developed with assistance from AI coding agents. All AI-generated code was manually reviewed, verified, and, where necessary, revised by the authors. Ethics Statement
This paper introduces an end-to-end dialogue model capable of both speech interaction and gesture-expression generation, representing a step toward more comprehensive dialogue systems. While improving the performance and naturalness of human-like intelligence remains a central objective, we place equal emphasis on ensuring AI safety. This includes mitigating harmful, discriminatory or biased outputs, as well as developing reliable detection mechanisms to identify AI-generated content. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of transparency: users should be clearly informed when they are interacting with an AI system.

A.1 Factorized Gesture and Expression Representation
Upper-body and hand gestures are encoded by separate RVQ-VAEs with six residual codebooks per branch. Facial expression uses six further codebooks in FLAME parameter space. The encoders downsample gesture–expression sequences from 30 Hz to 7.5 Hz, and each latent step contains 18 indices with shared physical timestamps. Lower-body joints are excluded from the learned representation. The facial tokenizer excludes global head rotation, which is supplied by the body pose; rendering therefore uses the combined body–face output. The facial metrics in Appendix C.5 hold head and neck pose fixed; MHD measures head-mesh deformation from expression and jaw articulation.

A.4 Semantic-Call Prediction and Supervision
A lexicon associates each normalized multiword phrase with one action family. At a generated-text endpoint, the router retains the longest matching phrase ending there and attaches the candidate to its final subword token. This identifies an available action; the call head assesses its appropriateness in the current context. For a candidate at token ii, the head mixes the hidden states from backbone layers 16,20,24 and predicts the semantic call probability. The call head is a learned three-layer mixture followed by LayerNorm, a linear layer, SiLU, dropout 0.1, and a scalar sigmoid head. The inputs contain the causal response prefix and previously observed dialogue context. Calls require pi≥τp_{i}\geq\tau and a uniquely identified family, with two-token non-maximum suppression. Within a family, templates are ranked by semantic confidence, gesture quality and visibility, and the default router selects the highest-ranked template. A rejected or absent call leaves generation unconditioned on a template. The 87.8% F1 and 87.0% accuracy in Section 5.2 measure contextual appropriateness on a balanced, candidate-conditioned test set. The decision is whether an available gesture fits a proposed lexical endpoint. The locked test confusion matrix is TP/FP/FN/TN =144/30/10/124=144/30/10/124.
Policy supervision distinguishes an observed gesture event from a judgment that a gesture would be appropriate. Two language models, Seed and GPT, independently score the naturalness and informativeness of the specified candidate action given its description and the dialogue context up to the endpoint; neither future words nor the original observed-event label are supplied. They return si(m)∈{0,1,2,3,4}s_{i}^{(m)}\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}, denoting clearly inappropriate, weak or redundant, optional or insufficiently supported, natural and informative, and strongly supported, respectively. Annotation uses GPT endpoint gpt-5.4-2026-03-05 and the Seed deployment Seed-2.0-lite-260428. Each lexical endpoint is judged separately, including multiple candidates in one sentence, with at most 2,400 characters of causal context. The action description and response prefix are supplied without observed-event labels. The complete annotation prompt and JSON schema are preserved with the scoring protocols in Appendix G.
Development and test labels are constructed from the same two-model annotations using a separate hard-label rule, preserving the session-disjoint splits. With mean score s¯i=(si(1)+si(2))/2\bar{s}_{i}=(s_{i}^{(1)}+s_{i}^{(2)})/2, we assign yi=1y_{i}=1 when s¯i≥3.5\bar{s}_{i}\geq 3.5 and yi=0y_{i}=0 when s¯i≤1.5\bar{s}_{i}\leq 1.5; endpoints with intermediate scores are excluded from evaluation. This yields 156 positive and 156 negative development endpoints. The call-probability threshold τ\tau is selected by event F1 on balanced development data and fixed for testing. Event matching uses a one-token tolerance after two-token suppression. Within each response, adjacent positive endpoints separated by at most two tokens form a target event. Predicted endpoints are considered in descending probability, suppressing any within two tokens of a retained peak. Each retained peak matches the nearest unmatched target group within tolerance; matching is one-to-one. A.5 Template-Guided Gesture Generation
An accepted call retrieves a gesture exemplar and its semantic anchor. The fixed-window format contains 192 frames in eight chunks and the word-aligned format retains the relevant event span. Delimited guide tokens precede the corresponding speech conditions and target-code tokens, distinguishing conditioning context from generated output. The generator learns continuation in the presence of a guide, so template poses are not directly substituted for predicted poses. In the joint configuration, guides condition the twelve upper-body and hand codebooks. Facial and mouth targets remain those of the current dialogue, avoiding transfer of the template speaker’s articulation. The eight-chunk training guide is exposed chunk by chunk. Causal attention allows each target to see the current guide and both current speech conditions, its previous target steps, and previous intervals. Guide and acoustic positions have label −100-100; only target-code positions enter the categorical losses. Direct guide embeddings use body/hand codes only. Shared transformer states and subsequent autoregression can nevertheless change facial outputs indirectly. In evaluation, gesture decoding is greedy. The first block uses the style context and its aligned speech conditions, without generated target history. Guides use the verified event span, quantized on the 133 ms latent grid and grouped into at most six guide steps per interval. The final partial group ends the guide rather than repeating the action indefinitely. Once the span ends, unguided continuation resumes.
Once a semantic call is triggered, the template timing is determined based on the timestamp of the anchor phrase’s endpoint word. The semantic template is then scheduled such that the corresponding semantic gesture is temporally aligned with this endpoint. Successful execution requires sufficient lead time to accommodate both the template’s preparatory motion and the computation required for gesture generation. The availability of look-ahead response text provides this lead time, enabling the template to be scheduled before the target semantic moment while preserving real-time generation.
Guided evaluation uses predicted gate probabilities at τ=0.706\tau=0.706. The archived semantic outputs contain 83 candidate records: 54 scheduled, 28 below threshold, and one removed by token suppression. Scheduled guides occur in 53/71 semantic clips; all 18 remaining clips are included in the semantic mean. Duplex outputs have two scheduled events in 2/67 clips. There are no recorded conflict or out-of-range rejection statuses.

A.7 Model Specifications
The dialogue backbone and speech synthesizer choices follow the exact choices of SALMONN-omni. The gesture–expression transformer is initialized from Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and has 24 layers, hidden size 896, 14 query heads, two key/value heads, and feed-forward size 4,864. Eighteen independent embeddings and output heads use vocabularies of 2,048 codes. ELLSA 2 has 10.78B parameters, while the 776M trainable groups contain 696M generator parameters, 15M added gesture-connector parameters, 13M LLM LoRA parameters, 1M synthesizer LoRA parameters, 38M speech-connector parameters, 10M speech synthesis-connector parameters, 2M semantic-head parameters, and 16K added special-token parameters.

B.3 Semantic Exemplar Library Construction
The semantic exemplar construction pipeline involves multiple stages. First, Gemini inspects source video with its transcript to propose time-stamped, explicitly meaningful actions and their descriptions. A separate video-verification pass checks each proposed segment for the described visible action. Recordings without a retained event are omitted from this semantic candidate pool. This yields 29,248 recordings containing 77,585 annotated events. The annotations establish positive evidence for candidate actions. Table 7 traces the subsequent reductions.
Each event defines a 192-frame (6.4 s) reference window centered near the event midpoint, with its start aligned to the 24-frame (0.8 s) generation grid. Pose screening requires valid-frame fraction ≥0.999\geq 0.999, sufficient movement clarity, acceptable spine posture and bounded boundary velocity. This leaves 46,894 candidates. Text classification uses the event description and nearby transcript to assign an action family and an exact spoken anchor. Unambiguous rule matches are resolved directly. Otherwise, GPT classifies the candidate, and a subsequent canonicalization pass merges families with equivalent visible actions and semantic functions. Empty transcripts, non-exact anchors and generic beats are excluded. Of 35,436 text-accepted candidates, 34,817 also meet the stronger video-confidence (≥0.9\geq 0.9) and combined visibility (≥0.8\geq 0.8) requirements. This step reuses the recorded video-verification evidence.
Boundary speed is the sum of mean pose-vector displacement over the first and last twelve frame transitions of the candidate window, in axis-angle coordinates. Screening requires this value ≤2.0\leq 2.0, movement clarity ≥0.15\geq 0.15, first-spine forward rotation maximum/95th percentile ≤0.55/0.50\leq 0.55/0.50 radians, and summed three-spine rotation-norm maximum/95th percentile ≤0.80/0.70\leq 0.80/0.70 radians. Movement clarity is clip⁡(0.55​d+0.45​e−0.20​b,0,1)\operatorname{clip}(0.55d+0.45e-0.20b,0,1), where d=min⁡(1,log⁡(1+D)/log⁡2)d=\min(1,\log(1+D)/\log 2) for midpoint displacement DD, e=min⁡(1,E/0.35)e=\min(1,E/0.35) for mean pose-vector speed EE, and b=min⁡(1,B/0.75)b=\min(1,B/0.75) for boundary speed BB. The video confidence is the verifier’s self-reported confidence. Combined visibility is 0.700.70 times that confidence plus 0.300.30 times movement clarity.
Library construction ranks these events by semantic/family confidence, gesture quality, visibility, posture and boundary continuity, while limiting each family to twelve examples and each speaker or session to two contributions within a family. A transcript-retrieval check requires the annotated family to appear among the five highest-ranked lexical candidates. The resulting broad library has 7,665 exemplars. Requiring the product of semantic and family confidence to exceed 0.8 leaves 3,672. Phrase disambiguation then assigns each normalized anchor or retrieval phrase to one family, resolving conflicts by the gesture’s meaning, direction, hand shape and target. The final inventory contains 3,227 exemplars, 1,125 families, and 2,072 uniquely assigned phrases.
The initial library-ranking score is 3​c​f+c+v+0.5​f+q+p−b−a3cf+c+v+0.5f+q+p-b-a, for semantic confidence cc, family confidence ff, visibility vv, motion quality qq, posture quality p=1/(1+spine95)p=1/(1+\text{spine}_{95}), boundary speed bb, and normalized anchor-to-window-center distance aa. Confidence and phrase filters subsequently define the final lexical inventory. This curation preference concerns clear, reusable actions.

Two language models judge whether a candidate action would be natural and informative at a lexical endpoint, even if the source speaker did not perform it. Annotation implementation and provenance.
The archived video-proposal and verification scripts use gemini-2.5-pro-preview-03-25 as their default endpoint. Proposal sends the source video with at most 10,000 transcript characters, requests a JSON array of time spans and descriptions. Verification re-encodes each event with one second of context on either side at 10 fps and requests exists, confidence, and visible evidence. Proposal exceptions permit two retries. Malformed arrays or failed verification are recorded as invalid. The later text-classification and family-canonicalization use gpt-5.4-2026-03-05.
B.4 Human-Verified Dialogue Test Set
Test curation combines transcript-based scene identification, target/partner voice activity, pose-fit validity and rendered-person visibility before video review. Human reviewers inspect both the visible reference behavior and its correspondence to the conversation; only explicit acceptance is retained. Duplex categories comprise 22 backchannels, 20 overlapping-speech events, 15 cases where the target interrupts the partner, and 10 cases where the partner interrupts the target. Thus both continuing to speak and changing to a listening role occur in the evaluation. Semantic review accepts 71 clips with meaningful visible gestures supported by the current semantic exemplar library. All 138 clips span 20 s, including 82 naturalistic and 56 improvised examples. As test set is selected from the test split of Seamless Interaction dataset, it ensures no overlapping with training dataset. Objective activity and facial metrics use 4–16 s, leaving context for gesture preparation and completion. The inherited event windows supplied to the MLLM judges are specified in Appendix C.3.

Appendix C Evaluation Details
C.1 Speech Interaction
Speech interaction evaluation uses 300 Llama Questions, 2,032 Web Questions, 1,000 TriviaQA questions and 199 AlpacaEval instructions. QA scoring normalizes predicted and reference text and accepts a match to any non-empty reference alias. Native generated text supplies S2T responses and Whisper-large-v3 transcriptions of generated audio supply S2S responses. Alpaca response quality uses the inherited GPT-4.1 rubric for accuracy and reasonableness on a 1–5 scale with the same prompt used in SALMONN-omni. For full-duplex evaluation, turn-taking is considered successful if the model produces a response within two seconds after the end of the user’s query.
C.2 Gesture Activity and Prosodic Alignment
For the activity ratio, All systems use 13 upper-body joints on a common zero-shape, root-fixed skeleton with fixed lower limbs. Let vtv_{t} be mean Euclidean joint displacement between adjacent frames, and let ESE_{S} and ELE_{L} be its means on valid speaking and listening-only frames in the central scoring interval. We compute
RSL=ESEL.R_{\mathrm{SL}}=\frac{E_{S}}{E_{L}}.
(24)
Target and partner voice-activity detection on the cropped audio timeline defines the states. Target speech, including overlap, belongs to SS; target silence with partner speech belongs to LL; mutual silence is excluded. Displacements are evaluated at 30 Hz, assigned to the later frame of each adjacent pair. Speech intervals are derived from metadata VAD annotations. C.3 Reference-Based MLLM Scores
Gemini-2.5-Pro and Seed each score every applicable clip twice using the same reference-based rubric and 5 fps video input. The MLLM duplex score is D0=0.45​T+0.45​P+0.10​VD_{0}=0.45T+0.45P+0.10V, combining timing (TT), conversational appropriateness (PP), and visibility (VV). The MLLM semantic score is S0=clip⁡(0.35​V+0.45​M+0.20​K−0.30​F,0,1)S_{0}=\operatorname{clip}(0.35V+0.45M+0.20K-0.30F,0,1), combining visible evidence, meaning match (MM), concreteness (KK), and a generic beat/fidget penalty (FF). Components are normalized to [0,1][0,1].
Both scores additionally account for behavior outside the annotated event through Q=Q0​(1−0.45​U−0.35​O)Q=Q_{0}(1-0.45U-0.35O), where UU penalizes unjustified movement during target-silence intervals and OO penalizes overactivity elsewhere. Silence candidates use 20 ms audio windows below −40-40 dBFS, trimmed by 0.3 s at both boundaries and retained only if at least one second remains. Judges must corroborate these intervals and provide timestamped evidence relative to the synchronized reference. The two penalties cannot count the same interval twice. Natural gesture preparation, returns, and listener feedback are exempt. Each judgment is penalized before the four judgments are averaged, followed by equal-weight clip averaging over the 67 duplex or 71 semantic items.
Executable request and aggregation protocol.
The versions of used MLLM judges are gemini-2.5-pro and Seed-2.0-lite-260428. The main tables report MLLM scores paired with the human ratings in Appendix C.4. Each request contains a single user message: task instructions, clip-relative transcript/event context and acoustic low-energy windows, followed by labeled reference video and candidate video as separate media inputs, in that order. Both retain target-person audio; partner speech is supplied as transcribed context, without a separate partner-audio input. Gemini temperature is zero; Seed uses the API default; no sampling seed is sent. The maximum output length is 30,000 tokens.
Components are requested directly as numbers in [0,1][0,1]. The activity severities U/OU/O are judge-assigned holistic values using anchors 0,0.25,0.50,0.75,10,0.25,0.50,0.75,1 for absent, mild isolated, moderate sustained/repeated, frequent pronounced, and pervasive severe problems. They are not sums over evidence intervals. The parser checks finite component ranges, timestamp bounds, at least one concrete interval for every positive penalty, independently confirmed absence of target speech for silence evidence, and nonoverlap between the two penalty types. A silence interval must last at least one second and lie wholly within an advisory low-energy window. Without an eligible window, U=0U=0. Full prompts, schema, and an illustrative output are given in Appendix G.

Appendix D Training Data
D.1 Speech Understanding and Interaction
We follow the speech-data preparation route of SALMONN-omni (Yu et al., 2025), combining speech recognition, spoken question answering, and synthetic multi-turn conversation. These sources cover instruction following, factual questions, longer answers, and conversational responses. Available question recordings are retained, while response speech is synthesized with CosyVoice2-0.5B (Du et al., 2024). For text-only sources, the inherited preparation pipeline uses the base LLM to produce conversational answers and synthesizes both sides of the interaction.
Multi-turn training follows SALMONN-omni’s construction of conversations from QA material. Prepared examples retain speaker turns and include interruption and competing-speech variants, allowing the speech system to learn when to continue, yield, or respond. Stage 2 uses the spoken-QA and conversation pool to connect synthesis and learn dialogue timing; Stage 4 reuses this pool to retain speech capability during joint optimization. Appendix F Limitations.
While ELLSA 2 represents progress toward more comprehensive dialogue modeling, several limitations remain. First, the current framework does not incorporate visual perception, despite vision being an important component of human face-to-face interaction. Future work could integrate visual inputs into the unified framework to support richer multimodal understanding and more comprehensive dialogue modeling. Second, the current semantic exemplar library is constructed solely from the Seamless Interaction dataset. Expanding the library with high-quality exemplars curated from larger and more diverse data sources could improve semantic coverage and further enhance the quality and robustness of template-guided gesture generation.
Appendix G Annotation and Scoring Prompts
The following are the verbatim saved task instructions, with line wrapping for readability. In these prompts, the silence penalty is named SS; the paper denotes it by UU to distinguish it from the semantic score.
G.1 Duplex MLLM score
Two synchronized 20-second videos are provided. VIDEO 1 is the human-verified GROUND-TRUTH reference. VIDEO 2 is the CANDIDATE to score. Score VIDEO 2 only. Use VIDEO 1 to locate the intended interaction event, but accept a visibly supported functional fragment or alternative response; exact pose, side, amplitude, and full trajectory need not match.
ANTI-HALLUCINATION RULE: transcript, VAD, category, audio, and VIDEO 1 identify what and when to inspect, but they do not prove that VIDEO 2 performs a motion. Independently verify the candidate’s visible change. Do not copy the reference description into the candidate description.
Mandatory observation:
1. Locate VIDEO 1’s clearest full-duplex event and state its time, body parts, starting pose, visible change, and ending pose.
2. Inspect VIDEO 2 at the same time, including before and after, and state its actual starting pose, visible change, and ending pose.
3. Compare the visible evidence and judge whether VIDEO 2 contains a full match, a useful functional fragment, a weak boundary-related cue, or only unrelated motion.
This is a sparse strongest-event metric, not a whole-clip average. Give substantial credit when any short candidate segment visibly captures part of the intended listening/speaking transition, interruption reaction, overlap behavior, or acknowledgement. A good local response is not cancelled by generic motion elsewhere. Do not require a large gesture, exact reference trajectory, return motion, or dense coverage.
Functional evidence includes:
- backchannel: a discrete nod, acknowledgement, orientation change, or intentional listening response;
- interruption target: a visible launch, escalation, turn claim, or newly initiated gesture near entry;
- interruption partner: a visible stop, reduction, withdrawal, yielding, reorientation, or transition toward a listening pose after being cut in;
- overlap: a visible change or maintained interaction behavior associated with the overlap boundary or interval.
Tiny renderer jitter, finger noise, a fully unchanged pose, or generic motion with no temporal relationship to the event receives little credit. A modest but clearly visible boundary-related change may receive partial credit even when its function is not completely unambiguous. Audio or transcript alignment alone cannot make Timing high: when the visible candidate cue is faint, generic, or ambiguous, Timing must not exceed 0.37 even if it happens at the annotated time.
Scoring anchors for each dimension:
- 0.00-0.10: no independently visible candidate change, or the claimed event exists only in text/audio/reference.
- 0.11-0.16: only generic motion, micro-fidget, continuous pre-existing motion, or clearly wrong timing.
- 0.17-0.29: a visible change occurs near the interaction event and weakly suggests the intended function, but is ambiguous, incomplete, or nonspecific.
- 0.30-0.46: one useful local functional fragment is visible, such as a partial stop, launch, nod, withdrawal, or state change, despite substantial mismatch elsewhere.
- 0.47-0.66: a clear correctly timed functional response with a noticeable deficiency relative to VIDEO 1.
- 0.67-0.90: a strong, specific, nearly equivalent response.
- 0.91-1.00: the relevant candidate and reference events are visually identical or functionally indistinguishable after separate inspection.
Dimensions:
- Timing: alignment of the independently visible candidate cue with the conversational event, subject to the 0.37 cap for a faint/generic/ambiguous cue.
- Appropriateness: degree to which the visible cue supports the intended interaction function.
- Gesture backchannel visibility: clarity of the strongest visible full-duplex cue; this legacy field covers every category.
Return exactly one JSON object and no other text:
{
 "Analysis": "reference time/start-change-end; candidate same-time start-change-end; strongest local evidence; comparison judgment",
 "Timing": 0.0,
 "Appropriateness": 0.0,
 "Gesture backchannel visibility": 0.0
}
Duplex Fit Score = 0.45 * Timing + 0.45 * Appropriateness + 0.10 * Gesture backchannel visibility.
G.2 Semantic MLLM score
Two synchronized 20-second videos are provided. VIDEO 1 is the human-verified GROUND-TRUTH semantic-motion reference. VIDEO 2 is the CANDIDATE to score. Score VIDEO 2 only. Use VIDEO 1 to locate and interpret the intended meaning, while crediting any visibly verified candidate gesture or fragment that supports part of that meaning.
ANTI-HALLUCINATION RULE: transcript, category, audio, annotation, and VIDEO 1 tell you what and when to inspect, but they are not evidence that VIDEO 2 moves. Independently state VIDEO 2’s actual visible pose or trajectory. Never invent a candidate action from the words or copy VIDEO 1’s trajectory into VIDEO 2’s description.
Mandatory observation:
1. State VIDEO 1’s clearest semantic event: time, target meaning, body parts, starting pose, visible trajectory/configuration, and ending pose.
2. Inspect VIDEO 2 at the same time, including before and after, and state its actual starting pose, visible trajectory/configuration, and ending pose.
3. Identify the strongest visibly shared semantic property: for example direction, side, height, size, number, shape, grouping, comparison, spatial layout, object handling, action component, emblem, or metaphorical trajectory.
This is a sparse strongest-event metric. One clear semantic gesture or one genuinely useful semantic fragment can earn substantial credit even if the rest of the clip is generic or mismatched. Do not average over every phrase. Do not require the complete reference trajectory, exact pose, exact side, large amplitude, or an independently recognizable rendition of the entire phrase.
A candidate fragment receives partial credit whenever its visible form shares a relevant coarse semantic property with VIDEO 1 at the target time, even if the full intended meaning would remain ambiguous without the reference. The reference may help interpret an actually visible candidate property; it may not supply motion that is absent. Do not dismiss such visible property matches as merely generic beats.
Mandatory partial-credit examples:
- a visible upward move for reaching, height, or increase;
- a sideward indication for a location or side;
- a compact hand shape, pinch, or clench for something small;
- visible separation or convergence for size, grouping, distance, or comparison;
- synchronized forward/back travel during "back and forth," even if the two hands do not alternate;
- a partial object-manipulation action or brief emblematic configuration.
These examples normally belong in 0.25-0.44 or above when visibly present at the target time. Use the 0.11-0.24 generic-only tier only when no relevant direction, configuration, spatial relation, or action component is visible.
Do not interpret arbitrary arm motion as a named action. Generic beats, fidgeting, self-touch, posture drift, or motion only coincident with a word should remain low when no relevant visible property is present.
LOW-SCORE CALIBRATION: Reserve a final zero only for an unusable video, absent person, or image corruption so severe that the candidate cannot be observed. If VIDEO 2 is a valid observable render but remains static or has no semantic gesture, use about 0.06-0.10 for all three positive dimensions and zero Beat/fidget penalty. This is still a clear failure, not semantic credit. Do not apply a beat/fidget penalty to a static candidate. A visible but unrelated generic motion may score slightly above this floor for Visual clarity, while semantic match and Concreteness remain low.
Scoring anchors for Visual clarity, Text-motion semantic match, and Concreteness:
- 0.00-0.05: candidate cannot be reliably observed because the video/person is absent or severely corrupted.
- 0.06-0.10: valid observable candidate, but static or completely missing the target semantic event.
- 0.11-0.24: visible but generic beat/fidget/motion with no relevant semantic property.
- 0.25-0.44: a coarse but visibly shared semantic property or action component appears at the target time; useful as a fragment but ambiguous or incomplete.
- 0.45-0.64: a meaningful partial gesture visibly supports the target meaning, although trajectory, specificity, or clarity is substantially weaker than VIDEO 1.
- 0.65-0.84: one clear correct semantic gesture or strong fragment, with a noticeable deficiency.
- 0.85-0.94: a strong and specific semantic equivalent with only minor ambiguity.
- 0.95-1.00: the semantic event is visually identical or functionally indistinguishable from VIDEO 1.
Beat/fidget penalty:
- Use 0.00-0.08 when a real semantic event or useful fragment is the strongest local evidence; unrelated motion elsewhere should not erase it.
- Use 0.09-0.15 when a coarse but relevant visible property is present but generic motion obscures it.
- Use 0.16-0.25 when generic beat/fidget is the main evidence and no relevant semantic property is visible. This penalty should keep a valid generic-motion candidate low but normally should not clip its final score to zero.
- Use 0.26-0.40 only when severe unrelated motion or artifacts make even a weak relevant fragment difficult to observe.
- Use 0.00 for a static candidate because there is no beat/fidget to penalize.
Return exactly one JSON object and no other text:
{

}
Semantic Support Score = clip(0.35 * Visual clarity + 0.45 * Text-motion semantic match + 0.20 * Concreteness - 0.30 * Beat/fidget penalty, 0, 1).
G.3 Shared Activity Addendum
This addendum overrides the earlier output schema and the instruction that motion outside the strongest event cannot affect the score. Preserve the earlier metric dimensions as a LOCAL BASE score. Then separately judge inappropriate activity over the FULL 0-20 second candidate clip. Do not lower the base dimensions merely to apply the same global penalty twice.
More movement is not better evidence. Before crediting a semantic property or duplex event, inspect nearby before/after behavior: does the candidate actually change trajectory/configuration in relation to the event, or is essentially the same repeating gesture occurring regardless of speech and meaning? A coincidental instant in a ubiquitous repetitive motion is not sufficient evidence of a meaningful gesture. Name a concrete visible property and its temporal relationship; do not invent a semantic action because a word happens to coincide with motion. Specific meaningful fragments still earn local credit. This check may change the local base assessment and must be explained separately from global deductions.
Evaluate two distinct penalties S and O, each from 0 to 1:
S = Silence motion penalty: sustained unjustified arm/hand gesticulation when the TARGET is not speaking. Candidate acoustic low-energy windows are provided in clip-relative seconds. They are hints, not proof of silence. Corroborate absence of target speech by listening. Only cite S evidence wholly inside one of these windows and lasting at least 1 second. If no qualifying windows exist or no independently verified problematic motion exists, S=0. Compare with VIDEO 1 at the same time.
Silence does NOT require freezing. Do NOT penalize breathing, small head/posture adjustments, a relaxed hand hold, a natural gesture return or carry-over near a boundary, preparation for an imminent turn, or a distinct meaningful nod/listening backchannel while the partner speaks. The acoustic windows already exclude 0.3 seconds near detected speech boundaries; still allow clearly justified carry-over. Penalize continued unrelated co-speech-like waving, repetitive large beats, looping, or excessive arm/hand travel that fails to settle while the target is silent and lacks a listening function. If movement is justified by a visible reference event or partner turn, explain the exemption and use S=0 for that event. Never infer motion merely from text or audio.
O = Overactivity penalty: excessive, distracting, repetitive, poorly controlled or functionally irrelevant activity during speech or other intervals NOT used for S. Evaluate purposeless repetitions, repeated large excursions, or an unchanging motor loop across different meanings/states. Compare the candidate’s range, frequency and purpose with the SAME-TIME human reference; do not reward amplitude or speed by themselves. Do NOT punish lively natural speaking gestures, a single expressive gesture, stylistic variation, or useful sparse gestures simply for moving more. A static candidate has S=0 and O=0, but still receives a low local task score if the target event is absent.
NO DOUBLE COUNTING: a time interval penalized under S cannot also be evidence for O. Local Beat/fidget penalty remains about evidence for the selected semantic event; O must cite additional excessive behavior rather than recoding that same local generic beat. Assign a quiet-interval problem to S first. When no distinct additional problem remains, O=0. Do not reduce S or O just because a strong task gesture exists elsewhere.
Shared severity anchors, incorporating duration, frequency, amplitude and functional justification:
0.00: absent, unobservable, or fully justified; no penalty evidence needed.
0.25: a clearly visible but mild isolated problem, limited duration/extent.
0.50: repeated or sustained moderate unjustified motion over a material portion of eligible time.
0.75: frequent pronounced purposeless movement, many repetitions or long failure to settle.
1.00: pervasive severe, nearly continuous unjustified gesticulation across most eligible intervals.
Choose proportionately; do not assign 1.0 for a single brief uncertain event. No eligible silent time means S=0, not missing data. In uncertain cases, state the uncertainty and do not invent penalty evidence. Scoring is blind to the system name and should not target any particular model or desired ranking.
Return one JSON object retaining ALL earlier LOCAL dimension fields and Analysis, and ADD:
"Silence motion penalty": 0.0,
"Overactivity penalty": 0.0,
"Silence evidence": [],
"Overactivity evidence": []
For every evidence entry use numeric "start_sec", "end_sec" within 0-20, strings "candidate_motion", "reference_motion", "why_unjustified". For Silence evidence also include "target_speech_absent": true, only if independently confirmed. Evidence intervals for S and O must not overlap. Positive penalties require concrete timestamped evidence. Zero penalties may use empty arrays. In Analysis separately explain local event evidence, globally excessive activity or its absence, and legitimate motion exemptions.
The scorer computes Base using the earlier formula and Final = Base * (1 - 0.45*S - 0.35*O). Do not return a fabricated final value in place of the required dimensions. Both base and final will be saved so global penalties and changes in local interpretation can be distinguished. These weights are fixed for this experiment and do not depend on system rankings.
G.4 Request Context and Output Example
The dynamic context contains the clip identifier, local event interval, mapping to source time, text-only event evidence, target role, target and partner transcripts with their time basis, and available reference-motion annotations. Optional absent fields are omitted. Acoustic low-energy intervals are then appended with the instruction to corroborate silence from the target audio and to allow legitimate feedback to partner speech. The reference video is labeled VIDEO 1: HUMAN-VERIFIED GT REFERENCE; the candidate is labeled VIDEO 2: CANDIDATE TO SCORE. Each is a separate media item sampled at 5 fps.
For illustration only, the following valid semantic response describes a hypothetical upward fragment.
{

The resulting semantic score is 0.420.42. For a positive deduction, every evidence object additionally contains numeric start_sec/end_sec and text candidate_motion, reference_motion, and why_unjustified; silence evidence also requires target_speech_absent: true. The parser enforces the temporal constraints in Appendix C.3. Format-recovery requests in the ablations append validation feedback about eligible intervals and the required schema, without changing the rubric or selecting among valid scores.
G.5 Contextual-Call Annotation
Call annotation prompt.
You are independently annotating a deterministic semantic gesture policy for a streaming expressive avatar.
At each item, decide whether inserting exactly the supplied action_family gesture immediately when the marked trigger phrase ends would be semantically natural and useful. Score rubric:
4 strong_yes: the completed causal meaning clearly supports this exact distinctive gesture and it should be inserted.
3 yes: the gesture is natural, context-supported, and adds useful visible meaning.
2 optional: it could be acceptable, but doing nothing is equally natural or evidence is insufficient.
1 no: weak, awkward, overly repetitive, generic emphasis, or probably not useful here.

Rules:
- Judge the supplied family, not any gesture in general.

- Use the full score range. Keep reason concise and specific. Return every id exactly once as JSON only.

Proposal prompt.
You are given a video of a natural conversation (with audio). Find ONLY segments where the speaker makes an EXPLICIT semantic gesture that unambiguously encodes concrete meaning visible from the gesture itself (no guessing).
Definition (EXPLICIT): A reasonable viewer can identify the intended meaning from the gesture alone with high confidence, and the spoken words merely confirm it.
Include ONLY these categories:
1) Emblems (conventional signs): e.g., phone-hand for ’call’, thumbs-up, OK sign, shush.
2) Deictic gestures: clear pointing/indicating a referenced person/object/location (including left vs right to separate two explicit options).
3) Iconic/mimetic gestures: tracing a shape, showing size/number with fingers, miming a described action/tool (e.g., drinking, writing, turning a knob).
Exclude (DO NOT output) if any of the following is true:
- The gesture is beat/emphasis, rhythmic timing, general expressiveness, fidgeting, posture change.

## 核心摘要

面对面交谈要求说话与倾听同时协调语音、手势与表情，现有全双工语音模型能同时听与说，现有手势模型多以后处理方式根据已给语音生成动作，缺少由对话理解统一调度可见行为的机制。ELLSA 2以连续对话骨干为中心，大语言模型骨干输出隐状态表征听到的对方语音声学上下文与对话状态，流式语音合成器输出隐状态表征自身说话内容与声音，两者与保留的预训练声学特征相加形成条件。手势表情合成器按0.8秒分块自回归生成上身、手部与表情编码，即使输出语音为静默也持续生成倾听反应，实现听说共用的在线非言语生成。对话骨干另设语义调用头判断当前文本上下文是否适合特定语义手势，触发后检索馆藏范例并作为引导插入生成序列，把是否调用与如何实现分开。在包含71个语义片段的人验测试集上，带模板引导的ELLSA 2的人类语义评分Human S（1-5分，越高越好）为2.711，高于无引导ELLSA 2的2.014。在TriviaQA语音问答的S2S回答准确率（%，越高越好）上，ELLSA 2为63.6%，高于SALMONN-omni的56.0%。结论适用于筛选后的可见说话人与短片段对话评估，视觉感知、馆藏覆盖以外的数据泛化尚未验证。原文未披露训练、推理或部署成本。

Repairing Speech Access After Text Updates
with Frozen Affine Fields
Ming-Hao Hsu
Yuxiang Wang
Yingda Shen
Zhizheng Wu
Affiliation: School of Data Science
Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, China
Email: wuzhizheng@cuhk.edu.cn
Abstract
Speech-capable language models inherit most of their knowledge from text-rich language backbones, and continued model maintenance is likewise dominated by text updates.
Knowledge acquired through a text update can nevertheless remain difficult to access when the same query is spoken.
We formulate this mismatch as post-update speech access repair, where the knowledge-bearing checkpoint stays frozen and a detachable operator repairs speech-only access in one model pass.
We introduce Affine Fields for Interface Repair across Modalities (Affirm), which first learns and freezes a base correction for speech hidden states, then adds query-specific corrections with zero mean over the operator-training queries.
Paired speech and text states provide the coordinates that condition these corrections on each query.
On balanced synthetic-speech PopQA, paired comparisons do not establish a clear advantage for Affirm over global SALSA steering or low-rank ReFT interventions under the same frozen single-state constraint.
On recorded SLUE-SQA-5 questions with text passages, a full-scale PopQA-fitted Affirm operator transfers without refitting and improves ROUGE-L by 0.0941 over its paired No Repair baseline.
Low-rank ReFT interventions also transfer positively, whereas the matched SALSA variant falls 0.0707 below its paired baseline.
These results show that text acquisition and speech access can diverge after an update and should be verified and repaired separately.
1 Introduction
Large language models increasingly serve as the reasoning core of interactive systems that use tools and act on external environments (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023).
Recent speech-language models extend this interaction from typed text to spoken input and output (Tang et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Shih et al., 2024).
Most general-purpose training data and factual maintenance material for these systems still come from text: web pages, documents, code, and manuals are available at far larger scale than paired speech supervision (Raffel et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023).
Speech-capable models therefore commonly attach audio encoders and alignment modules to a text-pretrained language backbone, while text remains the direct route for factual adaptation and targeted editing (Tang et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2023).

Figure 1: Decoupled knowledge acquisition and speech access repair.
(a) Text-only acquisition can leave a speech-access gap.
(b) Affirm combines a base correction (shared access parent) with a query-specific correction (centered route field) and edits the final prompt state with the acquired checkpoint frozen.
The example shows recorded outputs for one PopQA test question held out from operator fitting, with Affirm-Direct as the repair.
Native multimodality does not by itself make every text update equally usable from speech.
Studies of speech-language models report differences between matched spoken and typed inputs in semantic understanding, reasoning, and factual-recall pathways (Xiang et al., 2025; Cuervo et al., 2026; Modica et al., 2026; Hsu et al., 2026b; Hsu et al., 2026c).
We study a post-update instance of this mismatch: after a successful text-only update, a model may answer an updated fact when the question is typed yet fail when the same question is spoken.
The correct text response shows that the acquired checkpoint can express the updated fact, while the paired speech failure defines the post-update speech-access gap that we repair.
This problem arises whenever knowledge is maintained through text while users continue to query the resulting system by voice.
We consider a contract in which the acquired checkpoint is immutable and the repair remains detachable.
At deployment, the question is supplied only as speech, and the repair edits one decoder state in one model pass without a transcript.
The contract separates the knowledge-bearing checkpoint from the interface that makes its updated knowledge accessible (Figure 1).
The central design question is how to combine a base repair learned across speech queries with a correction tailored to each input.
We combine these roles in Affirm, or Affine Fields for Interface Repair across Modalities.
We first learn and freeze a base correction, called the shared access parent.
We then add a query-specific correction, called the centered route field, whose mean over the operator-training queries is zero.
Paired spoken and typed queries provide the hidden-state coordinates used to condition this correction.
The experiments first establish a large paired text–speech gap after successful text acquisition.
On balanced PopQA, paired bootstrap comparisons do not establish a clear advantage for Affirm-Direct over DiReFT, LoReFT, or SALSA.
When operators fitted on full-scale PopQA transfer without refitting to recorded SLUE questions, Affirm-Direct and ReFT improve over No Repair, whereas the matched SALSA variant degrades.
Parent comparisons and a two-seed depth sweep examine which design choices affect performance, and the compact variant also improves held-out access on Kimi-Audio.
Our contributions are:
• 
We formulate post-update speech access repair, separating text knowledge acquisition from detachable speech access through an immutable acquired checkpoint.
• 
We introduce Affirm, a staged affine field that combines a shared access parent with a centered query-specific route field learned from paired speech–text routes.
• 
We show that methods with comparable synthetic-speech performance can differ under recorded-speech transfer, where Affirm and ReFT improve over No Repair while the tested SALSA variant regresses.
2 Related Work
Text-centered speech language models and modality gaps.
Modern speech language models commonly connect an audio encoder to a pretrained text decoder through projectors, adapters, and staged multimodal training (Tang et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Hsu et al., 2026a).
Behavior alignment and cross-modal distillation train the speech route to reproduce capabilities available from text (Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026b; Hu et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026).
Speech inputs nevertheless remain weaker on some semantic and reasoning tasks, and representation similarity is associated with the remaining modality gap (Xiang et al., 2025; Cuervo et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a).
These studies improve speech during multimodal adaptation, whereas we address the later maintenance stage after a text update has established the target knowledge.
Cross-modal knowledge acquisition and access.
Multimodal models can store or acquire information through one route without making it equally available from another (Wen et al., 2025; Basu et al., 2024).
Speech and text can also rely on distinct factual-recall pathways inside a shared multimodal model (Modica et al., 2026).
Knowledge-editing methods change stored associations in language and audio-language models (Meng et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2023; Chung et al., 2026).
Our task instead begins after acquisition succeeds and repairs the route by which a frozen checkpoint accesses the acquired fact.
Frozen representation interventions.
A complementary line of work leaves pretrained model weights fixed and modifies behavior through narrow interventions on hidden representations.
Inference-Time Intervention learns directions at selected attention heads, while activation addition modifies residual-stream states with behavior-specific directions (Li et al., 2023; Turner et al., 2023).
ReFT generalizes learnable representation interventions at chosen layers and positions, including the DiReFT and LoReFT parameterizations (Wu et al., 2024).
These methods adapt behavior through a fixed text-model backbone, but they do not separate a text-acquisition stage from speech access to the acquired knowledge.
Affirm brings this intervention family to post-update speech access by learning from paired speech–text routes and retaining a detachable repair around a frozen shared parent.
Global and conditional steering.
Learned speech steering can optimize shared layer-wise additive directions with a frozen backbone (Yegorova et al., 2026).
Input-dependent steering predicts an intervention from each multimodal context (Parekh et al., 2025), while Steer-MoE dynamically mixes expert directions inside audio-encoder layers (Feng et al., 2025).
Angle and length interventions provide another representation-level route for reducing the speech–text modality gap (Xiang et al., 2025).
Together, these approaches establish global and input-conditioned steering as complementary mechanisms for reducing speech–text discrepancies.
Affirm addresses post-update factual access through a detachable operator that edits one decoder state of a frozen acquired checkpoint.
3 Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
3.1 Post-update access
Let Fθ+F_{\theta^{+}} be a speech-capable autoregressive checkpoint obtained by text-only answer-likelihood training from Fθ0F_{\theta_{0}}.

Affirm decomposes post-update repair into a shared access parent and a query-conditioned route field around that parent.

5 Experimental Setup
Model and factual acquisition.
We use Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (Xu et al., 2025).
For full-scale experiments, we fine-tune one checkpoint on text question–answer pairs from all 14,267 PopQA facts over 16 relations (Mallen et al., 2023) and another on all 4,000 TOFU questions over 200 fictional authors (Maini et al., 2024).
We then freeze each checkpoint and fit its repair operators.
We also evaluate compact operators on separately acquired Kimi-Audio-7B (KimiTeam et al., 2025) and MiMo-Audio-7B (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2025) checkpoints (Appendix D.5).
Full-scale operator splits.
For PopQA, we group questions linked by a shared subject or normalized question string before splitting, so no group crosses the 8,572/2,848/2,847 operator train/development/test split.
PopQA-20 and PopQA-60 use nested subsets of 2,853 and 8,560 training examples, approximately 20% and 60% of the full acquisition corpus, with the same development and test sets.
TOFU uses 120/40/40 train/development/test authors, yielding 2,400/800/800 examples without author overlap.
Balanced comparison and baseline fitting.
For the balanced PopQA comparison, we use a separate checkpoint acquired on 1,000 facts and a 600/199/201 operator train/development/test split that keeps duplicate questions together.
We separately fit each method on PopQA-20 for recorded-speech transfer and on TOFU training authors for author-disjoint evaluation.
Appendix B gives the implementation and development-selection details for every reproduced baseline.
Speech-only baselines.
The frozen-checkpoint comparison evaluates the following speech-only representation-level repair methods:
• 
No Repair applies the acquired checkpoint to speech without an added intervention.
• 
DiReFT and LoReFT (Wu et al., 2024) learn low-rank hidden-state interventions at a selected decoder state.
• 
L2S (Parekh et al., 2025) predicts an input-dependent steering intervention from the multimodal context.
• 
SALSA (Yegorova et al., 2026) learns one shared speech-aware steering activation vector with a frozen backbone.
All speech-only methods receive the question as audio, without its transcript or a paired text-question state, and use one pass through the frozen acquired checkpoint.
Speech LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), speech-to-text knowledge distillation (Wang et al., 2026b, S2T-KD,), a Whisper ASR cascade (Radford et al., 2023), and full speech supervision are reported separately as operational alternatives because they relax the frozen single-state deployment contract.
Donor-assisted controls.
Angle and Length (Xiang et al., 2025) modify speech representations through direction and norm adjustments using a paired text-question state as a per-example inference-time donor.
We report them separately because the additional typed question is unavailable to speech-only methods.
Speech and transfer.
CosyVoice renders the PopQA and TOFU questions used for fitting and evaluation (Du et al., 2024).
Our transfer evaluation uses all 256 recorded SLUE-SQA-5 questions from 50 human speakers and five source datasets (Shon et al., 2023).
Each SLUE input contains a text passage and a spoken question, so speech-only refers to the question modality.
We apply each frozen PopQA-20 operator with no SLUE training examples, refitting, or target-domain strength retuning.
The separate Angle and Length controls access the paired text question at inference.
This tests transfer to passage-based question answering under changes in task, prompt, speakers, and acoustics, rather than recall of the acquired PopQA facts.
Affirm variants.
Each variant combines a parent with the centered route field:
• 
Affirm-Direct combines a direct shared parent with the centered route field and is the primary Affirm variant.
• 
Affirm-Expert combines the expert parent with the centered route field after Stage A.
• 
Affirm-K1 uses a compact scale–direction parent for depth and cross-backbone characterization.
Optimization, selection, and metrics.
The hidden width is d=3,584d=3,584 and low-rank operators use r=64r=64.
Stage B freezes its parent and DD, trains zero-initialized UU, and deploys it with fixed β=0.25\beta=0.25.
We sweep ℓ∈{4,8,12,16,20,24,28}\ell\in\{4,8,12,16,20,24,28\} only on development data, calibrate matched edit norms before test generation, and report ROUGE-L recall (RL), normalized exact match (EM), and SLUE answer-span accuracy.
Appendix A gives complete schedules, doses, prompts, counts, seeds, and uncertainty procedures.
6 Results
6.1 The text update leaves a measurable speech-access gap
Text-only acquisition succeeds without making the acquired knowledge equally usable from speech.
On CosyVoice-rendered paired questions over all 14,267 PopQA facts, the acquired checkpoint reaches 0.9213 RL and 0.9187 EM through text, compared with 0.1840 RL and 0.1519 EM through speech.
The held-out PopQA and TOFU questions test access to facts included in text acquisition.
To test whether speech states retain question-specific information, we retrieve each speech state’s matching text state among 600 paired questions.
After subtracting each modality’s mean state, top-1 retrieval accuracy is 50.3%, compared with 0.17% chance (Appendix D).

8 Discussion and Conclusion
The experiments show that text acquisition and speech access can diverge after an update.
Affirm implements speech-access repair as a detachable operator, combining a shared access parent with a smaller centered route field for query-specific variation.
This structure complements speech-pathway retraining when checkpoint immutability and one-pass speech inference matter.
On balanced synthetic speech, paired comparisons do not establish a clear Affirm advantage over SALSA or ReFT.
Operators fitted separately on full-scale PopQA differ in transfer to recorded SLUE questions with text passages, where ReFT and Affirm improve over No Repair while the tested SALSA variant regresses.
With the centered route field included, the expert parent gives higher block-4 TOFU scores and the direct parent gives higher SLUE point estimates.
The compact TOFU sweep favors early decoder blocks.
Knowledge can be acquired through the richest supervision route, and speech access can then be verified and repaired without modifying the acquired checkpoint.
Limitations
We study short-answer factual access after text-only updates, primarily with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B.
Our PopQA and TOFU evaluations measure access to facts included in text acquisition, with disjoint operator-training, development, and test groups.
They therefore characterize transfer of the repair across acquired facts rather than acquisition of unseen knowledge.
The paired text–speech generation gap operationalizes access but does not localize every acoustic or internal cause.
Our PopQA and TOFU experiments use synthetic English speech from one fixed voice.
Recorded SLUE extends the evaluation to human speech, but jointly changes the task, prompt, speakers, and acoustics.
It also supplies a text passage, so this evaluation measures no-refit behavior transfer rather than closed-book recall of newly acquired facts from human recordings.
The transfer result concerns the complete fitted operator and does not isolate the centered route field’s contribution.
Kimi-Audio provides a locked-test evaluation of the compact realization, while MiMo-Audio gives mixed development results.
The single-state intervention restricts adaptation capacity, and broader speech fine-tuning or an ASR cascade can attain higher accuracy when the deployment contract is relaxed.
Long-form generation, multilingual access, repeated checkpoint updates, and architecture-specific scaling remain future directions.
Ethical Considerations
Our experiments concern access to factual information through spoken queries.
Improved access can make voice interfaces more useful, but an intervention can also change a previously correct answer or expose incorrect information stored by the model.
Aggregate benchmark gains do not establish reliability for consequential applications.
The English synthetic-speech and recorded-speech evaluations leave performance across languages, accents, and user groups incompletely characterized.
Use of the models and speech datasets remains subject to their respective licenses and usage conditions.
AI assistance.
Generative-AI tools assisted with planning, experiment orchestration, code review, literature synthesis, analysis, and editing.
The authors verified the retained measurements against experiment artifacts and take responsibility for the paper’s text, code, results, and claims.

A.5 Decoding, metrics, uncertainty, and failures
Evaluation uses greedy decoding with at most 160 new tokens on PopQA and TOFU and at most 64 new tokens on SLUE.
ROUGE-L is the recall form of the longest-common-subsequence score against the reference answer.
Exact match lowercases text, strips punctuation and articles, normalizes whitespace, and then tests equality.
SLUE answer-span accuracy credits a generation when its normalized text contains the normalized short reference answer.
Retention divides the number of no-repair-correct items that remain exact under intervention by the total number of no-repair-correct items.
We report paired test differences with bootstrap standard errors (SEs), computed as the sample standard deviation of 10,000 group-bootstrap estimates with seed 3407.
Balanced PopQA resamples duplicate-question groups.
Full-scale PopQA resamples bound subject–question components for direct-parent and route-field contrasts, and retains the original relation-group resampling for expert-parent contrasts.
TOFU resamples authors, and SLUE resamples speakers.
Inferential statements and bolding use paired percentile-bootstrap bounds, computed separately from the SEs.
A difference is resolved when its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles have the same nonzero sign.
These SEs quantify test-sample uncertainty, while Table 13 reports sample standard deviations across training seeds.
All reported evaluations cover their stated sample counts with no failed generations.
A.6 Software and hardware
Qwen experiments use PyTorch 2.3.1, a Transformers 4.52.0 development snapshot, qwen-omni-utils 0.0.9, NumPy 2.0.2, and Python 3.9.23.
Model execution uses BF16 on NVIDIA A800-SXM4-80GB accelerators, while learned operator tensors and calibration statistics are retained in FP32.
Each training or generation run uses one accelerator.
The operational timing study in Section E reports standalone end-to-end wall time and peak allocated CUDA memory for its matched runs.

## 核心摘要

本文研究文本更新后语音访问修复：检查点只经文本问答获得事实，解码前最终提示位置的隐状态在文本与语音路线下可直接比较，文本答对而配对语音答错即构成待修复差距。修复时已获知识的检查点保持冻结，可拆卸算子只编辑解码器一个隐状态，推理为一次语音前向，不提供转写、配对文本状态或第二遍解码。跨模态界面修复仿射场先经教师强制答案交叉熵学习并冻结共享访问父项，再叠加查询特定路由场，路由坐标来自配对语音与文本隐状态的无答案拟合，阶段B只训练读出矩阵并按金色答案对数概率优势选择教师分布蒸馏。与全局共享转向和低秩表示干预相比，该结构把公共平移与近似正交的小幅查询修正分开，平衡PopQA诊断中共享父项范数为31.48而路由修正均值范数仅8.69。在对256个带文本段落的录制SLUE-SQA-5问题免重拟合迁移评测中，PopQA-20拟合的Affirm-Direct以单次语音前向获得ROUGE-L召回率0.5376，高于配对无修复基线的0.4435。Affirm-Direct训练可训练参数为0.46M，推理只编辑解码器第20块单个隐状态，部署为外部单状态算子，结论限于短答案事实访问和英语语音，录制迁移带有文本段落且任务形式已变。
