Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking
Admir Krnić\dmkcorrauthormark
Affiliation: DeepMark
Kosta Pavlović
Affiliation: DeepMark
Petar Nedić
Affiliation: DeepMark
Željko Bolević
Affiliation: DeepMark
Slavko Kovačević
Affiliation: DeepMark
Igor Djurović
Affiliation: DeepMark
Abstract
Neural watermarking systems are typically trained as tightly coupled embedder-detector pairs and implicitly assume static deployment. In real-world deployments, embedders and detectors are frequently updated and selectively decoupled for security and versioning purposes, which can break detection in previously embedded content and, more critically, increase false-positive rates on embedders that a given detector is intentionally not intended to recognize.
In this paper the concept of backward compatibility in zero-bit audio watermarking is formalized. A training framework is proposed that pairs a new detector with a sequence of frozen legacy embedders (its legacy chain), using a performance-weighted sampling strategy so that the detector retains accuracy across all earlier versions. This coupling, while necessary for backward compatibility, is shown to induce an embedder-collapse effect that catastrophically degrades the true negative rate (TNR) against out-of-chain embedders. To counteract this, a Angular Diversity Loss (ADL) is introduced that explicitly forces each new embedder to occupy a distinct region of the output space. The combined approach restores near-perfect TNR with no measurable cost to detection accuracy or perceptual audio quality.
1 Introduction
Recent advances in generative AI have substantially increased the realism and accessibility of synthetic audio content. State-of-the-art audio generation techniques are capable of producing high-quality speech and audio at scale [1]. As a result, concerns surrounding large-scale misinformation, fraud and reputational damage have intensified, alongside a broader erosion of trust in digital media.
Audio watermarking, a technique that embeds imperceptible signals at generation time and later recovers them to verify provenance, has emerged as a practical mechanism for attribution and misuse prevention. It is also becoming a legal requirement: the European Union’s AI Act (Article 50) mandates that providers of generative AI mark and detect artificially generated content, and its accompanying Code of Practice further requires that a replacement detector be backward compatible, detecting previously marked content with no loss of capability [2].
A line of recent deep-learning approaches jointly trains embedders and detectors, which we survey in Section 2. These systems all share an implicit assumption: an embedder and its detector are trained as a single matched pair and deployed together. In practice, watermarking systems must evolve, with new embedder-detector pairs introduced over time to harden against new attacks, improve quality, or reduce cost, while previously distributed content stays in circulation and must remain verifiable. Existing methods provide no explicit mechanism for an updated detector to keep recognizing watermarks from earlier embedders while still rejecting unrelated content, leading to invalidated watermarks or elevated false positives after updates. Re-embedding old content is often infeasible, and maintaining many detector versions at inference is complex and itself raises the false-positive rate.
We call the ordered sequence of legacy embedders E1,…,Ev−1E_{1},\ldots,E_{v-1}, that a newly trained detector DvD_{v} must continue to support, the legacy chain. A backward-compatible DvD_{v} must (i) detect watermarks from all embedders in its chain, (ii) reject unwatermarked audio, and (iii) reject watermarks from embedders outside the chain. Objective (iii) is not merely an accuracy concern; it is what makes a compromised version revocable. If an embedder EiE_{i} is leaked, an adversary can stamp arbitrary audio with its watermark. The response is to revoke EiE_{i}, dropping it from every future detector’s chain so that any detector issued after the leak rejects it outright. Without this, a single leak permanently invalidates the watermark, as every newer detector keeps accepting the forgeries. This motivates strict version separation rather than monotone forward acceptance.
In this work, we conduct the first systematic study of backward compatibility in neural audio watermarking. The following contributions are made:
• 
The backward-compatibility objective for zero-bit watermarking is formalized, and the legacy-chain abstraction is introduced together with its security implications.
• 
A training framework is proposed that combines a performance-weighted sampling scheme across frozen legacy embedders with ADL applied to the new embedder.
• 
The framework is evaluated across eight model versions that span architectural changes in both embedders (DenseNet, ViTMAE) and detectors (ResNet, AST), and the ADL is shown to substantially restore TNR against out-of-chain embedders with no measurable degradation in detection accuracy or audio quality.
• 
The same mechanism is shown to enable revocation: a leaked embedder can be dropped from the legacy chain and reliably rejected by detectors trained without it.
2 Related Work
Deep-learning-based audio watermarking jointly trains an embedder and a detector to balance imperceptibility and robustness. RobustDNN [3] introduced the basic recipe, WavMark [4], AudioSeal [5], Timbre Watermarking [6], and SilentCipher [7] subsequently improved robustness to common signal-processing attacks. VoiceMark [8] extends robustness to zero-shot voice-cloning attacks. All of these systems train and deploy embedders and detectors as fixed pairs and provide no explicit mechanism for cross-version compatibility.
Petrov et al. [9] study the coexistence and ensembling of independently trained watermarks. Their setting differs from ours in two important ways: embedder-detector pairs are trained independently (with no shared parameters or training signal), and there is no obligation for a later detector to recognize watermarks from an earlier one. As a consequence, their reported interference is minimal. We instead consider the coupled-training setting required for backward compatibility, and show that this coupling introduces failure modes that independent training does not exhibit.
Continual learning addresses sequential task acquisition without catastrophic forgetting [10], through methods such as Elastic Weight Consolidation [11], Learning without Forgetting [12], and Synaptic Intelligence [13]. These approaches assume a single, architecturally fixed model updated over time and therefore do not accommodate the architectural changes that accompany real-world watermarking updates.
3 Problem Formulation
We first review zero-bit watermarking and then formalize the backward-compatibility objective on top of it.
Zero-Bit Watermarking. Zero-bit watermarking aims to decide whether a digital signal contains a watermark. Given an input signal x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, an embedder EE produces a watermarked signal xw=E⁡(x)x_{w}=E(x), where the perturbation E⁡(x)−xE(x)-x is imperceptible. A detector DD then produces a real-valued detection score D⁡(xw)∈ℝD(x_{w})\in\mathbb{R}, with larger positive values indicating the presence of a watermark and smaller (negative) values indicating its absence. A binary decision is obtained by comparing the score against a threshold. The pair (E,D)(E,D) is typically trained end-to-end: the detector learns to distinguish watermarked from unwatermarked audio, while the embedder learns to introduce minimal perturbations that the detector can reliably detect.
Backward-Compatibility Objective. We associate every training run with a discrete version index vv. For the initial version, v=1v=1, a single pair (E1,D1)(E_{1},D_{1}) is trained end-to-end. For each subsequent version v>1v>1, a new embedder EvE_{v} is trained jointly with a new detector DvD_{v}. The legacy chain at version vv is the set of earlier embedders {Ei:i<v}\{E_{i}:i<v\}, minus a revocation set RR of embedders deliberately dropped (e.g. a leaked one). The legacy chain is kept frozen during training, and DvD_{v} is trained against it together with EvE_{v}, so its compatible (in-chain) set is {Ei:i≤v}∖R\{E_{i}:i\leq v\}\setminus R. Every other embedder is out-of-chain: future versions EjE_{j} with j>vj>v that did not yet exist, and any revoked Ei∈RE_{i}\in R.
Formally, the detector DvD_{v} at version vv must satisfy:
• 
DvD_{v} correctly detects watermarks produced by every embedder from set: {Ei:i≤v}∖R\{E_{i}:i\leq v\}\setminus R (high TPR within the chain).
• 
DvD_{v} rejects raw audio (high TNR on clean inputs).
• 
DvD_{v} rejects watermarks produced by any embedder outside its legacy chain (high TNR against out-of-chain embedders): both future versions EjE_{j} with j>vj>v that did not yet exist at training, and any embedder from RR.
The last objective we refer to as the version boundary: the line a detector holds between the in-chain embedders it accepts and the out-of-chain ones it rejects, whether future or revoked. This is what distinguishes backward compatibility from standard multi-embedder training: an out-of-chain embedder is not merely absent, it must be actively rejected, which is precisely what makes revoking a leaked embedder possible.
4 Method
Although backward compatibility is a general concern, we focus exclusively on zero-bit audio watermarking in this work. Our method has three components: a backward-compatible training setup, a performance-weighted sampling strategy that allocates training iterations across the legacy chain, and a diversity loss that prevents the new embedder from drifting toward its predecessors.
Backward-Compatible Training Setup. Embedders operate in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain. The watermark is added to the magnitude spectrogram within the [500,4000][500,4000] Hz embedding band and the time-domain signal is reconstructed via inverse STFT using the original phase. Detectors mirror the embedder, they compute the STFT and a mel spectrogram restricted to the same embedding band, then feed it to the detection network.
We extend the idea from SilentCipher [7] of enforcing a hard constraint on the maximum perceptual distortion, which lets us train with a detection-only loss. This distortion constraint drives all embedders to a consistent quality level (PESQ 4.3–4.5). Because every model then sits at essentially the same perceptual quality, we can compare models by detection accuracy alone.
For the detection objective we adopt the push loss introduced by AWARE [14], which augments the standard detection MSE with a term that widens the margin between watermarked and unwatermarked frames:
ℒpush=MSE⁡(y^,y)−λ⁡(1|y≥0|​∑y≥0y^+1|y<0|​∑y<0(−y^)),\mathcal{L}_{\text{push}}=\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{y},y)-\lambda\left(\frac{1}{|y\geq 0|}\sum_{y\geq 0}\hat{y}+\frac{1}{|y<0|}\sum_{y<0}(-\hat{y})\right),
(1)
where the second term pushes positive logits (watermarked frames) up and negative logits (unwatermarked frames) down, scaled by the push weight λ\lambda.
For version v=1v=1, training follows the standard procedure: a single embedder-detector pair is trained end-to-end with the push loss alone. For versions v>1v>1, two things change with respect to the v=1v=1 recipe. First, the new embedder EvE_{v} and detector DvD_{v} may use a different architecture from any previous version. This is by design, since real watermarking deployments evolve their architectures over time (Section 5). Second, the training objective is extended with the diversity loss introduced below, which is needed to keep the new embedder distinguishable from the legacy chain and thereby preserve the version boundary.
At each iteration, the detector DvD_{v} is trained on the output of a single embedder sampled from the full chain {E1,…,Ev}∖R\{E_{1},\ldots,E_{v}\}\setminus R, chosen by the performance-weighted sampling scheme described in the next paragraph. Because the legacy embedders are frozen and each embedder is drawn independently by this scheme, the training of DvD_{v} does not depend on the order of the embedders within the chain. The version index reflects only the order in which the embedders were created.
Performance-Weighted Sampling. Let’s denote with 𝒞\mathcal{C} the chain of embedders the detector is trained to detect {E1,…,Ev}∖R\{E_{1},\ldots,E_{v}\}\setminus R. At each training iteration we sample a single embedder Ei∈𝒞E_{i}\in\mathcal{C} according to a probability distribution 𝐩\mathbf{p} over 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and perform the forward and backward passes for the pair (Ei,Dv)(E_{i},D_{v}). The distribution 𝐩\mathbf{p} is initialized to uniform. After each validation step we obtain a per-embedder accuracy Ai∈[0,1]A_{i}\in[0,1] for every Ei∈𝒞E_{i}\in\mathcal{C} and update 𝐩\mathbf{p} via a temperature-controlled softmax [15] over negated accuracies:
pi=exp(−k⋅Ai)∑Ej∈𝒞exp(−k⋅Aj),p_{i}=\frac{\exp(-k\cdot A_{i})}{\sum_{E_{j}\in\mathcal{C}}\exp(-k\cdot A_{j})},
(2)
where k>0k>0 controls how aggressively the budget is shifted toward weaker embedders. The scheme adaptively emphasizes the embedders on which the detector currently performs worst. Based on our experiments k=8k=8 yielded the best results.
Embedder Collapse and the Need for a Diversity Loss. Performance-weighted sampling together with push loss is sufficient to obtain high TPR within the legacy chain, but it leaves the new embedder EvE_{v} entirely free to position its residual watermark anywhere in the signal space. The detector DvD_{v} is itself trained from scratch, what is fixed are the legacy embedders E1,…,Ev−1E_{1},\ldots,E_{v-1}, whose residuals are frozen throughout training while EvE_{v}’s residual is the only one free to move. The easiest path to a low detection loss is therefore for EvE_{v} to drift toward the frozen legacy embedders’ residual distributions, so that DvD_{v} can satisfy every in-chain pair with a single decision boundary. We refer to this failure mode as embedder collapse: the new embedder’s residual ends up implicitly close to those of the frozen legacy embedders, destroying the version boundary.
Angular Diversity Loss. We treat the mel spectrogram of the audio watermarked by each embedder as a “class” on the unit sphere and separate these classes with an additive angular margin, inspired by the margin formulation from ArcFace [16]. The setting, however, is not the fixed-identity classification ArcFace was designed for: an embedder has no identity vector to learn, and only EvE_{v} is trainable while the legacy embedders are frozen. The ADL adapts the angular margin to this setting with two changes.
First, we remove ArcFace’s learnable per-class prototypes. Let fi​(x)f_{i}(x) denote the batch mean of the mel feature of the audio watermarked by embedder EiE_{i}. Each class center is then the normalized batch mean μi=f¯i/∥f¯i∥\mu_{i}=\bar{f}_{i}/\lVert\bar{f}_{i}\rVert, recomputed on every forward pass. Second, since only EvE_{v} moves, the margin is applied only to the mel features of the new embedder’s output. We denote by cos⁡θi(b)=⟨fv​(xb),μi⟩\cos\theta_{i}^{(b)}=\langle f_{v}(x_{b}),\mu_{i}\rangle the cosine similarity between mel features of the sample bb produced by the new embedder and class center ii. Let 𝒩v\mathcal{N}_{v} be the set of class centers from which EvE_{v} is repelled, typically 𝒩v\mathcal{N}_{v} contains all predecessors {Ei:i<v}\{E_{i}:i<v\}, with the option of removing revoked embedders, as in our revocation experiments. The loss is the additive-margin cross-entropy that pulls every sample toward its own class vv:
ℒdiv=−1B∑bloges​cos⁡(θv(b)+m)es​cos⁡(θv(b)+m)+∑i∈𝒩vescosθi(b).\mathcal{L}_{\text{div}}=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}\log\frac{e^{s\cos(\theta_{v}^{(b)}+m)}}{e^{s\cos(\theta_{v}^{(b)}+m)}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}_{v}}e^{s\cos\theta_{i}^{(b)}}}.
(3)
The margin mm pushes each sample of EvE_{v} at least mm radians away from every class center in 𝒩v\mathcal{N}_{v}, while the scale ss controls the softmax sharpness.
The proposed loss is essential for preserving the separation between model versions. Without it, the embedding spaces of the legacy and new embedders collapses, eliminating the intended version boundary. The mel spectrogram is a robust representation in which perceptually similar signals produce very similar mel features, so a strong margin or sharp scale would destabilize training. This is why weak parameters (m=0.1m=0.1, s=8s=8) suffice: the loss still enforces the separation, but needs only a gentle push.
Gradient Normalization. Combining ℒpush\mathcal{L}_{\text{push}} and ℒdiv\mathcal{L}_{\text{div}} through a fixed scalar weighting is brittle: the two losses operate on very different scales so one term tends to dominate the gradient. We instead balance them with a per-step gradient-norm scaling inspired by GradNorm [17].
At each step we compute the per-loss gradients with respect to the new embedder’s parameters, 𝐠push=∇ℒpush\mathbf{g}_{\text{push}}=\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\text{push}} and 𝐠div=∇ℒdiv\mathbf{g}_{\text{div}}=\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\text{div}}, and their L2L_{2} norms. We then rescale both to a common target norm n¯=12​(∥𝐠push∥+∥𝐠div∥)\bar{n}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\lVert\mathbf{g}_{\text{push}}\rVert+\lVert\mathbf{g}_{\text{div}}\rVert\right), and sum the result:
𝐠=n¯∥𝐠push∥+ϵ​𝐠push+n¯∥𝐠div∥+ϵ​𝐠div.\mathbf{g}=\frac{\bar{n}}{\lVert\mathbf{g}_{\text{push}}\rVert+\epsilon}\,\mathbf{g}_{\text{push}}+\frac{\bar{n}}{\lVert\mathbf{g}_{\text{div}}\rVert+\epsilon}\,\mathbf{g}_{\text{div}}.

Dividing each gradient by its own norm removes raw magnitude so both losses count equally, while the shared factor n¯\bar{n} rescales them to a common, representative size instead of unit norm.
5 Experimental Setup
This section describes the data, model architectures and evaluation protocol.
Dataset. Training data is drawn from the Mozilla Common Voice corpus [18], with all training audio resampled to 44.1 kHz during preprocessing. The test set consists of audio files sampled from three corpora, LibriSpeech [19], LJSpeech [20], and Mozilla Common Voice, and spans a range of native sampling rates, reflecting a realistic and heterogeneous evaluation condition.
Model Architectures. We evaluate two model families with complementary inductive biases: a convolutional family (DenseNet [21] embedder with a ResNet [22] detector) and a Transformer family (ViTMAE [23, 24] embedder with an AST [25] detector). Each architecture uses a fixed template, across versions we vary only its activation function and its depth, holding every other hyperparameter (widths, kernel sizes, attention heads, feature dimensions) constant. The depth knob is specific to each architecture: dense blocks for DenseNet, encoder/decoder layers for ViTMAE, residual stacks for ResNet, and encoder layers for AST. Modeling realistic architectural drift. We train a sequence of eight versions (v1v_{1} to v8v_{8}), one model, i.e. one embedder-detector pair, per version. Over time, practitioners swap in newer activation functions, enlarge networks, and eventually replace entire architecture families with newer ones. Our version sequence is designed to mimic this trajectory. Concretely, we choose architectures along two orthogonal axes:
1. 
Activation rotation. Within a fixed embedder/detector size, we rotate the activation function in the order in which it became standard in the deep-learning literature: ReLU [26] first, then Swish [27], then GELU [28]. This mimics a team that periodically swaps the activation function for a more recent one without otherwise changing the network.
2. 
Capacity step-ups. After the activation rotation has cycled through ReLU/Swish/GELU at the original size, we step up the network’s capacity (more dense blocks / more encoder-decoder layers) while keeping the most recent activation. This mimics a team that, after exhausting easy activation upgrades, decides to scale the model.
The same two-axis schedule is applied first to the convolutional family (v1v_{1}–v4v_{4}) and then repeated on the Transformer family (v5v_{5}–v8v_{8}), since Transformer-based audio models entered the field later than convolutional ones. The transition from v4v_{4} to v5v_{5} simulates the discrete jump that occurs when a deployment switches to a fundamentally newer architecture family rather than enlarging the existing one.
Training Details. All models are trained with Adam at a learning rate of 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, decayed by an exponential schedule (γ=0.95\gamma=0.95), with a batch size of 128128 and gradient-norm clipping at 0.10.1.
Evaluation Metrics. For each detector DvD_{v} we measure: TPR on in-chain pairs, TNR on unwatermarked audio and on out-of-chain pairs, respectively.
Results are presented as accuracy matrices, evaluated on the test set described above. A binary decision requires a confidence threshold τ\tau. We report two experiments: a base setup with performance-weighted sampling and the detection loss, and the full method that adds the ADL on top. Both use all eight versions with no revocation (R=∅R=\emptyset). Revocation is evaluated separately.

Revocation. Revoking a leaked embedder EiE_{i} means dropping it from every future detector’s legacy chain, which is considered successful if a detector trained without EiE_{i} still rejects it. Starting from the chain of versions v1v_{1} to v7v_{7}, we revoke a single embedder, either a convolutional-family one (v3v_{3}) or a transformer-family one (v5v_{5}), and for each retrain a new embedder–detector pair on the six surviving versions (v1v_{1} to v7v_{7} excluding the revoked one) under three conditions: (i) the baseline with no diversity loss, (ii) the diversity loss with EiE_{i} unused and (iii) the diversity loss with EiE_{i} added to the diversity term only (forcing the new embedder to differ from it) while kept out of the detection loss, so the detector is never trained to accept it. Table 3 reports TNR against EiE_{i}. The baseline barely rejects the revoked embedder, and merely omitting it from a diversity-trained chain is unreliable. Only when EiE_{i} is pushed away by the diversity loss does the new embedder produce distinct residuals, and the detector rejects the revoked embedder fully in both families.
Third-Party Watermarks. In production, our detectors must not accept third-party watermarks, and our watermarked content must not be accepted by third-party detectors. We tested both directions against the publicly released zero-bit AudioSeal model [5], using all eight pair of models trained with the full method: (i) the audio watermarked by each of our embedders is passed to the AudioSeal detector, and (ii) the audio watermarked by the AudioSeal embedder is passed to each of our detectors. Because AudioSeal operates at 16 kHz, audio is resampled to 16 kHz at its input.
We use AudioSeal’s default decision threshold of 0.50.5. For every one of the eight versions, and in both directions, not a single file is detected, so TNR is 100%100\% for every pair. This agrees with the negligible interference that Petrov et al. [9] report for independently trained watermarks.
7 Robustness Analysis
Maximizing robustness to signal-processing and codec attacks is out of scope, and none of our models are trained with attack augmentation. We ask a narrower question: does backward compatibility itself survive distortion? A deployed watermark is transmitted and edited before detection, so a framework that held only on clean audio would be of little practical use. We therefore test, rather than optimize for, robustness, re-running the evaluation under the DeepMark benchmark [29]. 8 Conclusion
We presented the first systematic study of backward compatibility in zero-bit deep-learning audio watermarking. We formalized the backward-compatibility objective via the legacy-chain abstraction, identified the embedder-collapse failure mode that breaks version boundaries when a new detector is trained against frozen legacy embedders, and proposed a training framework that combines performance-weighted sampling and push loss together with ADL balanced by gradient normalization. Across eight versions and two architecture families, the method restores out-of-chain TNR without degrading within-chain detection or perceptual quality, and the restored version boundary holds under distortion. The same mechanism enables revocation: a leaked embedder dropped from the chain is reliably rejected by detectors trained without it. We see the legacy chain as a useful abstraction for future watermarking systems that must evolve under deployment constraints, and we leave robustness under adversarial attack and multibit extensions to future work.

## 核心摘要
零比特音频水印以原始波形为输入，输出检测分数经阈值得到二值判定，难点在于嵌入器与检测器更新后旧内容仍要可验，而泄露版本还要可撤销。论文把新检测器必须支持的旧嵌入器集合定义为遗留链，要求对链内嵌入器高检出率，对干净音频与链外嵌入器高正确拒绝率，撤销的嵌入器则移出遗留链。新检测器在冻结的遗留嵌入器与可训练的新嵌入器组成的集合上训练，每轮按性能加权采样单个嵌入器的输出进行前向与反向传播，采样概率向当前准确率低的嵌入器倾斜，使检测器覆盖整条链。采样得到的水印与非水印帧先经推送损失扩大间隔，得到的新旧残差再经角多样性损失约束新嵌入器残差远离旧残差，两项对新嵌入器参数的梯度按各自范数归一到共同尺度后相加再更新参数。为兼容而耦合训练不同于独立训练水印共存，耦合在无约束时会诱发新嵌入器向旧残差靠拢，导致版本边界坍缩。在固定阈值0.99、无撤销的8版本序列评测设置下，相对无多样性损失的基线设置，完整方法使链外正确拒绝率（TNR）均值从11.3%上升到99.98%。在固定阈值0.99、无撤销的8版本序列评测设置下，完整方法链内检出率（TPR）维持在99.3%至100%均值99.9%，与基线均值99.8%相当。结论适用于零比特、短时傅里叶变换幅度嵌入与固定阈值的设置，多比特扩展与对抗攻击下的表现尚未验证，原文未披露训练、推理或部署成本。

Reference-Guided Turn-Taking Style Transfer 
for Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models
Yuxuan Chen
Yang Xiao
Jack Sun
Chak Sun
Brick Li
Sam
††thanks: 
†Corresponding author.
Abstract
Full-duplex spoken language models decide at every frame whether to take
the floor, defining a conversational personality — yet each set of weights
encodes exactly one, which human speakers bracket rather than share.
Existing controls mostly act from outside; none identifies the quantity that
sets how much the model speaks.
We identify it: a single late-layer residual-stream direction, the
initiative vector, extracted from the model’s own conversations
without training or annotation. The same direction reads the decision,
anticipating onsets up to 800 ms ahead, and shifts it: scaled during
generation, it moves speech ratio from 6–12% to 42–61% (no steering:
21–30%), consistently across conversations, weights, and corpora.
A short reference recording suffices to transfer a speaker’s turn-taking
style to the model, and the transfer is reference-specific: swapping in
another speaker’s reference worsens the match in 93–98% of cases, whereas the
best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no steering.
Turn-taking style is not frozen into the weights but a direction that can
be read, shifted, and calibrated per person.
Audio examples are available at
https://elpsykongloo.github.io/initiative-vector/.
Index Terms: Conversational Style Cloning, Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models, Conversational Dynamics
††address: 
1 The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
2 The University of Melbourne  3 Lulula
yuxuanchen5@link.cuhk.edu.cn, 
yang.xiao.1@student.unimelb.edu.au
jack@lulula.ai, 
chak@lulula.ai, 
brick@lulula.ai, 
sam@lulula.ai
1 Introduction
Figure 1: The initiative vector: extracted from the model’s own conversations,
read and written at L30. Top: among frames where the model has been silent,
the residual is averaged over frames followed by an onset within 800 ms
(𝝁+\boldsymbol{\mu}_{+}) and over frames that stay silent
(𝝁−\boldsymbol{\mu}_{-}); their normalized difference is 𝐮\mathbf{u}
(Eq. 1), with no training or annotation. Bottom: the projection
𝐡⋅𝐮\mathbf{h}\cdot\mathbf{u} rises before the model takes the floor, and adding
α​s​𝐮\alpha s\mathbf{u} at every frame sets how much it speaks.
Figure 2: The decision is linearly readable, deepest, and beyond both speakers’
timing. (a) Held-out AUC of a class-mean direction refitted at each of the 32
residual positions (position kk is the output of block kk); directions are
fitted on 100 conversations and evaluated on 500 held-out conversations per
weight. Taking the floor is strongest at the deepest positions on all three
weights (L31, 400 ms: 0.968 / 0.898 / 0.966), whereas yielding peaks
mid-network and decays (L26 / L22 / L19): taking and yielding the floor are
not the same axis at the same depth. “Speaking now” is about 0.99 from L0,
i.e., present in the input. The vertical line marks L30, the injection
site. (b) Per-conversation AUC gain of the fixed L30
direction over a timing baseline that sees both speakers
(Sec. 3): +0.115+0.115 / +0.185+0.185 / +0.172+0.172, positive on 449 / 497
/ 462 of 500 conversations. Circles are means over conversations.
Spoken language models are converging toward full-duplex
interaction [1, 2, 3],
listening while speaking and deciding at every frame whether to take the
floor rather than waiting for an explicit
endpoint [4, 5].
Collectively, this frame-level initiative defines a conversational
personality — eager or patient, interruptive or
deferential [6]
— and
different applications demand different ones: a tutoring agent should lead;
a companion should listen. Yet each set of weights encodes exactly one such
personality, fixed at training time [7], and no
default fits everybody: human speakers differ too much to share a
style [8, 9, 10]
and fall on both sides of whichever one a checkpoint encodes. A uniform
correction therefore
helps one group and hurts the other — the best we find is indistinguishable
from leaving the model alone (Sec. 4). What each user needs
is personal [11].
Most existing controls engineer turn-taking from the outside. Training-based
methods write a single style into the weights, from thousands of hours of
style-labeled data [12, 13] or from interactivity
rewards [14, 15, 16]: one
personality per checkpoint, bounded by the label set and prone to reward
hacking when timing itself is the reward. Instruction-based control avoids
retraining but is not reliably obeyed — on
Instruct-FD [17] the best system follows timing
instructions only 64.4% of the time. Turn-taking
predictors [5, 18, 19] read the
relevant signal but cannot act on the model. Activation steering acts on the
model
itself [20, 21, 22],
yet perception vectors set a binary listen/speak state at a fixed dose on one
checkpoint: a fix for interruption errors, not a variable to be set per person.
Whether a full-duplex spoken language model takes the floor is usually
treated as an emergent property of its next-token distribution, decodable
from internal states [23] but never set by degree. A
single direction in the residual stream, the initiative vector,
linearly encodes the model’s propensity to
speak [24, 25]; scaling the residual along
that direction during generation controls that propensity. Because the
direction is computed from the model’s own conversations, contrasting frames
that precede its speech onsets with frames where it stays
silent [26], each model yields its own vector under an
identical procedure (Fig. 1).
The direction reads the decision to take the floor: its projection
anticipates the model’s speech onsets well before they occur, above a
baseline built from both speakers’ timing, and remains
predictive even when no recent text is present (Fig. 2b).
It also shifts the decision: as the steering dose increases, the model’s
speech ratio rises monotonically, consistently
across conversations, weights, and corpora (Fig. 3). Refitting
such contrasts at every layer locates the computation: whether the model is
currently speaking is decodable
from the first layer, evidence for yielding the floor peaks in earlier
layers and then fades, and evidence for taking the floor strengthens
toward the final layer (Fig. 2a). The model thus decides to take
the floor late in
the network, well after its speaking state is available and at a
different depth from its decision to yield. Calibrated against a short
reference recording, the direction transfers a speaker’s turn-taking
style, and the transfer is reference-specific: neither a uniform dose nor
another speaker’s reference matches as well (Fig. 4).
Our contributions are as follows:
1. 
Initiative vectors. A single residual-stream direction,
extracted without training or annotation, both anticipates the model’s onsets
and sets how much it speaks — across weights and corpora.
2. 
Taking the floor is a late-stage computation, peaking in the
final layers, with the speaking state decodable in the first and yield
evidence peaking between them.
3. 
Reference-guided style transfer. A single short recording
suffices to transfer a speaker’s turn-taking style, with no retraining;
swapping in another speaker’s reference worsens the match in 93–98% of
cases.
2 Method
Figure 3: Adding the direction changes behavior, gradedly and on a second
corpus. (a) Speech ratio against steering dose, in units of each weight’s
listen-to-speak swing ss; 500 conversations per weight, and 500 CANDOR
segments with the same direction and scale. (b) Paired per-conversation
difference between +a+a and −a-a under the same input and seed; random
directions are norm-matched and applied at the same displacement; black bars:
95% intervals over conversations.
Figure 4: One dose per speaker transfers that speaker’s turn-taking style,
across three weights, 550 evaluation targets and 568 held-out references.
Distance (Eq. 3) is in reference SD and averaged over three
seeds; each reference’s dose is selected on 100 development targets only,
never on the targets used here. (a) Increase in distance when a reference is
steered with a dose kk grid steps away from its own. (b) Model speech ratio
after calibration, by decile of reference speech ratio. (c) Gain over the
best uniform dose against the number of conversations used to select each
dose (300 targets; shading: 95% interval). (d) Distance under each held-out
reference’s own dose against distance under the best uniform dose (568
references per weight).
Extraction. Let 𝐡t\mathbf{h}_{t} be the residual stream at frame tt
and position L30, the output of block 30 (zero-indexed) of the model’s
32-block temporal transformer. From the model’s own unsteered conversations we take the frames
at which it has been silent, and label a frame positive if the model starts
speaking within the next 800 ms and negative if it stays silent. With class
means 𝝁+\boldsymbol{\mu}_{+} and 𝝁−\boldsymbol{\mu}_{-}, the initiative
vector is
𝐮=(𝝁+−𝝁−)/∥𝝁+−𝝁−∥.\mathbf{u}=(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{+}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{-})\,/\,\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}_{+}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{-}\rVert.
(1)
The labels are the model’s own subsequent behavior, so extraction needs
neither training nor annotation.
Reading and writing. The projection ⟨𝐡t,𝐮⟩\langle\mathbf{h}_{t},\mathbf{u}\rangle
reads the model’s propensity to take the floor. Steering writes along the same
direction at every frame during generation,
𝐡t←𝐡t+α​s​𝐮,\mathbf{h}_{t}\leftarrow\mathbf{h}_{t}+\alpha\,s\,\mathbf{u},
(2)
where ss is the listen-to-speak swing of the projection, the gap between its
mean while the model speaks and while only the partner speaks, so that the
dose α\alpha is comparable across weights. L30 is the deepest position whose
perturbation is still processed by a full transformer block and written into
that block’s key–value cache; the shift therefore persists in the context
that later frames attend to.
Depth profile. To locate the decision, a class-mean contrast of the
same form is refitted at each of the 32 positions for four targets, each
scored by held-out AUC: taking the floor within 400 or 800 ms of a frame at
which both speakers are silent, being silent 800 ms after a frame of
sustained speech (yielding), and the current speaking state.
Reference-guided transfer. A speaker is summarized by three
descriptors of a five-minute reference recording: speech ratio, overlap
onsets per minute of partner speech, and response probability, the share of
partner turn ends (≥400{\geq}400 ms of partner silence) followed within 3 s by
the speaker’s onset before the partner resumes, with turn ends during the
speaker’s own speech kept in the denominator. With σk\sigma_{k} the standard
deviation of descriptor kk over training references, descriptors
𝐛\mathbf{b} and a reference 𝐫\mathbf{r} are compared by
d⁡(𝐛,𝐫)=(13​∑k=13(bk−rkσk)2)1/2.d(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{r})=\Big(\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k=1}^{3}\Big(\frac{b_{k}-r_{k}}{\sigma_{k}}\Big)^{2}\Big)^{1/2}.
(3)
The speaker’s dose minimizes the mean of d​(𝐛t​(α),𝐫)d(\mathbf{b}_{t}(\alpha),\mathbf{r})
over development targets tt, with 𝐛t​(α)\mathbf{b}_{t}(\alpha) the steered model’s
descriptors on tt, and is then applied unchanged to new conversations. Since
𝐛t​(α)\mathbf{b}_{t}(\alpha) does not depend on the speaker, it is computed once
per weight, and a new speaker is calibrated from the recording alone, without
running the model.
3 Experimental Setup
Models and conversations. We study three full-duplex weights that
share the Moshi architecture [1]: Moshika (base),
Moshika-RL, further aligned for interactivity [15], and
PersonaPlex [7], all operating on 80 ms frames.
Each model hears one side of a dyadic Seamless Interaction
recording [27] as its user stream (64 s, after
3 s of silence) and generates the other side. Directions and baselines are fitted on 100 conversations and evaluated on a
fixed set of 500 held-out conversations per weight. The same directions
and scale are applied, without refitting, to 500 CANDOR
segments [28]. Doses are
{−2​a,−a,0,a,2​a}\{-2a,-a,0,a,2a\} with a=0.125a=0.125 (Moshika, PersonaPlex) or 0.250.25
(Moshika-RL).
Readout. AUC is computed per conversation and averaged. The baseline,
trained on the same 100 conversations, is a logistic regression on timing
alone: recent activity of both speakers, the time since each last spoke,
activity rates, and the time since the model’s last text token.
Transfer. References are five-minute windows of Seamless
Interaction speakers from naturalistic and improvised conversations, with
descriptors extracted by Silero
VAD11
 1
 https://github.com/snakers4/silero-vad. Standard
deviations come from 120 training references, and the best uniform dose is
selected for them on 100 development targets; each individual dose uses the
same 100 targets alone, and transfer is evaluated on 550 targets for 568
held-out references, averaged over three seeds. Baselines are no steering and
the best uniform dose; the dose that is best in hindsight for each reference
serves as the upper bound. Intervals are 95% two-way bootstrap intervals over
targets and references (5,000 resamples, stratified by conversation type,
doses fixed).
4 Results
The direction reads the decision ahead of time. The fixed L30
projection separates frames followed by an onset within 800 ms from continued
silence with AUC 0.818, 0.830 and 0.898 on Moshika, Moshika-RL and
PersonaPlex (Fig. 2b). The timing baseline, which sees both
speakers, reaches 0.703, 0.646 and 0.725; the direction adds +0.115+0.115,
+0.185+0.185 and +0.172+0.172 and is ahead on 449, 497 and 462 of 500 conversations.
The gain does not come from the text stream: on frames with no recent text
token the AUC stays at 0.806, 0.823 and 0.893, at most 0.012 below the full
set.
Taking and yielding the floor peak at different depths. Across the
32 positions (Fig. 2a), onset evidence is strongest at the
deepest ones on all three weights (0.968, 0.898 and 0.966 at L31 for
onsets within 400 ms), whereas evidence for yielding the floor peaks
mid-network (L26, L22, L19) and then fades. Taking and yielding the floor are
thus separate axes at different depths. The speaking state is decodable at
about 0.99 from L0: it is present in the input rather than computed. The
model thus decides to take the floor late in the network.
Adding the direction sets how much the model speaks. Speech ratio
rises monotonically with the dose on all three weights, from 6–12% at −2​a-2a
to 42–61% at +2​a+2a, against 21–30% without steering
(Fig. 3a), and overlap onsets and response probability move in
the same direction. Under the same input and seed, moving from −a-a to
+a+a raises it by 20.1, 27.4 and 14.1 points, with increases on 480, 497 and
408 of 500 conversations (Fig. 3b). The effect belongs to the
direction rather than to the size of the perturbation: three norm-matched
random directions at the same displacement change speech ratio by at most
5.6 points. The same direction and scale carry over to CANDOR without
refitting (+20.3+20.3, +33.9+33.9 and +6.8+6.8 points).
One dose per speaker transfers that speaker’s style. On average,
the distance to a reference is smallest at its own dose on all three weights
(Fig. 4a). Swapping in another held-out reference’s dose,
whenever it differs, worsens the match in 92.7, 98.0 and 95.6% of cases,
and on average for 568, 568 and 566 of the 568 references. After calibration, the model’s speech ratio follows its reference across
deciles (Spearman 0.69, 0.60, 0.78; Fig. 4b).
The gain comes from personalization itself. References fall on both
sides of every model’s default (Fig. 4b), so no single
setting fits them: the best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no
steering on every weight, with all 95% intervals including zero. The per-speaker dose improves on it by 0.129, 0.208 and 0.164 reference SD,
93.1, 99.5 and 98.1% of the gain of the dose that is best in hindsight, and
it is strictly closer for 317/317, 257/257 and 270/289 of the
references whose dose differs from the uniform one (Fig. 4d).
Ten development conversations per weight already reach the plateau of this
gain (Fig. 4c). The dose a speaker needs is
also consistent across weights: the grid levels selected for the same
held-out reference correlate at Spearman ρ=0.81\rho=0.81 (Moshika–RL), 0.77
(Moshika–PersonaPlex) and 0.70 (RL–PersonaPlex), so calibration captures a
property of the speaker rather than of one checkpoint.
5 Conclusion
A full-duplex model’s turn-taking style need not be fixed at training time. A single late-layer direction, extracted from the model’s own
conversations without training or annotation, anticipates when the model will
take the floor, sets how much it speaks across weights and corpora, and,
from a single short recording, transfers an individual speaker’s style
without retraining. The benefit comes from personalization itself: turn-taking becomes a
setting that can be read, shifted, and calibrated per person.
6 Compliance with Ethical Standards
This study was conducted retrospectively using human subject data made
available for research by the Seamless
Interaction [27] and CANDOR [28]
corpora. Ethical approval was not required as confirmed by the licenses
attached with the data.

## 核心摘要
全双工语音语言模型需逐帧决定收听还是发声，累积成急切或耐心的会话风格，难点是每套权重只固定一种风格而不同说话人分布在其两侧，统一校正难以兼顾。论文从模型自身无干预对话中取静默帧，按八百毫秒内是否起始发声分成两类，以两类残差均值之差的归一化方向作为主动向量，无需训练与标注，在第三十个残差位置读出投影预判倾向，并在生成每帧沿该方向按听说摆动归一化剂量平移残差，经后块键值缓存持续影响后续帧。说话人由五分钟参考录音的说话占比、重叠起始率与回应概率表示，先一次性算好各剂量下操纵模型的描述子，再为新说话人在开发目标上选择平均标准化距离最小的剂量直接套用，无需再运行模型。在每权重500组留存对话上，固定该方向预测800ms内起始发声的AUC为0.818、0.830和0.898，高于只看双人计时的基线在同样留存对话上的0.703、0.646和0.725。在每权重500组对话上，剂量从-2a到+2a使说话占比从6-12%单调升至42-61%，高于无操纵时在同样对话上的21-30%。在550个评估目标和568个留存参考上，与使用自身参考剂量相比，换用他人不同剂量使平均标准化距离增大的情形占92.7%、98.0%和95.6%，方向为变差。结论限于Moshi架构80ms帧的三权重与Seamless Interaction及CANDOR验证，未验证其他架构与更长参考外推，原文未披露训练、推理或部署成本。

HRTF Upsampling and Personalization via Neural Operators 
Meenakshi Krishnan\sthanksWork done while at Dolby Laboratories. mkrishn9@umd.edu
You Zhang
Ramani Duraiswami
C. Phillip Brown
Abstract
Head-related transfer function (HRTF) spatial upsampling from sparse measurements is a fundamental challenge in personalized binaural audio. We formulate HRTF upsampling as an operator learning problem and introduce SPARO, a neural operator that maps sparse measurements at a set of spatial directions to the HRTF field, a continuous representation that can be queried at arbitrary positions. SPARO projects the measurements onto a learned set of spherical latent modes, processes the latent modes with Transformer blocks, and decodes the resulting representations at query directions. On SONICOM, using the LAP24 measurement configuration, SPARO attains the best log-spectral distortion (LSD) and interaural level difference (ILD) error at every sparsity level from 3 to 100 measurements (18% lower LSD and 43% lower ILD error than the strongest baseline at 100 measurements) while remaining competitive in interaural time difference (ITD) error. It reconstructs a dense HRTF 1515–373×373\times faster than the leading neural-field method RANF. We further validate the approach on HUTUBS, demonstrating its effectiveness across HRTF datasets.
Index Terms: Head-related transfer function, spatial audio, neural operator, upsampling, personalization
††address: 1University of Maryland, College Park    2Dolby Laboratories, Inc.
1 Introduction
Personalized spatial audio rendering for virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR) requires head-related transfer functions (HRTFs), which capture the direction-dependent acoustic filtering of a listener’s head, torso, and pinnae. As these filtering effects are highly anatomy-specific, the use of non-individualized HRTFs measurably degrades sound localization accuracy and perceptual attributes such as externalization and immersion [1, 2]. Personalized HRTFs are also relevant for hearing assistive devices (including hearing aids and cochlear implant processors) where accurate spatial rendering can improve speech intelligibility in multi-talker environments [3].
While acoustic measurement remains the gold standard for individual HRTFs, densely sampled datasets typically require impulse responses at hundreds of spatial directions, for example, SONICOM [4], CIPIC [5], and ARI [6] contain 793, 1250, and 1550 measured directions, respectively. Such acquisition is costly and impractical at scale, while practical rendering may additionally require HRTFs at arbitrary directions outside the measurement grid.
HRTF spatial upsampling addresses this bottleneck by estimating dense HRTFs from a sparse set of individual measurements [7, 8].
Figure 1: HRTF upsampling as operator learning. SPARO learns
the upsampling operator ℱ\mathcal{F} that generalizes across listeners and can be queried at arbitrary directions to produce the HRTF field.
Figure 2: Architecture for HRTF upsampling. Sparse HRTF observations are embedded by the branch projector and aggregated into a fixed set of learned spherical modes according to their angular similarity to mode centers on S2S^{2}. Transformer blocks model interactions entirely in the latent mode space. At arbitrary query directions, the transformed modes are interpolated using the same spherical mode geometry, and a final MLP produces the output HRTF.
Algorithmic upsampling methods such as barycentric interpolation and spherical harmonic decomposition [9, 10, 11] are effective when measurements are sufficiently dense, but degrade severely under high sparsity [12, 13]. Learning-based approaches have shown strong performance for HRTF upsampling from sparse measurements [7, 14]. In particular, neural field (NF) methods represent HRTFs as a function of sound source direction conditioned on subject-specific parameters, enabling a pre-trained generic model to be adapted to new subjects from sparse measurements [12, 15, 16, 17]. The Retrieval-Augmented Neural Field (RANF) [13], the winning system of Task 2 of the Listener Acoustic Personalization (LAP24) challenge [7], further augments this with similar-subject retrieval, achieving state-of-the-art performance in log-spectral distortion (LSD), interaural level difference (ILD) and interaural time difference (ITD) errors across sparsity levels of 3 to 100 measurements.
Neural-field approaches provide a flexible continuous representation of HRTFs [15], where personalization typically involves optimizing subject-specific representations or parameters from the available measurements. Many methods thus use per-subject iterative adaptation at inference, for example by optimizing low-rank subject-specific parameters [12, 13]. In this formulation, the sparse measurements primarily serve to identify a listener-specific field. Rather than representing each listener’s HRTF as a separate field, an alternative is to learn a single upsampling operator that maps sparse HRTF measurements to the corresponding HRTF field across listeners.
In general, operator learning methods aim to learn mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces, with the functions represented in practice by their values on finite sets of sample locations [18, 19]. They offer a discretization-invariant representation that is independent of the input-output dimensions, and prior architectures [20, 21] decouple input and output discretizations through a fixed latent representation. In this paper, we learn a shared upsampling operator across individuals that maps sparse measurements to the HRTF at arbitrary query directions, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
We therefore introduce SPARO, a sparse-to-dense neural operator for HRTF spatial upsampling. SPARO learns a direct mapping from sparse HRTF observations at measured directions to the HRTF field at arbitrary query directions through a learned spherical mode representation that decouples observation and prediction locations. SPARO couples the input and output mappings through a shared learned geometry on the sphere S2S^{2}: sparse observations are projected onto spherical latent modes, the resulting mode representations are transformed globally, and the learned mode geometry is used to interpolate the transformed representation at arbitrary query directions. We predict HRTF log-magnitude and ITD on SONICOM from sparse measurements, and evaluate under the LAP24 protocol [7]. SPARO achieves the lowest error on LSD and ILD at all sparsity levels and is competitive on ITD, pointing to operator learning as a promising direction for personalized spatial audio.
2 Methods
2.1 Preliminary and Notations: HRTF Upsampling
For subject ss, ear c∈{L,R}c\in\{L,R\}, and source direction
𝐝=(θ,ϕ)\mathbf{d}=(\theta,\phi) with azimuth θ∈[0,2​π)\theta\in[0,2\pi), and elevation ϕ∈[−π/2,π/2]\phi\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2], the HRTF is:
Hsc​(f,𝐝)=Pearc​(f,𝐝)Pfree​(f),H_{s}^{c}(f,\mathbf{d})=\frac{P_{\text{ear}}^{c}(f,\mathbf{d})}{P_{\mathrm{free}}(f)},
(1)
where PearcP_{\mathrm{ear}}^{c} is the sound pressure at the blocked ear-canal
entrance, PfreeP_{\mathrm{free}} is the free-field pressure at the head
center [22, 23], and ff denotes frequency. The HRTF is thus a complex-valued transfer function
encoding both magnitude and phase information as a function of frequency and
source direction. Its time-domain counterpart is the head-related impulse response
(HRIR).
Let 𝐇sc​(𝐝)∈ℂF\mathbf{H}_{s}^{c}(\mathbf{d})\in\mathbb{C}^{F} denote the HRTF at FF
frequency bins, and let 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒮\mathcal{S}
denote a dense spatial grid and the training subjects, respectively.
For a test subject s¯∉𝒮\bar{s}\notin\mathcal{S}, HRTFs are available only on a
sparse set 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}; the goal is to estimate
𝐇s¯c​(𝐝)\mathbf{H}_{\bar{s}}^{c}(\mathbf{d}) for all 𝐝∈𝒟\mathbf{d}\in\mathcal{D}.
Rather than predict the full complex spectrum, HRTF upsampling methods [12, 13, 24] often model log-magnitude
and ITD separately. HRTF magnitude carries direction-dependent spectral
cues important for elevation and front–back localization, while ITD and ILD
provide dominant binaural cues for horizontal localization
[25, 26]. Minimum-phase HRIRs are reconstructed from the predicted magnitudes and the predicted ITD applied as a fractional delay [27].
2.2 Formulating HRTF Upsampling as Operator Learning
Let 𝒟′={𝐝i′}i=1M\mathcal{D}^{\prime}=\{\mathbf{d}_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i=1}^{M} denote the set of MM
sparse measurement directions. SPARO learns an operator of the form
ℱ:{(𝐝i′,𝐮s​(𝐝i′))}i=1M⟼𝐮s​(𝐝),𝐝∈𝒟,\mathcal{F}:\left\{\bigl(\mathbf{d}_{i}^{\prime},\mathbf{u}_{s}(\mathbf{d}_{i}^{\prime})\bigr)\right\}_{i=1}^{M}\longmapsto\mathbf{u}_{s}(\mathbf{d}),\qquad\mathbf{d}\in\mathcal{D},
(2)
mapping sparse observations of a directional field on S2S^{2} to its value
at arbitrary query directions. We apply this formulation both to
the log-magnitude
𝐮s​(𝐝)=log10⁡|𝐇sc​(𝐝)|∈ℝF\mathbf{u}_{s}(\mathbf{d})=\log_{10}|\mathbf{H}_{s}^{c}(\mathbf{d})|\in\mathbb{R}^{F}
and to the scalar ITD field
𝐮s​(𝐝)=τs​(𝐝)∈ℝ\mathbf{u}_{s}(\mathbf{d})=\tau_{s}(\mathbf{d})\in\mathbb{R}.
2.3 SPARO Architecture
To support arbitrary sparse measurement and query locations, SPARO maps the HRTF at observed positions to a fixed set of latent modes, processes the latent representation,
and decodes the result at arbitrary query directions. The overall architecture is shown in Fig. 2. Since HRTFs are functions of direction on S2S^{2}, we parameterize these latent modes by learned spherical centers, and the prediction at a query direction attends to the processed modes with weights determined by angular proximity to these centers.
Input Embeddings. Following the branch–trunk construction used in neural operators such as DeepONet [19] and LNO [20], a branch multilayer perceptron (MLP) embeds each observed pair
(𝐝i′,𝐮s​(𝐝i′))(\mathbf{d}_{i}^{\prime},\mathbf{u}_{s}(\mathbf{d}_{i}^{\prime})), for i∈{1,2,…,M}i\in\{1,2,\dots,M\} as 𝐛i∈ℝD\mathbf{b}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, while a trunk MLP embeds a query direction 𝐝j\mathbf{d}_{j} alone as 𝐩j∈ℝD\mathbf{p}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. Since the branch requires an observed field value but the trunk requires only a direction, the branch is evaluated only at the measured locations, whereas the trunk can be evaluated independently at query directions.

Observations are weighted according to their angular similarity
to 𝐜k\mathbf{c}_{k}:

𝐛i∈ℝD\mathbf{b}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is the branch embedding of

independently for each mode, so each 𝐳k0\mathbf{z}_{k}^{0} is a weighted aggregate
of the observed field values associated with a learned region of the sphere.
The centers are initialized uniformly on a Fibonacci lattice on S2S^{2} and learned
jointly with the network, while τk\tau_{k} controls the angular concentration
of each mode.
Transformer Blocks. The latent representation
𝐙0∈ℝMz×D\mathbf{Z}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{M_{z}\times D} is then processed by LL standard
Transformer blocks [28], each comprising multi-head
scaled dot-product self-attention and a position-wise MLP with residual
connections and layer normalization. Since this
processing is performed only over the MzM_{z} latent modes, its cost is
independent of the number of output query directions.
Spherical Mode Projection Decoder.
To obtain the field value at an arbitrary query direction
𝐝j∈S2\mathbf{d}_{j}\in S^{2}, the decoder weights the transformed latent modes
according to their angular similarity to the same learned spherical centers:

(4)

vectors. The softmax is taken over the MzM_{z} latent modes independently for
each query, so each query representation is a location-dependent mixture of
the learned modes.
The encoder and decoder share the same learned spherical mode centers 𝐜k\mathbf{c}_{k} and temperatures τk\tau_{k}. The encoder projects sparse observations onto learned spatial modes on S2S^{2}, the Transformer models interactions between these modes, and the decoder interpolates the transformed modes at arbitrary query directions.
Local Cross-attention.
In the spherical-mode pathway, measured HRTFs influence a query only after
being aggregated into latent modes. To provide a direct
query-to-observation pathway, we apply cross-attention between
the query and the original sparse measurements. Using the trunk embedding
𝐩j\mathbf{p}_{j} of query direction 𝐝j\mathbf{d}_{j} as the query, and the branch
embeddings {𝐛i}i=1M\{\mathbf{b}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} as keys and values,

Here, 𝐮^s​(𝐝j)\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_{s}(\mathbf{d}_{j}) is the final prediction at query
direction 𝐝j\mathbf{d}_{j}. Each prediction thus attends directly to
available measurements, in addition to the representation through the
learned spherical modes.
2.4 Implementation and Test-time Personalization
HRTF Reconstruction.
For HRTF upsampling, we train two instances of the SPARO model: one for HRTF log-magnitude and one for ITD. The magnitude model maps sparse observations {(𝐝i′,log⁡|𝐇sc​(𝐝i′)|)}i=1M\{(\mathbf{d}_{i}^{\prime},\log|\mathbf{H}^{c}_{s}(\mathbf{d}_{i}^{\prime})|)\}_{i=1}^{M} to the log-magnitude response at arbitrary query directions. A second SPARO model predicts the scalar ITD field τs​(𝐝)\tau_{s}(\mathbf{d}), taking sparse ITD observations {(𝐝i′,τs​(𝐝i′))}i=1M\{(\mathbf{d}_{i}^{\prime},\tau_{s}(\mathbf{d}_{i}^{\prime}))\}_{i=1}^{M} as input. The two models are trained independently and their predictions are combined at inference to reconstruct the full HRTF.
Right Ear Handling.
Following [15], we represent right-ear measurements in a mirrored coordinate system. Specifically, right-ear azimuths are reflected as θ↦(360∘−θ)mod360∘\theta\mapsto(360^{\circ}-\theta)\bmod 360^{\circ}, allowing both ears to share a common left-ear convention and effectively doubling the number of training examples. This assumes approximate bilateral symmetry after reflection about the median plane.
Test-time Adaptation. For each test subject, we first encode the sparse observations to obtain the initial latent representation Z0Z_{0}. We then perform a short test-time optimization (TTO) using only the observed measurements, jointly updating Z0Z_{0} and the final output MLP head while keeping the latent Transformer blocks and all remaining model parameters fixed. The adaptation objective combines relative L2L^{2} error at the observed directions with penalties that keep the optimized latent and output-layer parameters close to their pretrained values to prevent overfitting on measurements. After adaptation, the optimized latent is decoded at all query directions to obtain the final HRTF prediction. The loss at test-time is thus:

We report results both for models trained at a single sparsity level and for a single model trained on all sparsity configurations jointly, evaluated at every level without retraining.
Evaluation: Evaluation uses the three objective metrics defined in the LAP24 challenge [7]. The LSD measures spectral

When comparing with [13], we use the same 20 test subjects; they hold out a validation set for checkpoint and hyperparameter selection, while we train for a fixed number of epochs with a fixed hyperparameter set on the remaining 179 subjects. 3.3 Experiments on the Simulated HUTUBS Dataset
For HUTUBS-simulated [30] we compare against SUpDEq [10] as a non-neural spherical-harmonic baseline, following the sampling and evaluation setup in [10], where the spherical-harmonic order is prescribed by the sampling grid. The LAP24 SONICOM configurations do not correspond to such grids, so applying SUpDEq there would require additional choices of interpolation order and regularization. The observed directions are Lebedev grids ranging from 6 to 170 directions (degree Q=1,…,10Q=1,\dots,10) and a degree-29 Fliege target grid containing 900 directions. We use subjects 2–95, excluding the KEMAR heads (subjects 1 and 96), with subjects 86–95 held out for testing and the remaining subjects used for training.

4 CONCLUSION
We formulated HRTF spatial upsampling as operator learning
and introduced SPARO, which maps sparse measurements to arbitrary query directions through a learned spherical mode representation.
SPARO achieves the lowest LSD and ILD error among the compared methods at all four SONICOM sparsity levels, with competitive ITD and substantially lower test-time cost than neural-field methods. Results on HUTUBS further support operator learning as an effective approach for personalized HRTF reconstruction.

## 核心摘要

个性化双耳渲染需要知道每个方向上头部、躯干和耳廓造成的滤波，即头相关传输函数，而密集测量采集成本过高且无法直接给出任意方向取值。论文把补全写成算子学习：输入是同一被试在少数方向上的对数幅度与两耳到达时间差，输出是任意查询方向上的对应场值，模型在多个被试间共享。稀疏观测先经分支网络编码，再按角度相似度聚合到一组中心可学习的球面隐模态，Transformer在模态间建模全局交互，解码按查询方向与同一组中心的相似度加权插值，并叠加直接指向原始观测的交叉注意力。与逐被试优化隐场的神经场方法不同，该算子一次前向即可给出连续场，测试时仅微调隐表示和输出头。在SONICOM按LAP24协议以100个测量点评估未测方向时，对数谱失真LSD为2.3 dB，低于最强基线IOA3D的2.8 dB。同样在SONICOM按LAP24协议以100个测量点评估未测方向时，两耳声级差误差ILD为0.4 dB，低于最强基线IOA3D的0.7 dB。在HUTUBS仿真集以6个Lebedev方向观测评估900个目标方向时，对数谱失真LSD为3.39 dB，低于球谐基线SUpDEq的5.32 dB。在A6000上重建793个目标方向时单被试推理耗时约0.56秒，随测量点基本不变，比神经场方法RANF快15–373倍；结论仅适用于给定稀疏幅度和时间差观测的补全，依赖左右耳镜像对称假设，未验证噪声较大或头部移动时的表现。

SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets
Yixian
Aulia
Jonathan
Kunat
Donghang
Anocha
Abstract
We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR–LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages—Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil—on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. We evaluate open-weight and commercial ASR–LLM systems using identical verifiers and quantify the speech gap as the difference between text and speech accuracy. Results show substantial degradation, with accuracy drops of 9.00–18.50 percentage points for multiple-choice reasoning and 20.00–42.86 points for instruction following. Tamil exhibits the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points. Our findings highlight the limitations of text-only benchmarks in predicting voice-agent reliability and demonstrate the value of SEA-HELM Audio for evaluating multilingual voice-agent systems.
keywordsautomatic speech recognition, multilingual evaluation, spoken language understanding, SEA-HELM Audio

1 Introduction
As artificial intelligence systems transition from text-based interfaces to conversational voice-enabled agents, evaluating the end-to-end accuracy of cascaded speech-language stacks has become a critical research priority. While text-based Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to achieve high benchmark scores, deploying these models within voice pipelines introduces acoustic transcription errors, phonetic ambiguities, and domain-specific degradation. Quantifying this degradation, specifically measuring the accuracy penalty a user incurs by speaking rather than typing, is essential for understanding real-world agent reliability across diverse tasks.
Existing spoken language model benchmarks, such as VoiceBench [1], evaluate capabilities including speech recognition, reasoning, and instruction following through spoken inputs. However, their predominantly English-language evaluation settings provide limited insight into how voice-agent systems perform on Southeast Asian languages and tasks. In particular, it remains unclear to what extent transcription errors alter task-critical information and how these errors affect downstream task performance, especially in the context of Southeast Asian languages.
To address the need for localized evaluation, AI Singapore developed SEA-HELM (Southeast Asian Holistic Evaluation of Language Models) [2]. SEA-HELM provides authentic per-language prompts and tailored programmatic verifiers across regional languages. However, SEA-HELM was engineered natively as a text-only benchmark, consisting exclusively of written prompts without paired audio recordings.
This paper addresses the central research question: How can a text-based, regionally grounded benchmark be adapted into a speech-based evaluation dataset to systematically measure the impact of speech input on downstream LLM task performance across Southeast Asian languages? By bridging SEA-HELM’s text prompts with synthesized audio pipelines, we establish a framework to quantify the Speech gap, the difference between Scoretext\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{text}} and Scorespeech\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{speech}}, across multiple Southeast Asian languages, providing empirical baselines for regional speech agent deployment.
2 Methodology
This section outlines the experimental framework, dataset selection, and evaluation metrics employed to systematically isolate and quantify the performance degradation introduced by the speech modality across our five target languages.
2.1 Experimental Design
Prior to finalizing the evaluation pipeline, we conducted an exploratory phase to establish a robust and regionally relevant testing environment. A primary distinction between our setup and existing voice evaluation frameworks lies in audio corpus generation: VoiceBench uses pre-recorded human speech, whereas SEA-HELM provides only text prompts. Consequently, our cascade architecture synthesizes its own input speech before evaluating downstream models.
To ensure audio fidelity across regional languages, we generated synthetic speech with OmniVoice [3] Text-to-Speech (TTS) engines, selected for acoustic naturalness, prosodic accuracy, and regional accent representation.
For task design, we selected multiple-choice and instruction-following formats, which are established in voice evaluation, and instantiated them with SEA-HELM text prompts. This approach preserves regional nuances, code-switching patterns, and local cultural contexts across Chinese, Malay, Tamil, Indonesian, and English. By evaluating each sample twice, once through the synthesized voice pipeline (Scorespeech\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{speech}}) and once via direct text prompts (Scoretext\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{text}}), we establish a controlled baseline to isolate and measure the precise performance penalty imposed by the speech-to-text layer.
2.2 Datasets and Task Selection
To evaluate the voice cascade cost-effectively and deterministically, we selected tasks from SEA-HELM that rely on rule-based scoring and closely align with established VoiceBench task types.
The evaluation suite draws from four primary SEA-HELM task subsets, summarized in Table 1.

2.2.1 Benchmark Alignment and Active Subset Scope
For the initial empirical runs detailed in this study, benchmarking focuses on the SEA-HELM IFEval and Global-MMLU-Lite subsets across our five focus languages (Chinese, Malay, Tamil, Indonesian, and English).
The selection criteria prioritized two key attributes:
1. 
Speakable Prompts: Prompts can be read aloud as natural speech without removing formatting or template markup first.
2. 
Verifiable Evaluation: All scoring is executed via programmatic, rule-based verifiers, so the text path and the speech path are scored in exactly the same way.
2.3 Evaluation Metrics
To formalize the measurement of the speech modality penalty, the following metrics were captured across every benchmark run:
• 
Text accuracy (Scoretext\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{text}}): The accuracy of the target LLM when provided with the original, ground-truth text input. This represents the theoretical performance ceiling for the task.
• 
Speech accuracy (Scorespeech\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{speech}}): The end-to-end accuracy of the target LLM when the prompt is spoken, synthesized by TTS and transcribed by ASR.
• 
Δ\Delta (The Gap): Δ=Scoretext−Scorespeech\Delta=\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{text}}-\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{speech}}. This absolute difference represents the modality penalty, quantifying how much task performance degrades due to transcription errors, phonetic ambiguities, or missing acoustic signals.
3 SEA-HELM Audio
SEA-HELM contains only written prompts, so SEA-HELM Audio creates the spoken input itself: each prompt is read aloud by a speech synthesizer, transcribed by the ASR system under test, and answered by the LLM. Comparing this against the same LLM answering the original text isolates the cost of the speech front-end.
3.1 Evaluation Flow
Each SEA-HELM prompt is evaluated in two ways (Figure 1). In the speech path, the prompt is converted to speech with TTS, transcribed back to text by ASR, and the transcript is answered by the LLM. In the text path, the LLM answers the original prompt directly. Both answers are scored by the same rule-based verifier, giving Scorespeech\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{speech}} and Scoretext\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{text}}. Because the two paths share the same LLM and the same verifier, the difference between them (Δ\Delta = Scoretext\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{text}} −- Scorespeech\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{speech}}) is the accuracy lost by speaking the prompt instead of typing it.
Figure 1: SEA-HELM Audio evaluation: speech path (TTS →\rightarrow Speech →\rightarrow LLM) vs. text path (LLM only).
3.2 Spoken Prompt Construction
The TTS system plays the role of the user. Its voice is chosen independently of the system being evaluated, so every ASR–LLM configuration hears the same spoken prompts and differences in Scorespeech\mathrm{Score}_{\mathrm{speech}} reflect the system rather than the input.
Only the content a user would actually say is synthesized. For multiple-choice tasks, this is a short instruction followed by the question and its four options; for instruction-following tasks, it is the prompt exactly as written. Written conventions that do not read naturally aloud are adapted per language: in Chinese, the option labels A–D and the answer marker are written as Chinese words. The answer key (the correct option, or the constraints an IFEval response must satisfy) is never spoken and is used only at scoring time.
3.3 Speech Recognition
The ASR system turns the synthesized speech back into text. We evaluate three systems chosen for their coverage of the target languages (Table 2): Qwen3-ASR-1.7B [7] as an open-weight multilingual baseline, MERaLiON3-ASR-3B [8] as a regionally adapted open-weight model for Tamil, and ElevenLabs Scribe Realtime as a commercial service. Open-weight models use greedy decoding so that transcripts are reproducible.
Transcription quality is also measured directly, as Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER) between the transcript and the original prompt. This separates how much the ASR changed the prompt from how much those changes affected the task.

3.4 Response Generation
The LLM answers the ASR transcript (speech path) and the original prompt (text path). We evaluate SEA-LION-4.5-27B [9], a regional open-weight model, and Gemini 3.5 Flash, a commercial model. Both use deterministic decoding (temperature 0), so any difference between the two paths comes from the input rather than from sampling.
3.5 Scoring
All responses are scored with rule-based verifiers taken from SEA-HELM, which keeps scoring deterministic, cheap to repeat, and identical across the two paths. For multiple-choice questions, the chosen option letter (A–D) is extracted from the response and compared with the answer key. For instruction following, each response is checked against the constraints stated in its prompt and is counted as correct only if it also uses the expected language.
4 Results
This section presents the empirical findings from our multi-lingual voice cascade evaluations. Performance is reported across two primary axes: task type (multiple-choice questions via Global-MMLU-Lite vs. instruction following via SEA-HELM IFEval) and pipeline configuration (Regional Open-Weight Baseline vs. Commercial Stack).
4.1 Multiple Choice Reasoning (Global-MMLU-Lite)
Evaluations on the SEA-HELM Global-MMLU-Lite subset were conducted for Chinese and English, assessing general domain knowledge under a multiple-choice format (400 samples per run). Across both languages, the commercial stack (ElevenLabs Scribe Realtime paired with Gemini 3.5 Flash) outperformed the regional open-weight baseline in both text accuracy and speech accuracy.
However, Chinese demonstrated a distinct resilience to the modality shift compared to English. For Chinese, Δ\Delta remained between 9.00 and 10.75 points, whereas English incurred a much steeper penalty of 15.50 to 18.50 points.

4.2 Instruction Following (SEA-HELM IFEval)
SEA-HELM IFEval provided multiple test of deterministic instruction adherence across English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil (105 samples per run). The text-only baselines achieved exceptionally high scores, peaking at 97.14% for English, but introducing the speech modality resulted in severe performance degradation across all tested languages.
The modality gap (Δ\Delta) expanded significantly in instruction-following tasks compared to the MCQ evaluations. Tamil suffered the steepest performance drops (exceeding 40 points) for both the specialized MERaLiON3-ASR-3B pipeline and the commercial ElevenLabs equivalent, indicating severe structural vulnerabilities in Tamil ASR transcriptions.
While the commercial stack generally outperformed the baseline, SEA-LION-4.5-27B proved highly competitive in text accuracy for Southeast Asian languages, notably surpassing Gemini 3.5 Flash in Indonesian IFEval (93.33% vs 89.52%). Despite this strong text foundation, the open-weight pipeline struggled to recover from ASR-induced errors, reflecting Δ\Delta of over 25 points in Malay and Indonesian.

5 Discussion & Analysis
The empirical results underscore a critical reality in voice-agent deployment: strong text-based LLM performance does not guarantee equivalent voice capabilities. The modality gap (Δ\Delta) observed across our evaluations highlights significant disparities driven by language, task structure, and pipeline composition.
5.1 Linguistic Resilience vs. Vulnerability
The most striking finding is the sheer variance in the gap across the five evaluated languages.
• 
Resilience in Chinese: Chinese exhibited the lowest performance degradation across all configurations, maintaining a Delta of approximately 9.00 to 10.75 points. This suggests two compounding advantages: first, modern ASR systems (both Qwen and ElevenLabs) possess highly robust acoustic models for Chinese; second, the downstream LLMs demonstrate strong semantic recovery, able to infer correct answers even in the presence of minor phonetic transcription errors.
• 
The Tamil Bottleneck: Conversely, Tamil suffered the most severe modality penalty, shedding over 40 points in accuracy when transitioning from text to voice. Despite SEA-LION-4.5-27B achieving a respectable 85.71% baseline accuracy on perfect text, the end-to-end performance collapsed to 42.86% utilizing the specialized MERaLiON3-ASR-3B model. This indicates a severe bottleneck at the acoustic processing layer, highlighting a critical data scarcity issue in Tamil ASR training corpora compared to high-resource languages.
5.2 Task Format Sensitivity: MCQ vs. Instruction Following
The data reveals that the modality gap is heavily influenced by the nature of the evaluation task.
On Global-MMLU-Lite (MCQ), LLMs could often recover from noisy transcripts because multiple-choice reasoning primarily requires identifying key semantic concepts to select an option (A, B, C, or D). If an ASR model slightly misheard a noun, the LLM could still deduce the correct multiple-choice letter from contextual clues.
IFEval, in contrast, scores each response against explicit lexical, length, and format constraints stated in the prompt. When ASR drops or substitutes a word that carries one of these constraints, the LLM answers a different instruction, and the rule-based verifier marks the response as a failure even if it is otherwise correct. This mechanism accounts for the larger IFEval gaps of 20 to 43 points.
5.3 Commercial vs. Open-Weight
While the commercial stack (ElevenLabs Scribe Realtime + Gemini 3.5 Flash) consistently delivered higher speech accuracy, analyzing text accuracy reveals a nuanced picture of regional model capabilities.
The SEA-LION-4.5-27B model proved highly competitive, and occasionally superior, in pure-text regional evaluations. Most notably, it outperformed Gemini in the Indonesian IFEval text baseline (94.29% vs. 89.52%). The fact that SEA-LION’s end-to-end voice performance drops so sharply (a 33.33 point penalty) confirms that the limiting factor in the open-weight pipeline is not the LLM’s regional reasoning capability, but rather the fragility of the open-weight ASR models (Qwen3-ASR-1.7B and MERaLiON3-ASR-3B) handling Southeast Asian accents and code-switching.
For organizations deploying regional voice agents, these findings suggest that heavily investing in localized ASR fine-tuning will yield a much higher return on investment than further scaling the LLM parameters.
6 Conclusion and Future Work
This study shows that a text-native benchmark, such as SEA-HELM, can be adapted to benchmark end-to-end voice pipelines, provided the evaluation tasks are highly deterministic. By measuring the modality gap (Δ\Delta) between pure text accuracy and speech accuracy across five languages, we have isolated the precise performance penalty introduced when a user speaks to a conversational agent rather than typing.
Our findings demonstrate that voice pipeline reliability is heavily dependent on the target language and the structural rigidity of the task. While Chinese multiple-choice reasoning exhibited a robust resilience to the modality shift (Δ<11\Delta<11 points), instruction following in Tamil suffered catastrophic degradation (Δ>40\Delta>40 points). Furthermore, while the commercial stack (ElevenLabs Scribe Realtime + Gemini 3.5 Flash) provided the most stable end-to-end performance, the strong pure-text baseline of SEA-LION-4.5-27B suggests that the primary bottleneck for regional open-weight deployments lies in the acoustic transcription layer, not the language model’s reasoning capabilities.

## 核心摘要
这项工作要回答文字基准如何变成语音评测，以及用户用说话代替打字会在东南亚多语言任务上损失多少准确率。输入是SEA-HELM的文字提示，输出是同一提示经朗读、识别、作答后的任务得分，难点在于转写错误会改动题干中的关键约束。语音合成以提示中可说内容为输入朗读生成音频且不读出答案钥匙，与被测系统无关的同一音频直接作为待测自动语音识别的输入被转写为文本。转写文本与原始文字分别送入同一大语言模型作答，两种回答再交由同一规则验证器打分得到语音准确率与文本准确率，两者差值记为语音差距，转写质量另用词错误率和字错误率衡量，从而区分改动了多少字和对任务影响多大。与用英文真人录音的已有语音评测不同，该框架保留了SEA-HELM的本地表达和多语言验证器。在SEA-HELM IFEval泰米尔语评测中，以ElevenLabs v3合成语音为输入、每轮105个样本时，MERaLiON3-ASR-3B搭配SEA-LION-4.5-27B的语音准确率为47.62，低于同一模型文字直接作答的文本准确率87.62，两者相差40.00个百分点，说明指令跟随对转写改动很敏感。该结论仅适用于已实测的Global-MMLU-Lite选择题与IFEval指令跟随及中、英、马来、印尼、泰米尔语合成语音条件，SEA-HELM NLU问答与Safeguard拒绝任务仍列为未来工作，真人发音与更多口音尚未验证。原文未披露训练、推理或部署成本。

From Detection to Anticipation: Continuous Onset Forecasting for Stuttered Speech
Tampu Ravi Kumar
Ayoub Daliri
Vivek Gupta
Abstract
Automatic stuttering systems primarily detect dysfluencies after they have occurred, limiting their use for anticipatory intervention. We address this gap by formulating stuttering prediction as continuous causal time-to-event forecasting, where a model estimates the risk of an upcoming stuttering onset every 100 ms using only preceding speech. To support this task, we augment FluencyBank Timestamped for 36 speakers with manually reviewed repetitions, prolongations, and blocks, yielding 2,872 forecasting events. We then model the temporal evolution of frozen Whisper-large-v3 speech representations using a compact causal Conformer with 3.67M trainable parameters. The proposed approach achieves an AUROC of 0.63. Temporal analysis further shows that explicitly modeling preceding speech states outperforms simply increasing the static acoustic window, while a discrete-time survival formulation provides coherent forecasts from 300 ms to 1.5 s using a single model. These results provide initial evidence that stuttering onset is preceded by measurable temporal information in speech and establish a framework for future anticipatory stuttering systems.
Index Terms: stuttering, onset forecasting, time-to-event prediction, causal modeling, Conformer, Whisper
