2College of Health Solutions, Arizona State University, USA
{traviku2, ayoub.daliri, vgupta140}@asu.edu
1 Introduction
Developmental stuttering is a speech fluency disorder characterized by repetitions, prolongations, and blocks, affecting approximately 1% of adults and 5-8% of children [27]. Behavioral therapy and altered auditory feedback (AAF) can improve fluency, but treatment responses vary substantially across individuals and situations. Wearable AAF devices such as SpeechEasy provide continuous modified auditory feedback during speech and show heterogeneous benefits during long-term, naturalistic use [17, 19]. A system capable of anticipating stuttering onset could eventually trigger such feedback only when needed rather than continuously.
Most computational work, however, focuses on stuttering detection: models classify speech segments that already contain a dysfluency [13, 3, 21]. Recent work extends this setting by predicting whether the next three-second speech segment will contain stuttering [12], but segment-level prediction neither localizes event onset nor continuously estimates its imminence. Motivated by behavioral and neurophysiological evidence that information associated with stuttering can precede overt onset [11, 24, 6], we ask: can stuttering onset be forecast continuously from speech observed strictly before the event?
To our knowledge, we are the first to formulate stuttering prediction as continuous causal time-to-event forecasting. Every 100 ms, the model observes only preceding speech and estimates the probability that a new stuttering event will begin within a future horizon. We study this problem using FluencyBank Timestamped(FBT) [20] dataset, augmented with manually reviewed repetitions, prolongations, and blocks because the existing annotations are not comprehensive for our forecasting analysis. We represent local speech using frozen Whisper-large-v3 [18] and model its temporal evolution using causal architectures. Our contributions are:
• 
We formulate stuttering anticipation as continuous causal
time-to-event forecasting, producing onset-risk estimates every 100 ms from
speech observed strictly before the event.
• 
We build the onset-aligned annotation layer on existing FBT annotations: 2,872 forecasting events across 36 FBT
speakers, including 129 prolongations and 150 blocks annotated manually.
• 
We characterize forecastability across event types, speakers, and
horizons from 300 ms to 1.5 s, and evaluate forecasts at the event
level under an operational duty-cycle constraint, covering 58.6% of events
with feedback active only 25% of the time.
2 TASK FORMULATION AND DATA
2.1 Data and Annotation Augmentation
We use the FBT dataset, comprising
36 speakers with 6.41 h of recordings and 5.13 h of transcribed participant
speech. FBT provides word-level timestamps and repetition annotations, but its
labels are not comprehensive for the event types our forecasting task
requires, so we augment it with manually reviewed repetitions, prolongations,
and blocks. We first generate verbatim word-level transcripts and timestamps
with CrisperWhisper2.0 [28] and align them with the existing FBT annotations. A
human annotator then listens to each recording end-to-end, rather than
reviewing only automatically flagged regions, and adds missed sound and word
repetitions, prolongations, and blocks; automatic transcripts and existing
annotations serve only as review aids, and all added events are manually
verified. To estimate reliability, a second annotator independently labeled 185 clips
from four speakers (44 repetition,
60 prolongation, 56 block, and 25 event-free clips), without access to the
first annotator’s labels. Following SEP-28k [13], we compute
Fleiss’ κ\kappa per event type on clip-level labels: κ=0.54\kappa=0.54
[0.37, 0.69] for repetitions, 0.730.73 [0.62, 0.83] for prolongations, and
0.560.56 [0.41, 0.69] for blocks. For matched events, the median absolute
onset discrepancy was 80 ms overall.
Figure 1: Continuous onset forecasting. The encoder is run once per 100100-ms
grid point over its own preceding 22 s, so consecutive windows overlap by
1.91.9 s; the causal Conformer then attends over 200200 such states (2020 s),
giving a total reach of ≈22\approx 22 s. The 22 s window sets how finely
audio is summarized, not how far back the model can see. Nothing the model
reads extends beyond tt.
We place event boundaries at the acoustic manifestation of the dysfluency:
repetition onset at the beginning of the first repeated fragment,
prolongation onset at the beginning of the abnormally sustained sound, and
block onset at the point where speech stops or an articulatory posture is
established, i.e. the start of the silent or tense interruption rather than
the onset of the subsequent word. Temporally adjacent dysfluencies that
overlap, or that occur within 0.5  s without an intervening completed fluent
word, are consolidated into a single forecasting event, merging 73 of 2,945 raw
dysfluency annotations. The resulting inventory contains 2,872 events: 2,593
repetitions, 129 prolongations, and 150 blocks, the latter two annotated
entirely by hand. Per-speaker event counts range from 11 to 210 (median 65).
CrisperWhisper is not used by the acoustic forecasting model.
2.2 Forecasting Target
Conventional stuttering detection determines whether an observed speech
segment already contains a dysfluency. We instead predict whether a new event will begin in the future.
For each recording, we construct a regular prediction grid at 100-ms
intervals. The grid begins at t=2t=2\,s. The earliest annotated onset in the corpus occurs at 3.37 s, so no event is lost to the grid start. Let s+​(t)s^{+}(t) denote the onset of the next
repetition, prolongation, or block beginning strictly after prediction time
tt. We define the time to the next event as
Tt=s+​(t)−t.T_{t}=s^{+}(t)-t.
(1)
For a future horizon Δ\Delta, the forecasting target is
yt(Δ)=[0<Tt≤Δ].y_{t}^{(\Delta)}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[0<T_{t}\leq\Delta\right].
(2)
The model estimates
pt(Δ)=P⁡(Tt≤Δ∣𝐱≤t),p_{t}^{(\Delta)}=P\!\left(T_{t}\leq\Delta\mid\mathbf{x}_{\leq t}\right),
(3)
using only speech observed at or before tt. Thus, the target event itself is
never contained in a positive input.
Scorable frames. Of 229,966 grid points, we exclude 20,107 frames falling inside an active stuttering event, because the event has already begun and the task would become detection rather than forecasting, and a further 45,165 frames outside transcribed participant-speech segments. Silence occurring within a transcribed segment remains scorable, since a deployed system would have to produce a decision there. This yields 164,694 scorable frames. At the primary Δ=300\Delta=300ms horizon, 8,121 frames are positive, a prevalence of 4.93%.
Composition of the negative class. Because stuttering events cluster in time, a model could appear to forecast by recognizing that an event occurred recently rather than by extracting pre-onset information. 25.4% of positive and 19.8% of negative frames fall within 2 s of a previous onset, so the two classes are comparably situated in this respect.
2.3 Multi-Horizon Formulation
A fixed binary horizon imposes a hard boundary on a potentially evolving pre-onset state. We therefore additionally evaluate forecasting over Δ∈(0.3,0.5,0.75,1.0,1.5)\Delta\in{(0.3,0.5,0.75,1.0,1.5)} s. A discrete-time survival model predicts 15 conditional hazards at 100-ms intervals from a single forward pass. Let
ht,k=P⁡(Tt∈(τk−1,τk]∣Tt>τk−1,𝐱≤t),h_{t,k}=P(T_{t}\in(\tau_{k-1},\tau_{k}]\mid T_{t}>\tau_{k-1},\mathbf{x}_{\leq t}),
the probability of onset in bin kk given that no onset has occurred earlier, where τk=0.1​k\tau_{k}=0.1ks. The cumulative probability of onset within τk\tau_{k} is
P⁡(Tt≤τk∣𝐱≤t)=1−∏j=1k(1−ht,j).P(T_{t}\leq\tau_{k}\mid\mathbf{x}_{\leq t})=1-\prod_{j=1}^{k}(1-h_{t,j}).
The model is trained by masked binary cross-entropy over at-risk bins, i.e. the negative log discrete-time survival likelihood. A frame is at risk in bin kk only if that bin lies within the transcribed segment containing tt; otherwise it is right-censored and contributes no further bins, rather than being silently labelled negative as the fixed-horizon target requires. The evaluable set therefore shrinks with the horizon (156,669 frames at 0.3 s to 128,167 at 1.5 s).
This formulation produces a coherent, non-decreasing risk trajectory from a single model rather than requiring a separate binary classifier for every horizon.
3 Causal Temporal Forecasting
We separate local acoustic representation from longer-range temporal
modeling (Fig. 1). Every 100 ms, a frozen encoder turns
the preceding 2 s of audio into a single vector; a lightweight causal model
then runs over the sequence of those vectors, attending back up to 200 steps.
The 2 s window therefore sets how finely the audio is summarized, not how far
back the model can see: at a 200-step span the receptive field reaches roughly
22 s, as 2 s summaries spaced 100 ms apart. Everything the model reads at
time tt ends at or before tt.
3.1 Acoustic Representation
We use the frozen encoder of Whisper-large-v3.
Because it applies bidirectional self-attention, encoding a full recording
would expose future audio, so we independently encode only the 2-s waveform
ending at tt, giving 𝐳t∈ℝ1280\mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{1280}. The encoder
expects a 30-s log-mel input; we zero-pad and retain only the 100 frames
corresponding to real audio. Frames are emitted at 50 Hz and averaged in
non-overlapping groups of five into one state per 100 ms, matching the
forecasting grid, giving the causal sequence 𝐙≤t\mathbf{Z}_{\leq t}. We use the
final encoder layer, selected on validation average precision from
{8,16,24,32}\{8,16,24,32\} in a preliminary sweep; layer-wise probes of stuttering
detection locate dysfluency information in middle
layers [21, 2], but forecasting an event absent
from the input is a different task, and here the final layer was best.
Representations are extracted once and cached (0.9 GPU-hours), after which
each temporal model trains in minutes on one GPU.
3.2 Temporal Model
Our primary temporal model is a four-block
Conformer [10]. Each Whisper state is normalized and
projected to 192 dimensions; each block has macaron feed-forward modules
(192→768→192192\to 768\to 192), four-head causal self-attention, and a causal
depthwise convolution with kernel size 15. Three choices prevent future
information from reaching a prediction: attention sees only current and
preceding states, convolutions are left-padded, and we use LayerNorm rather
than temporal BatchNorm, which would normalize using whole-sequence
statistics. Attention uses a maximum left context of 20 s (200 states) and
carries no positional term, so ordering reaches the model only through the
stacked causal convolutions. The final state maps to a frame-level onset-risk
probability; the model has 3.67 M trainable parameters and Whisper remains
frozen. We compare against a static Whisper predictor that attention-pools
the 2-s window, a causal TCN [1] (1.12 M parameters), and a causal GRU [5]
(1.12 M), all sharing representations, targets, and folds.
3.3 Training
We optimize focal loss [14] (γ=2\gamma=2, α=0.75\alpha=0.75) to
counter the 4.93% prevalence, with AdamW [16], learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4},
weight decay 0.010.01, dropout 0.20.2, gradient clipping at 5, and early
stopping on validation AP with patience 8. Training sequences span 40 s: a
200-step causal buffer, which supplies context but no loss, followed by 200
scored steps. For multi-horizon forecasting we keep the architecture and
replace the binary output with the 15-bin hazard head, trained with plain
binary cross-entropy over at-risk bins rather than focal loss: focal
reweighting distorts predicted probabilities, and calibrated hazards are the
point of that formulation (dropout 0.30.3, 50-step buffer).
4 Experiments and Results
4.1 Setup
We use six speaker-disjoint folds over the 36 speakers; for each test fold a
disjoint fold is used for validation and the remaining speakers for training.
All models share folds, grids, and targets, so comparisons are paired. We
train three seeds per fold and average their predictions before computing
out-of-fold metrics. Since only 4.93% of frames are positive, accuracy is
uninformative: we report average precision (AP), its lift over the prevalence
floor, AUROC, and within-speaker AUROC (wAUROC), computed within each
speaker and averaged, which removes differences in baseline stuttering
propensity. Intervals and model differences come from paired speaker-level
bootstrap resampling. Operating thresholds are selected on each validation fold and applied unchanged to its test fold. The static Whisper predictor approximates the segment-level setting of [12] at our temporal resolution.
4.2 Does Temporal Modeling Improve Forecasting?
Table 1 compares architectures at the 300-ms horizon. The causal
Conformer is strongest, with AP 0.07690.0769 (1.56×\times the prevalence floor)
and AUROC 0.63000.6300, improving pooled AUROC over the TCN by 0.04110.0411 (95% CI
[0.0196,0.0615][0.0196,0.0615]); the GRU does not improve over the TCN. The gain is not
explained by exposure to more audio: widening the static Whisper window from
2.0 to 3.8 s moves AUROC from 0.5682 to 0.5666 (AP 0.0522 to 0.0512),
whereas modeling the temporal sequence raises it to 0.6300. Useful pre-onset
information therefore lies in the temporal evolution of locally
contextualized speech states rather than in a larger static window.

4.4 Multi-Horizon and Operational Forecasting
Table 3 compares the discrete-time hazard model with
independently trained binary classifiers and with independent cumulative
outputs. The hazard model is competitive with five separately trained binary

Frame-level discrimination does not show whether forecasts could drive an
event-triggered intervention. We therefore merge positive decisions into
warning episodes and measure event-level sensitivity against alarm duty
cycle, the fraction of time a feedback system would be active. At a 25% duty
cycle the Conformer anticipates 58.6% of scorable events, against 57.4% for
the TCN and 53.8% for the GRU; at a higher-recall point it anticipates 91.6%
at 66.5% duty. At the validation-selected maximum-F1 threshold it anticipates
43.9% of events with a mean lead time of 196 ms, but produces 27.6 false
warning bouts per minute. These operating points quantify the trade-off
between feedback exposure and event coverage; whether selectively triggered
AAF at these lead times improves fluency requires prospective intervention
studies.
5 Related Work
Forecasting is plausible because stuttering is not distributed uniformly
through speech: it concentrates on particular sounds, word classes, and
utterance positions [4, 26],
and speakers often report anticipating upcoming moments of
stuttering [11]. Neural
differences precede overt blocks [24], and adults who
stutter show reduced pre-speech auditory modulation [6].
Das et al. [7] predicted upcoming dysfluent trials from
pre-speech facial muscle movements. The listener study of Liu and
Howell [15] and the surprisal analysis of Warner et
al. [25] are closest to our setting and both ask whether pre-onset material predicts the event, but
neither builds an acoustic predictor.
The only audio-based predictor we are aware of is that of
Kozak [12], who trains a compact CNN on SEP-28k to
predict whether the next 3 s clip contains a dysfluency and finds signal
concentrated on blocks and sound repetitions. Our formulation differs in three
respects: it produces a risk estimate every 100 ms rather than one decision
per clip, it targets exact annotated onsets at sub-second horizons, and it
evaluates event-level coverage under an alarm duty-cycle budget. More broadly,
continuous causal prediction of upcoming speech events has been studied for
turn-taking, where models project future voice activity from preceding
audio [22, 8]; our event-level evaluation,
sensitivity against time spent in warning, follows practice in seizure
prediction [23], and our multi-horizon head uses a
discrete-time survival formulation [9].
6 Conclusion
In this work, we formulated stuttering anticipation as continuous causal time-to-event forecasting, constructed the required onset-aligned corpus layer, and established a benchmark framework for evaluating pre-onset risk trajectories. Our findings demonstrate three key insights: (1) speech preceding stuttering onset carries statistically measurable predictive structure; (2) modeling the sequential evolution of contextualized speech states provides significant gains over expanding static acoustic context; and (3) a discrete-time survival formulation produces coherent, multi-horizon forecasts without violating temporal ordering. Although current operational trade-offs indicate that pre-onset forecasting remains an open challenge, this work provides a formulation, empirical baseline, and evaluation methodology to guide future research toward deployable anticipatory interventions.
7 Limitations and Future Work
While this work establishes a baseline for continuous onset forecasting, several challenges remain before such models can drive real-time clinical interventions. The primary constraint remains annotation scale. Continuous time-to-event forecasting requires precise, frame-level onset timestamps that existing segment-level stuttering corpora do not provide. While our augmented layer of 2,872 events across 36 speakers represents a critical first step, scaling onset-aligned annotations to larger, more diverse cohorts will be essential to fully unlock fine-grained anticipatory modeling.
8 Compliance with Ethical Standards
This work uses the publicly available FluencyBank Timestamped (FBT) dataset under its existing license and our augmented annotations contain no additional PII beyond what FBT already provides. The proposed forecasting models are intended as a research step toward clinician- or user-supervised assistive tools, not as a standalone diagnostic or autonomous intervention system.
9 Acknowledgments
We conducted this research as a collaborative effort at Arizona State University. We thank the Complex Data Analysis and Reasoning Lab within the School of Computing and Augmented Intelligence at Arizona State University for providing computational resources and institutional support. We also sincerely thank Manan Roy Choudhury and Tejas Anvekar for their valuable feedback during the ideation stage of this work.

Bias Mitigation in Audio-Enabled LLMs through 
Adversarial Training and Distillation Methods
Adnan Al Ali, 
Jindřich Libovický, 
Anne Lauscher
Affiliation: Charles University, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Czech Republic
Affiliation: Trustworthy AI Lab, University of Hamburg, Germany
Correspondence:alali@ufal.mff.cuni.cz
Abstract
Audio-enabled large language models (AuLLMs) allow users to interact with them simply by talking to them, without the need for an intermediate transcription. This expands the models’ accessibility and capabilities by encoding non-verbal cues. However, using non-verbal cues leads to biased behaviour based on the attributes inferred (or assumed) from them. Attribute-based biases have been reported in recent work, but their mitigation is understudied. In this work, we focus on the gender attribute and show that models’ perception of it can be unlearned using adversarial methods without a loss in performance on other benchmarked tasks. Such models are useful in situations where gender inference is unwanted.
Yet in other practical settings, gender perception (without bias) may be desired.
As a less radical measure, we distil the gender-agnostic model, creating a model that perceives gender but responds similarly to the gender-agnostic teacher, unless explicitly asked.
We apply our newly proposed methods to three AuLLMs and obtain satisfactory results in the gender-unlearning part and partially satisfactory results in the distilling part.
1 Introduction
Figure 1: Outline of the two proposed methods: adversarial-only (blue part) and adversarial/distillation pipeline (whole figure).
Audio-enabled large language models (AuLLMs) improve accessibility, particularly for the elderly (Yang et al., 2024) and those in early education (Aguilera et al., 2024), potentially bridging the digital divide in LLM adoption (Suárez and García-Mariñoso, 2025). Moreover, a built-in voice encoder (without intermediate transcription) retains prosody and avoids transcription errors (Kharitonov et al., 2022; Deshmukh et al., 2024).
Audio support is standard in commercial models (OpenAI et al., 2024; Comanici et al., 2025) and increasingly common in open-weight ones (Liu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2026, inter alia). Thus, with the growing adoption of AuLLMs, especially among people with limited digital literacy, fairness becomes critical.
While text-only LLMs have exhibited biased behaviour (Wan et al., 2023; Gallegos et al., 2024; Rowe et al., 2025, inter alia), voice encoder outputs also contain paralinguistic cues that enable inference of attributes such as gender or age, which usually cannot be inferred from text, introducing a risk of additional biases. Holtermann et al. (2026) found that AuLLMs produce different, stereotypically biased outputs for the same recording content for feminine and masculine voices.
We address the concerns raised by Holtermann et al. (2026) and develop two successive methods – an adversarial-only method and an adversarial/distillation pipeline – for bias mitigation in AuLLMs.
The methods provide a general framework for mitigating biases in AuLLMs based on attributes such as age, group-specific accents, or gender. In our case study, we demonstrate them on gender bias.
In the first method (Section 4), we use adversarial training to remove the gender signal from the audio encoder, creating a gender-unaware model (GUM). Aside from gender perception, the GUM retains audio understanding comparable to the original model and can be used when gender perception is unwanted.
Building on it, in Section 5 we combine the outputs of the original model and the GUM to distil a model that retains gender perception but produces comparable outputs for masculine and feminine voices when gender is irrelevant.
Our contributions are the following:
(1) Providing an insight into the understudied topic of bias mitigation in AuLLMs.
(2) Demonstrating how gender perception can be removed from the models and what the side effects of it are.
(3) Presenting an approach for mitigating bias while preserving the gender perception, demonstrating its limitations and proposing ways to improve it.
We release the code and the trained models.11
 1
 https://github.com/adnan-al-ali/speech-llm-bias-mitigation/, 22
 2
 https://hf.co/alalia/speech-bias-mitigation/
2 Related Work
Text-only LLMs have been thoroughly observed to reproduce and amplify stereotypically biased narratives (Gallegos et al., 2024). Various datasets measure LLMs’ biased behaviour based on gender, race, age, disability, sexual orientation, and others (Parrish et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023; Rowe et al., 2025, inter alia), and most current models still exhibit some form of undesirable behaviour (Comanici et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2026; Anthropic, 2026).
AuLLMs are considerably understudied compared to their text-only counterparts.
Holtermann et al. (2026) provided a comprehensive evaluation of biases in AuLLMs and found that they infer attributes such as gender from paralinguistic cues and, based on them, produce stereotypically biased outputs even without any explicit mention of the attributes in the user prompt. They observed this in both open- and closed-weight models, in both option-choosing and open generation.
Bias mitigation and value alignment approaches for text-only language models include reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF; Ouyang et al., 2022), parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) on an augmented dataset (Lauscher et al., 2021), and adversarial training (Rekabsaz et al., 2021), among others. However, these can rarely be applied directly to AuLLMs due to architectural differences, the scarcity of multimodal data, and different manifestations of bias.
Holtermann et al. (2026) also provided insight into bias mitigation, namely pitch modification. They found that increasing the pitch led to more stereotypically feminine terms being generated, and vice versa. Targeted pitch modulation could therefore push the model towards less gendered outputs. However, it would inevitably degrade performance on tasks such as pitch detection (trivially), sound identification, or gender detection (which may or may not be intended), and may not completely eliminate gender perception.
We confirm these concerns in Table 1 and opt to avoid pitch modification. Instead, we adapt methods from text-only models (adversarial learning, PEFT) to AuLLMs.
3 Datasets, Evaluation Metrics, Models
Figure 2: Fightin’ Words method applied to the open generation adjectives from the Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni model (before any training), sorted by log odds ratio (LOR).
In our methods, we use multiple datasets to evaluate and train gender detection, gender bias, and general audio capabilities. We use the corpus annotation data as the source of speaker gender information.
3.1 Gender Detection
Following Holtermann et al. (2026), we use the British Dialects (Demirsahin et al., 2020; 500 recordings) and the Speech Archive (Weinberger, 2015; 470 recordings) corpora, which contain short English recordings of speakers varying in age and accent, balanced by gender. We prompt the model for the speaker’s gender (‘M’/‘F’), allowing a third ‘X’ option if unclear, and measure absolute accuracy, refusal rate, and accuracy on non-refused samples.
3.2 Gender Bias Evaluation
We reproduce the experimental setup of Holtermann et al. (2026) and measure gender bias in both restricted-option choice and open generation, using the same recordings as in Section 3.1. For prompting details, refer to the original article, section Prompting Setup.
For the option choice evaluation, we measure the association between the speaker’s gender and stereotypical words. We feed the model a pair of gender-polarised terms (such as ‘collaborative’ vs ‘independent’) and prompt it to decide which better describes the person in the recording. From the outputs, we compute c⁡(audioM,wordM)c(\mathrm{audio}_{M},\mathrm{word}_{M}) – the number of cases where the speaker is male and the model chose the stereotypically masculine option – and the other three M/F combinations defined analogously. From those, we define the log odds ratio (LOR) as:
log⁡c⁡(audioM,wordM)⋅c⁡(audioF,wordF)c⁡(audioM,wordF)⋅c⁡(audioF,wordM).\log\frac{c(\mathrm{audio}_{M},\mathrm{word}_{M})\cdot c(\mathrm{audio}_{F},\mathrm{word}_{F})}{c(\mathrm{audio}_{M},\mathrm{word}_{F})\cdot c(\mathrm{audio}_{F},\mathrm{word}_{M})}.
(1)
Positive LOR values indicate a stereotypical association, while negative values indicate an anti-stereotypical one. In total, we have 23 280 samples (recording-prompt pairs).
We analyse the open generation qualitatively. We present the model with two concatenated recordings with the same linguistic content, one from a man and one from a woman (in either order), and prompt it to write short profiles for both speakers and to decide which is better suited to which of two gender-polarised roles. The prompt templates represent three categories: power, science, and career, and refer to the speakers as Speaker A and Speaker B.
We then prompt GPT-OSS-120B (OpenAI et al., 2025) to extract the adjectives associated with Speaker A and B. Importantly, the extraction model has no access to the recordings or the speakers’ actual genders, to avoid introducing additional bias. We then apply the Fightin’ Words method (Monroe et al., 2017) to find words systematically associated with masculine and feminine voices, yielding LOR scores for each word, of which we keep only the statistically significant ones. The result is a list of words sorted by LOR, as illustrated in Figure 2.
3.3 Misgendering Evaluation
When gender perception is unavailable, the risk of misgendering (e.g., using the wrong gendered pronoun) increases, as the model may choose pronouns arbitrarily. We therefore also evaluate the misgendering rate. Using the voice corpora from Section 3.1, we remove samples whose transcription contains gendered pronouns. We then ask the model to describe the speaker’s voice, including age (see Listing 3), which works best, as models often respond with ‘in his/her twenties/thirties/…’.
From the response, we parse the most prominent gender by pronouns,33
 3
 We consider he, she, they, and their inflexions. LLMs generated no other gendered pronouns (e.g., neopronouns). with four outcomes: ‘M’ (male), ‘F’ (female), ‘X’ (neutral they), and ‘_’ (no pronouns or tie). We call this benchmark misgend.
3.4 Implicit Gender Stereotype Signals
To distinguish gender bias evaluation from its unlearning during distillation (Section 5), we create a dataset of more natural prompts. While the evaluation offers the model one stereotypical and one anti-stereotypical option, here the stereotypical answer is possible but not stated. Examples include ‘Why is this speaker popular among men?’ and ‘What is this speaker doing in a kindergarten?’ (see Section C.1 for the full list). We pair these with VCTK voice recordings (Yamagishi et al., 2019; 240 random recordings per prompt, 8160 samples total) and call this dataset ImpGender.
3.5 General Audio Tasks
For fine-tuning the models for general instruction-following audio tasks (e.g., transcription, pitch and emotion detection), we use a subset of the sift-50m corpus (Pandey et al., 2025) that contains only recordings from the VCTK corpus, due to its availability. sift-50m contains samples that explicitly or implicitly train for gender detection. During the adversarial training, this would interfere with the gender unlearning. To avoid the interference, we filter out samples containing words such as ‘gender’, ‘man’, ‘woman’ (full list in Listing 2) from the original dataset and refer to the filtered version as sift-50m\neuter\neuter. This filters out most prompts that ask for gender (based on manual evaluation of a small subset), but some information about gender may still be implicitly retained, e.g., in pronouns.
To evaluate general audio understanding, we use the mmau (mini subset: 1000 samples) benchmark (Sakshi et al., 2025). Since we have a separate benchmark for gender detection, we analogously create mmau\neuter\neuter (908 samples) to decouple the tasks. Because we do not use the gendered variant, we simply refer to the ungendered dataset as mmau.
3.6 Models
In our experiments, we work with three AuLLMs, each with a different audio encoder:
(1) Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct(Chu et al., 2024)with the Whisper encoder Radford et al., 2022, which Holtermann et al. (2026) also evaluated,
(2) Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B(Xu et al., 2025)with its custom AuT encoder, and
(3) Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B(NVIDIA et al., 2026)with the Parakeet encoder (Sekoyan et al., 2025).
To ensure comparable results, we disable the chain-of-thought reasoning stage for all models.
All of these models can predict gender well (Table 2) but also produce gender-stereotypical outputs (Table 3, Figures 2, 8, 10). Qwen2-Audio, an older, smaller model, exhibits more bias and considerably worse audio understanding (Table 1).
4 Adversarial Training
In the first method, our goal is to completely remove gender representation from the voice encoder’s output, resulting in the gender-unaware model (GUM). We employ adversarial training (Elazar and Goldberg, 2018) using a gradient reversal layer (GRL; Ganin and Lempitsky, 2015), which effectively multiplies the gradient with a negative constant -​α\text{-}\alpha (a hyperparameter) during the backward pass.
4.1 Experimental Setup
During the training, we make the following temporary modifications to the model:
(1) We freeze the parameters except for the audio encoder, which is the source of gender perception. As the encoder is relatively small (<1<1B parameters), we employ full fine-tuning.
(2) We mean-pool the final representations from the encoder into a single vector of dimension dencoderd_{\mathrm{encoder}} and pass it through the GRL.
(3) We pass the GRL output to a binary gender classification head.
Figure 3 shows the setup.
We use the output from the newly attached head to compute the gender classification cross-entropy loss. Additionally, to prevent catastrophic forgetting, we combine it with the language model (LM) cross-entropy loss computed from the language model head. We sum the losses with a hyperparameter γ\gamma:
ℒcomb=ℒgender+γ​ℒLM.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comb}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gender}}+\gamma\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}.
(2)
Figure 3: Training setup for the adversarial stage.
For the dataset, we subsample the sift-50m\neuter\neuter dataset (see Section 3.5). Each speaker in the VCTK corpus has a gender label, which allows computing both losses for the same sample. We train the models on 4 000 gender-balanced samples for one epoch at a constant learning rate and checkpoint the encoder every 125 optimisation steps.
From the saved checkpoints, we select those with absolute gender detection44
 4
 We measure gender detection by direct prompting, having discarded the gender classification head after training. accuracy below 60%60\% (see Section 3.1). From the selection, we use the checkpoint with the highest mmau benchmark accuracy for the next step.
4.2 Training and Evaluation
We train the model and grid-search for the optimal hyperparameters (48 combinations, four checkpoints each; see Section B.1). Table 1 shows the best-performing hyperparameter configuration for each model. In all three cases, adversarial training successfully degraded gender detection to random levels, creating a GUM. The minimal trade-off for this targeted unlearning is the slight degradation (<4%<4\%) in general audio understanding for Qwen3-Omni and Nemotron-3-Omni. This is possibly due to imperfect filtering of tasks that require gender detection from mmau. Interestingly, audio understanding for Qwen2-Audio improved, perhaps by learning new skills from the sift-50m\neuter\neuter dataset. Qwen3-Omni was the most difficult model to train, with only two checkpoints achieving below 60% gender detection accuracy, and mmau results comparable to the original model.

5 Distillation Stage
Building on the success of the first method, we extended it by combining the original model’s full capabilities with the GUM’s gender neutrality to create a model that perceives gender, but behaves gender-agnostically, unless explicitly asked about the gender. We do this by distilling the logits from both models in a mixed dataset.
5.1 Experimental Setup
Suppose we have a model ℳ\mathcal{M} and its gender-unaware variant ℳGUM\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GUM}} from the adversarial training stage. We fine-tune another instance of the model ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} using the outputs from the two models. We train ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} using low-rank adaptation (LoRA; Hu et al., 2022) applied to all attention weights in the decoder only.
When extracting the logits from the original model ℳ\mathcal{M}, we aim to preserve its behaviour as much as possible. For that, we create sift-50mℳ\textsc{sift-50m}^{\mathcal{M}} – a variant of sift-50m, in which we only take the user prompts from sift-50m and generate the answers using ℳ\mathcal{M}. Then, we generate the answers to the ImpGender prompts using ℳGUM\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GUM}}, creating ImpGenderℳGUM\textsc{ImpGender}^{\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GUM}}}. We use top-k sampling with temperatures of 0.5 and 0.7, respectively.
After generating the two datasets, we extract the logits from the language modelling head. For each dataset, we extract the logits from the same model as we used to generate it. We cap the total number of samples to 4 000 per dataset and mix them together, yielding 8 000 samples. From those, we filter out samples whose logits exceed 150 MB to prevent out-of-memory issues. Such samples are usually a result of broken, repetitive generation. During training, we use the KL divergence loss and normalise the per-sample loss by its length. We train for one epoch with checkpointing every 80 steps.
5.2 Training and Evaluation
As before, we train the LoRA adapters and grid-search for the optimal hyperparameters (eight combinations, ten checkpoints each; see Section B.2). After one epoch, the loss converged and oscillated around a stable value for most hyperparameter configurations. From the checkpoints, we select the ones that:
(1) have gender accuracy detection ≥70%\geq 70\% and
(2) have mmau accuracy no worse than 97%97\% of the original performance.

6 Discussion
In the first part of this work, we presented a method that lowers gender detection accuracy to near-random levels. While the results looked satisfactory, they raised a question: how is this result achieved? Ideally, the gender-unaware model should have no perception of gender but should also be aware of this limitation and refuse to answer (a valid option in our prompts). In practice, models tend to use shortcuts. Qwen3-Omni achieved near-random results by confidently choosing the ‘F’ label 95.5% of the time. The other two models refused far more often but frequently gave the correct answer otherwise, suggesting residual gender perception. This shows qualitative analysis is needed beyond absolute accuracy, which alone can be misleading.
The successive distillation method exposes new challenges. Contrary to our expectations, most distilled checkpoints for Qwen3-Omni and Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni produced more biased outputs than their original models (although a non-trivial subset showed slight improvement). We believe this is due to the use of the sift-50m dataset. The dataset is designed to train the model on benchmarkable, factual skills rather than to provide considerate answers with discussion and explanation. We even found samples explicitly rewarding stereotypical outputs, shown in Section A.
By training on a dataset with short, exact answers, we reward the model for making assumptions and override its often fragile safety guardrails. Yet alternative datasets for instruction tuning AuLLMs are scarce. A partial solution would be to generate longer, more suitable answers to the prompts using existing models (similarly to sift-50mℳ\textsc{sift-50m}^{\mathcal{M}}). However, aside from error accumulation and stereotype-enforcing questions, the prompts are formulated so that even models trained to generate rich text switch to ‘benchmarking mode’ and produce short, on-point answers, as observed for Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni when generating its sift-50mℳ\textsc{sift-50m}^{\mathcal{M}} dataset.
Our findings also bring a more optimistic takeaway: the two methods we propose require relatively small datasets, thanks to selective and parameter-efficient training. Therefore, a smaller (∼\sim15k-sample), carefully curated dataset would be feasible to produce and would likely yield more satisfactory results.
7 Conclusion
In this work, we presented two novel methods for bias mitigation in audio-enabled large language models (AuLLMs). While the general outline of the methods can be used to mitigate bias based on any attribute inferred from speech, we demonstrate it specifically on gender bias, using three different AuLLMs. In the first method, we use adversarial training methods to remove the gender perception from the models’ audio encoders. The resulting models are useful in settings where gender inference is undesired. This method was largely successful, although an in-depth analysis revealed that in some cases, the perception was not entirely removed, and in others, the model would confidently make claims about the gender it no longer perceived.
Extending the first method, we combined the outputs of the original models and their gender-unaware variants to balance the original capabilities with gender-agnostic behaviour. We did this using parameter-efficient logit distillation. From the trained checkpoints, we chose those for which gender perception and general audio understanding were comparable to the original model, and selected the least-biased checkpoint.
While we were able to create a less biased model than the original, the improvement was marginal for two of the three models. We further found that most of the distilled checkpoints were more biased than the original baseline. We attribute this change to the dataset that we used, which rewards short answers and assumptions over explanation and discussion.
We present this work as early findings on the possibilities for gender bias mitigation in AuLLMs and invite future work to further expand these studies. We believe that a carefully crafted dataset would achieve more satisfactory results.
Limitations
Data availability.
Our approach is vastly limited by the available datasets. As we discuss in Section 6, the dataset available to us contains prompts with short, factual answers that are optimised for benchmarks rather than for everyday use. Such prompts reward making assumptions rather than acknowledging limited knowledge. This may be counterproductive when trying to mitigate stereotypical assumptions from the model. The dataset further contains samples that encourage biased behaviour, shown in Appendix A. Yet, alternative datasets suitable for our use are scarce.
Custom datasets scale.
Our ImpGender dataset for distilling the gender-unaware model contains 34 unique prompts, covering areas such as professions, work/school relationship dynamics, self-perception and others. These prompts are repeated 240 times with different audio recordings. While this serves as a proof of concept, an ideal dataset would contain hundreds of prompts covering diverse areas, each repeated only a few times. Crafting datasets to address this and the previous issue would be resource-intensive, but feasible for future work.
Lack of real-world evaluation.
Our evaluation metrics are formatted as a sample with unrelated content and a prompt. This does not correspond to real-life use, where the instruction itself is often stated in the recording. Previous work also reported this challenge (Holtermann et al., 2026).
Language coverage.
Our work focuses on English alone. Additional languages, especially the gendered ones, might bring new challenges, particularly to filtering gendered prompts.
Binary gender model.
Our gender modelling is based on the dataset annotation, which is limited to the ‘male’ and ‘female’ labels. This, however, does not reflect the complex nature of gender identities.
Ethical Considerations
We do not anticipate any negative ethical implications arising from this study. We used AI-assisted coding (GitHub Copilot) and AI tools (Claude, ChatGPT, and Grammarly) for grammar checking and minor sentence rephrasing.
The models we work with are licensed under the Apache 2.0 license (Qwen2-Audio and Qwen3-Omni) and the NVIDIA Open Model Agreement (Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni). The British Dialects and the Speech Archive corpora are licensed under CC-BY-SA-4.0. The VCTK corpus is licensed under the Edinburgh DataShare depositor agreement. The sift-50m dataset is licensed under CDLA-SHARING-1.0 and the mmau benchmark is licensed under CC-BY-NC-4.0. The code released by Holtermann et al. (2026) is licensed under the MIT License.
Appendix A Stereotypes in SIFT-50M
Upon manual inspection, we found that the sift-50m dataset often encourages models to produce stereotypically biased outputs. We list some examples below:
• 
Q: How does the gender of the speaker influence the tone and delivery of the message in the audio? 
A: The female gender of the speaker contributes to a nurturing and gentle tone in the delivery, which may make the message seem more approachable and less authoritative.
• 
Q: Explore the cultural and regional implications of the speaker’s accent on the reception of the audio’s content. 
A: The Irish accent adds a distinct cultural and regional flavor to the audio, which can influence the listener’s perception of the speaker’s background and credibility. […]
• 
Q: How might the speaker’s age category (twenties) and gender (Female) influence the perceived authority and credibility of the message about medical concerns? 
A: The speaker’s young age and female gender might influence some listeners’ perceptions of her authority and credibility on medical concerns, potentially leading them to question her experience or expertise despite her clear and confident delivery.
Appendix B Technical Details
For training, we used the Hugging Face Transformers library (Wolf et al., 2020) and our custom training loop, using the AdamW optimiser (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019). For inference, we used the vLLM library (Kwon et al., 2023). We used GPUs with 48 GB of VRAM (Nvidia A40 and L40) and 95 GB of VRAM (Nvidia H100 and RTX 6000 Pro). We used Accelerate (Gugger et al., 2022) for distributed training. Table 5 shows the memory consumption for each model. Training for one epoch took approximately two hours.
B.1 Adversarial Training Hyperparameters
The fixed hyperparameters for training were: effective batch size = 8, weight decay = 5×10−35\times 10^{-3}. The grid-searched hyperparameters were: learning rate ∈(5×10−6,10−5,5×10−5,10−4)\in(5\times 10^{-6},10^{-5},5\times 10^{-5},10^{-4}), weight for ℒLLM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LLM}} (γ\gamma) ∈(0.5,1,2)\in(0.5,1,2), gradient reversal weight (α\alpha) ∈(0.025,0.05,0.1,0.2)\in(0.025,0.05,0.1,0.2).
B.2 Distilling Hyperparameters

## 论文评价
论文把语音大模型中的性别偏见拆成两种使用需求，分别给出去除性别感知和保留感知但降低偏见的训练流程，并在 3 个模型上验证了效果与代价。最有力的证据是性别探测准确率降到 50% 附近且通用音频理解基本保持，但蒸馏阶段多数检查点偏见反而加重，说明第二阶段结论还不稳定。

## 核心摘要
语音使能大语言模型（Audio-enabled Large Language Model，AuLLM）直接以语音为输入，输出文本回答，语音中的副语言线索会让模型推断说话人性别并产生刻板关联，这是本文要处理的问题。第一步用对抗训练只更新音频编码器，性别分类头前加入梯度反转层（Gradient Reversal Layer，GRL），同时保留语言模型损失以维持通用能力，得到性别无感知模型。对抗阶段在 Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B 上把性别探测绝对准确率从 99.9% 降到 54.5%，而 mmau 通用音频理解准确率保持在 71.3%。第二步用原始模型回答通用指令、用性别无感知模型回答隐式性别刻板 prompt，再以 KL 散度（Kullback-Leibler Divergence，KL）蒸馏到只训练解码器注意力的低秩适配器中，希望恢复性别识别但输出更中性。蒸馏后 Qwen2-Audio-7B 的选项偏见对数优势比从 0.40 降到 0.23，但另两个大模型改善很小。该路线依赖小规模英文语音和指令数据，开放式生成评估依赖外部大模型抽取形容词，结论尚未覆盖真实对话、其他属性和性别化语言。训练成本披露为单轮约 2 小时及各模型推理与训练显存占用，未给出延迟与吞吐测量。

## 方法概述和架构
输入是英文语音录音加文本指令，最终输出是文本回答或选项判断。处理链路是语音先经过音频编码器变成表示，再送入大语言模型解码器生成回答。论文把性别线索的来源定位在编码器输出，因此后续干预围绕编码器和解码器分两阶段展开。第一阶段只训练编码器，目标是去掉其中的性别信号，同时不破坏转写，音高和情感等通用理解能力。第二阶段固定大部分参数，只训练解码器上的适配器，把两个教师的行为合并到一个学生模型里。

对抗训练组件包含均值池化，梯度反转层和二分类性别头。均值池化指把编码器输出的变长序列表示平均为一个单一向量，向量维度为 $d_{\mathrm{encoder}}$，用于后续分类。梯度反转层（Gradient Reversal Layer，GRL）是连接编码器和性别分类头的特殊层，前向传播时它是恒等映射，不改变数值，反向传播时把梯度乘以 $-\alpha$ 再传回编码器。性别分类头是新加的二分类头，接收梯度反转层的输出并预测男声或女声。数据流是编码器序列表示经过均值池化得到单一向量，再经过梯度反转层进入性别分类头。这里存在反馈，编码器因此朝让性别分类变难的方向更新，而分类头本身仍朝分类准确的方向更新。

组合损失同时约束去性别化和能力保留，公式为 $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comb}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gender}}+\gamma \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}$$ 其中 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gender}}$ 是性别分类交叉熵，$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}$ 是语言模型头的交叉熵，$\gamma$ 控制保留通用能力的强度。原文给出同时计算两个损失的设计理由是防止灾难性遗忘，即避免编码器为了骗过性别分类而丢失正常语音理解。训练数据来自过滤后的 sift-50m neuter，每条 VCTK 语音同时有性别标签和指令回答，因此同一条样本可以同时算出性别损失和语言模型损失。训练时冻结除编码器外的参数，编码器规模小于 10 亿参数，采用全量微调，每 125 个优化步保存一次编码器检查点。

检查点选择不看对抗头准确率，而是用直接提问测性别。提示要求模型回答 $\boxed{M}$，$\boxed{F}$ 或 $\boxed{X}$，统计绝对准确率，拒答率和非拒答准确率。论文保留绝对准确率低于 60% 的检查点，再按 mmau 基准选通用能力最高者，称为性别无感知模型（Gender-Unaware Model，GUM）。这种选择方式有意避免被对抗头自欺，因为直接提问能暴露模型用全猜女性或大量拒答来压低准确率的捷径。

蒸馏组件包含两个数据生成分支和一个低秩适配学生。低秩适配（Low-Rank Adaptation，LoRA）指只在原有权重旁训练小规模低秩矩阵，推理时与原权重合并生效，用于低成本调整大模型。记原始模型为 $\mathcal{M}$，性别无感知模型为 $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GUM}}$，新训练的模型为 $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$。第一分支取 sift-50m 的用户 prompt，用 $\mathcal{M}$ 以温度 0.5 的 top-k 采样生成回答，构成 sift-50m$^{\mathcal{M}}$，目的是保留原始行为和长度风格。第二分支用自建的 ImpGender 隐式性别 prompt 集合，配 VCTK 录音，用 $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GUM}}$ 以温度 0.7 生成回答，构成 ImpGender$^{\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{GUM}}}$，目的是让学生在容易触发刻板联想的地方模仿中性教师。每类数据集最多取 4000 条，混合为 8000 条，过滤掉单条 logit 超过 150 MB 的破裂重复样本。

训练时的数据传递是按样本来源区分教师，蒸馏目标来自生成该样本的同一教师模型的语言模型头 logit。KL 散度（Kullback-Leibler Divergence，KL）在这里指衡量学生输出分布与教师输出分布差异的损失，训练按长度归一化后优化 $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$。LoRA 只加在解码器全部注意力权重上，编码器和解码器其余参数固定。两个阶段的连接是第一阶段产出的 GUM 成为第二阶段隐式性别分支的教师，与保留原始能力的教师共同决定学生的训练信号。选择标准是性别探测准确率不低于 70% 且 mmau 不低于原始性能的 97%，再按选项偏见的对数优势比选最低者，目的是在恢复性别识别和通用理解的前提下挑选偏见更小的适配器。

## 核心创新点
第一项是把文本偏见缓解中的对抗遗忘搬到语音编码器，并给出可操作的性别去除流程。已有音高变换做法会损伤音高探测等任务且未必去掉性别感知，本文冻结语言模型、只用梯度反转更新编码器，再用组合损失防止灾难性遗忘，使去除动作集中在性别信号来源处。
第二项是区分两种部署需求并给出两段式路线。完全不希望推断性别时直接使用性别无感知模型，希望保留性别问答但减少刻板输出时再做蒸馏，这种按需求拆分比单一去偏更贴合实际使用中的矛盾要求。
第三项是构造隐式性别刻板数据集 ImpGender 用于蒸馏。评测用的选项题直接给出刻板与反刻板选项，容易与训练混淆，ImpGender 改用更自然的场景提问，例如演讲者进入手术室或幼儿园时在做什么、为什么受男同事或女同事欢迎，刻板答案可能出现但未被明示，从而把缓解目标与评测题目分开。
第四项是对捷径和副作用的细致核查。论文同时报告绝对准确率、拒答率、误性别代词分布和回答长度，发现 Qwen3-Omni 靠 95.5% 猜女性压低准确率，另两个模型拒答上升但非拒答准确率仍达 80.8%，Nemotron 在误性别测试中仍有 72% 正确代词，说明性别感知并未完全去除。
第五项是揭示指令数据对去偏的反作用。作者发现 sift-50m 鼓励短而确定的事实回答，甚至包含把女性声音描述为温柔但不够权威等刻板样本，这会奖励模型做假设并冲掉安全约束，解释了蒸馏阶段多数检查点偏见加重的原因，也为后续构造小而精的数据集留下依据。

## 实验结果
为检验对抗去性别是否同时降低偏见并保留通用能力，以及蒸馏能否在恢复性别感知后保持低偏见，本文在同一语音评估条件下对比 3 个模型的原始版本、性别无感知模型（Gender-Unaware Model，GUM）和蒸馏版本。保留这 9 个版本是因为它们直接对应两阶段路线的主张，且覆盖 Qwen2-Audio-7B、Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B 和 Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B 三种不同音频编码器。

| 模型版本 | 性别探测绝对准确率 % ↓ | 非拒答准确率 % ↓ | 拒答率 % | mmau 准确率 % ↑ | 选项偏见 LOR ↓ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2-Audio-7B 原始 | 81.5 | 90.7 | 10.1 | 42.1 | 0.40 |
| Qwen2-Audio-7B GUM | 46.0 | 64.5 | 28.8 | 46.6 | 0.10 |
| Qwen2-Audio-7B 蒸馏 | 70.4 | 87.7 | 19.7 | 41.3 | 0.23 |
| Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B 原始 | 99.9 | 99.9 | 0.0 | 75.0 | 0.24 |
| Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B GUM | 54.5 | 54.5 | 0.0 | 71.3 | 0.10 |
| Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B 蒸馏 | 99.9 | 99.9 | 0.0 | 76.2 | 0.22 |
| Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B 原始 | 96.4 | 96.6 | 0.2 | 75.3 | 0.25 |
| Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B GUM | 50.8 | 80.8 | 37.1 | 73.5 | 0.18 |
| Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B 蒸馏 | 93.4 | 93.7 | 0.3 | 73.4 | 0.21 |

对抗阶段把 3 个模型的性别探测都压到 60% 以下，Qwen3-Omni 和 Nemotron 的 mmau 分别下降约 3.7 和 1.8 个百分点，Qwen2-Audio 的 mmau 反而从 42.1% 升到 46.6%。选项偏见的对数优势比（Log Odds Ratio，LOR）在对抗后分别降到 0.10、0.10 和 0.18，正值表示刻板关联，越接近 0 越中性。蒸馏恢复了性别探测，Qwen2-Audio 的 LOR 从 0.40 降到 0.23，另两个模型只从 0.24 降到 0.22、从 0.25 降到 0.21。论文还报告 Qwen3-Omni 和 Nemotron 的蒸馏检查点中分别有 86.3% 和 83.8% 比原始模型更偏，开放式生成的 Fightin' Words 词表在 Qwen2-Audio 上刻板程度下降最明显，Nemotron 词表变少主要与回答变短有关。

蒸馏阶段的取舍需要单独核对，因为选择标准同时约束性别恢复和通用能力，再按偏见排序。为此保留每个模型满足性别探测准确率不低于 70% 且 mmau 不低于原始性能 97% 的最优低秩适配（Low-Rank Adaptation，LoRA）检查点，与原始性能并列，只训练解码器注意力权重，数据为最多 8000 条的 sift-50m 与 ImpGender 混合蒸馏集。

| 模型检查点 | 学习率 | LoRA rank | 训练步数 | 性别探测准确率 % ↑ | mmau 准确率 % ↑ | 选项偏见 LOR ↓ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2-Audio-7B 原始 | — | — | — | 81.5 | 42.1 | 0.40 |
| Qwen2-Audio-7B 蒸馏最优 | 5e-5 | 32 | 720 | 70.4 | 41.3 | 0.23 |
| Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B 原始 | — | — | — | 99.9 | 75.0 | 0.24 |
| Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B 蒸馏最优 | 5e-5 | 16 | 400 | 99.9 | 76.2 | 0.22 |
| Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B 原始 | — | — | — | 96.4 | 75.3 | 0.25 |
| Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B 蒸馏最优 | 5e-5 | 16 | 800 | 93.4 | 73.4 | 0.21 |

最优蒸馏检查点都恢复了性别探测并守住了 mmau，但偏见改善幅度分化明显。Qwen2-Audio 因原始 LOR 高达 0.40，下降 0.17 个单位的空间较大；另两个大模型仅下降 0.02 和 0.04，且多数候选检查点反而更偏，说明按长度归一化 KL 散度（Kullback-Leibler Divergence，KL）蒸馏并不能稳定继承 GUM 的中性行为。证据支持范围限于英文 VCTK 语音、隐式刻板 prompt 和 4000 条加 4000 条的蒸馏规模，论文将原因归于短回答数据集奖励简短断言而非解释讨论，训练成本为单轮约 2 小时，延迟与吞吐论文未给出具体数值。

## 细节详述
性别探测评测用 British Dialects 的 500 条录音和 Speech Archive 的 470 条录音，性别 balanced，覆盖不同年龄和口音。选项偏见评测共 23280 个录音 prompt 对，用 23 对左右的性别极化词让模型二选一，按男性语音选男性刻板词等四格计数计算 LOR。开放式生成把同一文本的男声和女声拼接后要求写人物小传并分配权力、科学和职业类角色，再用 GPT-OSS-120B 只看文本抽取形容词并用 Fightin' Words 方法排序。误性别评测用上述语音库去掉转写含性别代词的样本，要求描述嗓音年龄和音色，从 he、she、they 及其屈折形式解析代词性别。ImpGender 含 34 类独特 prompt，每类配 240 条随机 VCTK 录音，共 8160 个样本。通用指令训练用 sift-50m 中仅来自 VCTK 的子集并过滤含 gender、male、female、man、woman 等 18 个词的样本，记为 sift-50m\neuter，目标回答平均长 75.2 个字符。通用理解评测用 mmau 的 mini 子集 1000 条，过滤性别相关题目后剩 908 条。对抗训练固定有效批量 8，权重衰减 $5\times 10^{-3}$，训练 4000 条性别 balanced 样本共 1 个轮次，学习率在 $5\times 10^{-6}$、$10^{-5}$、$5\times 10^{-5}$、$10^{-4}$ 中搜索，$\gamma$ 在 0.5、1、2 中搜索，梯度反转权重 $\alpha$ 在 0.025、0.05、0.1、0.2 中搜索。蒸馏固定有效批量 8，权重衰减 $5\times 10^{-3}$，LoRA dropout 为 0.05，LoRA alpha 为秩的 2 倍，学习率在 $10^{-6}$、$5\times 10^{-6}$、$10^{-5}$、$5\times 10^{-5}$ 中搜索，秩在 16、32 中搜索，训练 1 个轮次，每 80 步保存检查点。模型规模为 Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct 70 亿参数，另两个为 300 亿参数的混合专家结构。推理关闭思维链，训练用 Hugging Face Transformers 自定义循环和 AdamW，推理用 vLLM，用 48 GB 的 A40、L40 和 95 GB 的 H100、RTX 6000 Pro，单轮次约 2 小时。解码温度如上，未说明束搜索宽度和流式设置。

## 评分理由
* 创新性 (1.2/2)：问题在语音大模型中较少被系统缓解，编码器对抗遗忘加双教师蒸馏的组合有新意，但对抗和蒸馏本身是已有技术迁移，蒸馏收益有限故未达突破。
* 技术严谨性 (1.0/1.5)：组合损失、梯度反转和检查点筛选逻辑完整，作者主动揭露猜女性和拒答捷径，但蒸馏偏见加重的因果解释停留在数据观察，缺少对照验证。
* 实验充分性 (1.0/1.5)：3 个编码器、4 类评测和超参数网格覆盖较好，保留了负结果和细分行为，但开放式生成依赖外部模型抽取且无统计显著性说明，蒸馏阶段缺少更强基线。
* 清晰度 (0.7/1)：流程图和公式含义清楚，数据过滤和选择标准可跟随，但表格与正文数字分散，部分图注和附录 prompt 细节需要来回对照。
* 影响力 (0.8/1.5)：语音是核心实验对象，性别公平对语音助手有实际意义，但只做英语二元性别，蒸馏效果不稳定，后续直接复用价值受限。
* 开源 (1.2/1.5)：论文给出 GitHub 代码库和 Hugging Face 模型集合，核心材料开放但输入未提供文档完整度和 ImpGender 是否完整发布的信息，故取开放但不完整档。
* 可复现性 (0.3/0.5)：超参数网格、批量、优化器、硬件和筛选阈值披露较多，但随机种子、数据划分细节和部分生成参数缺失，只能支持大部分复现。
* 工程/实践价值 (0.8/1.5)：两段式部署思路和训练检查点选择方法有参考价值，也有显存占用和时长记录，但缺少延迟、吞吐和真实对话部署测量，未形成完整生产流程。

## 局限与问题
作者明确承认的局限包括可用指令数据偏向短而确定的基准答案并含有刻板样本，ImpGender 只有 34 类 prompt 且靠重复录音扩充，评测是录音加文本 prompt 而非真实场景中指令本身在录音里，只做英语且性别建模限于男性和女性标注。潜在问题是绝对准确率会掩盖捷径，Qwen3-Omni 全猜女性和另两个模型高拒答下的高非拒答准确率都说明残留感知，误性别测试中 Nemotron 仍有较高正确率也支持这一点。蒸馏阶段多数检查点比原始模型更偏，说明当前数据混合和 KL 目标不足以稳定实现感知保留加输出中性，需要更谨慎的数据构造才能成立。

## 开源详情
- 代码：https://github.com/adnan-al-ali/speech-llm-bias-mitigation/
- 模型权重：https://hf.co/alalia/speech-bias-mitigation/
- 数据集：论文提到了 sift-50m、mmau、VCTK、British Dialects、Speech Archive 和 ImpGender 等数据集名称，论文中未提及数据集获取链接。
- Demo：论文中未提及
- 复现材料：论文在附录 B 中给出了训练配置，固定超参数包括有效批量大小为 8 和权重衰减为 5×10−3，对抗训练阶段在 4000 个性别均衡样本上训练 1 个轮次并每 125 个优化步骤保存编码器检查点，蒸馏阶段混合了 8000 个样本并每 80 个步骤保存检查点，单轮训练耗时约为 2 小时，论文中未提及独立的检查点下载链接。
- 论文中引用的开源项目：未提及

via Event-Centric Alignment

Abstract
Abstract
Recent advances in Omni Language Models (OLMs) provide a unified solution for audiovisual video captioning.
Nevertheless, existing approaches predominantly treat captioning as an unstructured text generation process, neglecting the inherent semantic structure of videos and leading to suboptimal fine-grained audiovisual alignment.
To bridge this gap, we propose EVA-Cap, a novel framework that decomposes captions into atomic audiovisual events and transforms unstructured text supervision into event-centric alignment.
We train EVA-Cap via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a self-curated dataset, EVA-Data, which is built with event-centric quality control.
During the GRPO phase, the model is explicitly optimized against three event-centric alignment targets: global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap significantly outperforms existing methods in event-centric evaluation (e.g., +9.0% average gain on ChronusAV), while achieving competitive performance on general audiovisual captioning benchmarks (e.g., +3.3% on WorldSense).

1 Introduction
Video captioning [3, 13, 37, 61, 48] aims to extract rich semantic content from videos and generate coherent natural language descriptions.
As a fundamental task in video understanding, it underpins various downstream applications, including video retrieval [39, 47, 57, 34], video reasoning [38, 11, 56, 10, 28], and video generation [2, 40, 54, 36, 35].
Recently, advances in Transformer-based end-to-end models have revolutionized the conventional modularized video caption pipelines.
Especially, Omni Language Models (OLMs) [29, 20, 53, 46, 52, 7] have driven a paradigm shift from visual-only modeling to an omni-modal paradigm that integrates audio and visual signals, enabling more effective cross-modal reasoning and stronger generalization in real-world audiovisual scenarios.
Despite its promise, achieving factually accurate and comprehensive audiovisual captioning remains difficult due to the intrinsic complexity and dense interdependence between visual and auditory content.
Existing methods treat video captioning as a text generation problem for OLMs based on caption-level supervision [4, 43].
This overlooks the structured semantics inherent in videos, meaning a generated caption may be linguistically correct but misaligned with the logical structure and event-level correspondences.
While some recent research has incorporated additional supervision over specific aspects (e.g., dialogue [5, 30] or object attributes [19, 6]), such narrowly scoped supervision still struggles to achieve fine-grained audiovisual alignment.
Consequently, a critical bottleneck stems from the lack of an effective caption representation that unifies video-grounded structural semantics with general language modeling.
To address this issue, we propose framing video captioning as assembling discrete, atomic audiovisual event sequences through joint optimization of event content and their correspondences.
As illustrated in Fig. 1, a video consists of multiple audio and visual events, where each event is represented as a tuple of type, character, and content.
These events can be aligned temporally to form a coherent caption clip, linked via shared semantic content and explicit synchronous connectors (e.g., “as”, “at the same time”).
Crucially, such an event-centric perspective bridges audiovisual events and captions by modeling both intra-event attribution (i.e., whether the attributions of a single event are correct?) and inter-event synchronization (i.e., what are the temporal order and synchronization of different events?).
While such an event-centric perspective provides a structured semantic understanding of videos beyond mere language modeling, effectively integrating such insights into OLMs post-training remains an open question.
This gap is largely due to (1) the scarcity of high-quality audiovisual caption data with event-level fidelity, and (2) the absence of dedicated event-centric frameworks for leveraging supervision with event-level heuristics.
Figure 1: Illustration of the event-centric representation of audiovisual captions, where aligned audiovisual events are composed into the predicted caption.
To this end, we propose EVA-Cap, which builds upon Qwen2.5-Omni [45] and unifies event-centric alignment within the language modeling post-training phase.
Specifically, we first construct EVA-Data, a 63K audiovisual video–caption dataset, via an automatic initialization–refinement pipeline followed by event-centric quality control.
In this process, timestamped audiovisual events are extracted from raw videos and subjected to per-event verification to ensure high fidelity.
Furthermore, we introduce a two-stage post-training strategy to facilitate event-centric alignment, which consists of SFT (SFT) and GRPO (GRPO) [27] on the EVA-Data.
During the GRPO stage, three event-centric rewards are designed to enforce global completeness (via event recall), intra-event attribution (via character matching), and inter-event synchronization (via cross-modal retrieval).
Collectively, these post-training objectives enhance the fine-grained alignment of audiovisual events, enabling factually accurate, event-grounded audiovisual caption generation.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap outperforms existing open-source models across 6 audiovisual benchmarks.
For example, on general captioning benchmarks, EVA-Cap achieves a total error rate of 34.6% on video-SALMONN-2 testset [29] and surpasses existing methods by a clear margin of 3.3% on WorldSense [15].
Most importantly, on event-centric evaluation with ChronusAV [7] and AV-SpeakerBench [23], EVA-Cap exhibits substantial advantages with an accuracy of 55.4%, 56.2%, and 40.1% for Visual-to-Audio (V2A) inference, Audio-to-Visual (A2V) grounding, and speaker attribution, respectively.
These results underscore the capability of EVA-Cap in generating highly faithful captions with precise temporal alignment and accurate event attribution.
2 Related Work
2.1 Audiovisual Video Captioning.
Recent advancements in Omni Language Models (OLMs) [29, 20, 53, 46] have significantly improved multimodal perception in complex real-world scenarios, thereby promoting the development of audiovisual captioning [21, 12, 18]. However, existing approaches remain constrained by the scarcity of high-quality audiovisual caption data, and largely rely on either coarse-grained supervision or focus on limited aspects of the task. For instance, AVoCaDO [4] constructs large-scale audiovisual video-caption pairs through temporal orchestration, but suffers from insufficient factual verification and coarse-grained temporal alignment. UGC-Captioner [43] relies on holistic caption-level supervision, whereas DiaDem [5] and D-ORCA [30] focus narrowly on specific aspects of captions, failing to capture fine-grained event-level correspondences. In contrast, we introduce an event-centric perspective for audiovisual captioning. We construct an event-enhanced dataset with event-centric quality control, and propose an event-centric training strategy that explicitly models event-level alignment, enabling accurate and event-grounded audiovisual caption generation.
2.2 Reinforcement Learning for Visual Content Captioning.
Reinforcement learning [27, 55, 60] plays an increasingly important role in caption optimization, spanning from visual-only to omni-modal scenarios. CapRL [44] and RubiCap [16] design verifiable rubrics for dense image captioning. OwlCap [61] and VideoCap-R1 [22] improve video captioning by matching key information extracted from visual content. In the audiovisual domain, D-ORCA [30] introduces dialogue-oriented rewards focusing on speaker and ASR consistency, while TimeChat-Captioner [51] optimizes timestamp alignment under structured caption formats. However, these approaches typically focus on limited aspects and struggle to achieve fine-grained audiovisual alignment. In this paper, we develop three event-centric rewards that jointly enforce fine-grained supervision within and across modalities. This approach provides more precise event alignment than prior methods, which either focus on modality-specific objectives [30, 5] or rely on coarse audiovisual synchronization [4, 51].
3 Method
This section introduces the construction of EVA-Cap, which is built upon Qwen-2.5-Omni [45] and optimized for audiovisual video captioning via event-centric alignment.
First, we address the scarcity of high-quality data by curating EVA-Data, a 63K-scale audiovisual captioning dataset.
The dataset is generated using an automated pipeline with rigorous event-centric quality control (Sec. 3.1).
Next, we introduce a two-stage training strategy comprising SFT and GRPO to improve EVA-Cap with event-centric alignment.
The training process integrates a suite of event-centric rewards to effectively exploit event-level supervision (Sec. 3.2).
3.1 EVA-Data Construction
3.1.1 Annotation Pipeline
We develop an automatic annotation pipeline to construct audiovisual video–caption pairs with event-level fidelity. As shown in Fig. 2, the pipeline comprises three main stages:
Stage 1: Initialization. We first utilize the open-source audiovisual captioner AVoCaDO [4], which excels in holistic perception, to generate initial audiovisual descriptions for raw videos. This provides a coherent narrative of each video and captures key events and details, covering scene backgrounds, interactive actions, and audio transcriptions. We then filter out samples with repetitive descriptions or abnormal text lengths.
Stage 2: Refinement. We then feed both raw videos and initial descriptions to the advanced omni-model Gemini-2.5-Pro [8] for content refinement and temporal alignment. Guided by raw audiovisual signals, we instruct the model to strengthen the temporal synchronization of audiovisual events and revise event character attribution, while preserving the original natural language style. This yields refined descriptions with precise audiovisual event alignment, achieving fine-grained annotation.
Stage 3: Event-Centric Quality Control. To ensure the quality of the curated data, we introduce an aligned event hit mechanism for the automatic validation of refined descriptions. Specifically, we employ Gemini-2.5-Pro to extract timestamp-grounded audiovisual event tuples directly from raw videos. We then input all event tuples together with refined descriptions to GPT-4.1 [1] to verify whether each event tuple is hit in the caption. An event hit requires both audio and visual events to be entailed with consistent temporal synchronization. This process jointly assesses the accuracy of audiovisual synchronization and event attribution in captions. We discard samples with an event hit ratio below a threshold of 0.8. In this way, we build a large-scale audiovisual caption dataset, EVA-Data, which provides high-quality event-level supervision for event-centric post-training.

3.1.2 Data Statistics
To guarantee both diversity and quality, we collect 100K audiovisual videos (each under 200 seconds in duration) from LLaVA-Video [58], FineVideo [9], and Shot2Story [14]. Through the annotation pipeline, EVA-Data ultimately yields 63K audiovisual video-caption pairs with event-level fidelity. Fig. 3 (b) illustrates the duration distribution of these videos. On average, each video lasts 73.7 seconds, while the corresponding captions average 504.3 words. We further randomly sample 20K videos from EVA-Data and analyze the distribution of audio and visual events in the corresponding captions, as shown in Fig. 3 (c). The results demonstrate that the annotated videos contain rich audiovisual information and the captions are free of modality bias, thus providing effective supervision for event-centric alignment.
3.2 Post-Training of EVA-Cap
Leveraging this dataset, we propose EVA-Cap, an audiovisual captioner optimized via event-centric alignment. We first present our two-stage training pipeline in Sec. 3.2.1, and then introduce the event-centric reward functions dedicated to fine-grained alignment in Sec. 3.2.2.
3.2.1 Training Pipeline
We build EVA-Cap upon the Qwen2.5-Omni Thinker module, which jointly encodes audio and video into a unified, temporally interleaved token sequence to facilitate synchronous audiovisual understanding. We then adopt a two-stage post-training pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
In the first phase, we perform SFT on our constructed 63K EVA-Data to empower the model to generate detailed captions that integrate both audio and visual modalities.
In the second phase, we further optimize the SFT model with GRPO on 3.2K rollout videos from EVA-Data (details of the rollout process are provided in Appendix A.2.2).
To enhance fine-grained alignment in audiovisual captions, we design event-centric rewards covering three dimensions: event completeness, character attribution, and audiovisual synchronization.
The detailed SFT and GRPO objectives are provided in Appendix A.1, and the reward design is elaborated in Sec. 3.2.2.

4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Setup
Implementation Details: We adopt Qwen2.5-Omni-7B [45] as our backbone model. During training, the vision and audio encoders are kept frozen, while only the adapters and LLM parameters are updated. Videos are sampled at 2 FPS, with a maximum per-frame pixels of 512×28×28512\times 28\times 28 and total pixels of 30×512×28×2830\times 512\times 28\times 28. And the maximum generation length is set to 2048. For SFT, we train the model for two epochs with a batch size of 128 and a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}. For GRPO, we conduct training for two epochs with a batch size of 16, a learning rate of 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}, a KL penalty of 0.04, and a group size of 8, following a progressive reward weighting strategy.
We employ Qwen3.5-27B [33] as the reward judge. All training is conducted on 32 NVIDIA H20 GPUs.
Benchmarks: For general audiovisual captioning, we evaluate EVA-Cap under two settings: direct quality assessment (video-SALMONN-2 testset [29] and UGC-VideoCap [43]) and QA-cascaded evaluation (Daily-Omni [62] and WorldSense [15]). The former directly evaluates the overall quality of generated captions through dedicated scoring mechanisms, while for the latter, we first generate descriptive captions with our model and then adopt Gemini-2.5-Pro [8] to answer QA questions solely based on the produced captions.
To assess the capabilities in event-centric alignment, we further conduct evaluations on subsets of ChronusAV [7] and AV-SpeakerBench [23]. For ChronusAV, we select 1,066 videos under 200 seconds to assess audiovisual synchronization via video-to-audio (V2A) and audio-to-video (A2V) grounding. Evaluation follows a two-stage protocol: Gemini-2.5-Pro first generates answers for the V2A and A2V grounding queries conditioned on the model-generated captions, and Seed-1.6 [31] subsequently scores the outputs to compute VDCscore [3] and accuracy. For AV-SpeakerBench, we adopt 422 QA samples from its Speaker Recognition subset to assess audio event attribution, using the same QA-cascaded evaluation paradigm with Gemini-2.5-Pro.

Performance on direct quality assessment. We evaluate EVA-Cap on two representative general audiovisual captioning benchmarks.
Those benchmarks assess the overall captioning performance from multiple dimensions, including video content omission, hallucination, and multi-aspect scoring.
The comparison with existing audiovisual models is presented in Tab. 1.
EVA-Cap achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results across various metrics, e.g., a total error rate of 34.6% on the video-SALMONN-2 testset [29] and an average score of 76.9 on UGC-VideoCap [43], surpassing both unified OLMs, e.g., Qwen3-Omni-Instruct [46] and task-specific captioners, e.g., DiaDem [5].
On the video-SALMONN-2 test set, EVA-Cap demonstrates the lowest miss rate of 17.6%.

We further investigate the effects of three event-centric rewards during the GRPO phase.
The global event completeness reward ℛcomp\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{comp}} penalizes event omission, thereby boosting model performance across all dimensions (+8.5%, +2.1%, and +3.7% accuracy on V2A, AV-Speaker, and Daily-Omni).
Furthermore, integrating the inter-event synchronization reward ℛsync\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sync}} and intra-event attribution reward ℛattr\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{attr}} yields consistent gains on corresponding tasks (+2.1% on A2V and +3.1% on AV-Speaker in terms of accuracy), while also improving the overall captioning performance steadily.
Collectively, these three rewards enable precise alignment in both event content and event correspondence, facilitating factually accurate, event-grounded audiovisual video captioning.
To further dissect our two-stage GRPO design, we conduct additional ablations. Introducing attribution reward ℛattr\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{attr}} as early as the first round not only compromises general performance but also degrades event-centric alignment. We hypothesize that injecting both ℛsync\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sync}} and ℛattr\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{attr}} prematurely leads to optimization conflicts between inter-event relations and intra-event accuracy. Conversely, a progressive strategy facilitates a gradual alignment process, from global coarse-grained structures to fine-grained character-level details. Moreover, comparisons against a baseline that sustains only ℛcomp\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{comp}} and ℛsync\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sync}} in the second round demonstrate that the sustained improvements stem from effective reward design rather than mere data scaling.

For instance, the audio ASR event "Puppy: I know. You saw me and took pity on me" occurs when characters converse on the sidewalk. This example demonstrates that our model can produce high-fidelity captions in complex audiovisual scenarios involving multi-view transitions and multi-object interactions, and further underscores the efficacy of the event-centric alignment mechanism for long-form audiovisual captioning.

5 Conclusion
This paper presents EVA-Cap, an audiovisual video captioning model with a training framework that transforms holistic caption optimization into event-centric alignment.
To support event-level supervision, we first constructed EVA-Data with event-centric quality control and adopted a two-stage post-training strategy with SFT and GRPO.
Then, by decomposing captions into modality-grounded events, EVA-Cap elaborates fine-grained GRPO rewards tailored to event completeness, character attribution, and audiovisual synchronization.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that SFT on EVA-Data significantly improves OLMs to internalize event-centric knowledge.
Furthermore, the subsequent GRPO optimization improves event-centric alignment while maintaining strong general captioning performance.
These results suggest that event-centric alignment offers an effective path toward more faithful and temporally coherent audiovisual video captioning.

A.2 More Implementation Details
A.2.1 Details about the Construction of Reference Structures
We filter 6.4K videos from EVA-Data, all of which achieve a 100% hit ratio in Stage 3 of the annotation pipeline, ensuring highly accurate event-level supervision signals. To facilitate efficient reward computation for both GRPO training and rollout, we construct reference structures for these 6.4K selected videos. Specifically, this involves extracting audiovisual event units ℰ⋆\mathcal{E}^{\star} from the ground-truth captions y⋆y^{\star} and formulating audio-to-visual synchronization queries 𝒬⋆\mathcal{Q}^{\star}.
We employ the reward judge LLM, Qwen3.5-27B [33], prompting it to sequentially extract audio events and visual events from the given caption to form a unified event list ℰ⋆\mathcal{E}^{\star}. Each extracted audio event serves as a separate query. We input the complete ground-truth caption along with all the extracted visual events into the LLM, prompting it to select the temporally synchronized visual events corresponding to the current audio event (i.e., the current query) from all the input visual events.
Each visual event is assigned a unique index based on its chronological extraction order (i.e., the first extracted visual event has an index of 1). Since all visual events are extracted sequentially, we discard audio events whose matched visual event index span exceeds 5.
This filtering step excludes audio events that cover an excessively long temporal range (e.g., background music that plays throughout the entire video), as such coarse-grained audio events provide limited support for fine-grained audiovisual alignment. Next, we construct a candidate visual event set containing 5 visual events by selecting those adjacent to the indices of the selected synchronized visual events. This strategy naturally incorporates neighboring visual events, which are prone to misalignment with the audio events—thereby creating challenging hard negative samples for subsequent reward assessment.
Collectively, the filtered audio events paired with their corresponding constructed visual candidate sets form the final synchronization queries 𝒬⋆\mathcal{Q}^{\star}.
As a result, we obtain an audiovisual event unit set and an audio-to-visual synchronization query set for each video. These well-defined reference structures enable reliable event-level reward calculation and support the subsequent GRPO training pipeline.
A.2.2 Details about the Rollout Process
SFT initializes the audiovisual captioning format of the model and enables preliminary event alignment capabilities. For GRPO, we first conduct the rollout process to identify qualified videos and yield high-quality event-level supervision signals. We perform rollout on the videos selected in Sec. A.2.1, all equipped with the well-constructed reference structures (i.e., sets of audiovisual event units and audio-to-visual synchronization queries). Each selected video is then inferred 8 times (i.e., group size) using the SFT model.
Leveraging the constructed reference structures, we compute two types of event-level rewards for each generated caption during the rollout process: the intra-event attribution reward and the inter-event synchronization reward.
Specifically, the intra-event attribution reward focuses on evaluating the proportion of events that are correctly attributed to the appropriate characters, while the inter-event synchronization reward quantifies the alignment between audio events and the constructed candidate visual events by calculating the F1-score.
To ensure the quality of supervision signals for subsequent preference training, we implement a two-stage filtering mechanism at the query level and the video level. At the query level, invalid audio-to-visual synchronization queries are filtered by the inter-event synchronization reward. Specifically, we aggregate reward values for each individual query across the 8 generated captions, and retain only queries whose average synchronization reward falls within the interval (0,0.75)(0,0.75), following the filtering protocol of HumanOmniV2 [49].
At the video level, filtering is performed based on the sum of intra-event attribution reward and inter-event synchronization reward. We first eliminate videos with fewer than 5 valid synchronization queries, as such cases lack sufficient synchronized semantic information to support reliable training. We then compute the standard deviation of the combined reward scores across the 8 generated captions per video, and finally retain the top 50% of qualified videos, yielding 3.2K valid video samples for downstream GRPO training.
We conduct two rounds of GRPO training, with one training epoch set for each round. In the first round, we only leverage Global Event Completeness and Inter-Event Synchronization for model optimization. Accordingly, the rollout video selection relies solely on the standard deviation of the inter-event synchronization reward. In the second round, we incorporate all three designed reward components into the joint training objective. Correspondingly, the rollout selection strategy is updated to adopt the standard deviation of the sum of inter-event synchronization reward and intra-event attribution reward as the screening criterion.
